docs.title: Trigger Settings
docs.text: The following sections describe the trigger settings so you can choose the one that best suits your capture. Because there are many trigger types, they are split into separate sections for easy reference.

docs.title: Trigger Conditions
docs.text:
Trigger Conditions

These are the common conditions that you can find everywhere in the trigger settings. The trigger conditions are:

  • 0 - LOW level
  • 1 - HIGH level
  • X - Don't care term (Any value is allowed)
  • ↑ - Rising edge
  • ↓ - Falling edge
  • Either - Any edge (Rising or Falling edge)

docs.title: Single Level Trigger
docs.text:
A single capture will record data until a digital trigger is found on a single channel.

Configuration

Per Channel Trigger Settings

All the channels can be configured with the Trigger Conditions listed above. You can choose the one that is most suitable for your capture. The most common use case is to trigger on a rising edge of a clock signal.

We also provide trigger from a specific binary pattern from a specific channel label (e.g. I2C).

Trigger from a specific binary pattern
  • Trigger Delay: The amount of time the condition must hold before triggering. Default is 0 (trigger immediately).
  • Pass Count: Number of matching trigger events to ignore before triggering. Default is 0 (trigger on first match).

docs.title: Multi-level Trigger
docs.text:
Multi Level triggering is composed of multiple single-stage trigger conditions. You can create complex trigger conditions using multiple stages (up to 16 states).

Warning

Multi-level Trigger is not supported when sampling frequency is ≥ 2 GHz.

Configuration

Multi-level Trigger Settings

Each state is configured like a single-level trigger (as shown in the right side of the figure).

States can be connected with:

Next IF

Continuous trigger conditions (signals must match on adjacent sample clocks)

  • Signals captured by two adjacent sample clocks must meet the conditions
  • Typically used with synchronous or state mode measurements
  • Signals are in a continuous, predictable state

Then IF

Non-continuous trigger conditions (signals can match with any number of samples between)

  • Triggers when both conditions are met, regardless of signals between them
  • Suitable for asynchronous or timing mode
  • Ideal when edge transitions must meet conditions but intermediate states don't matter

You can also add an OR (OR IF) statement to run conditions in parallel.

OR IF

Establish parallel trigger conditions. Any matching condition will trigger.

An example is shown in the figure below. Either of the two patterns starting with P1 or P2 will trigger in the capture.

OR IF Example

Sequence by

By default, the trigger conditions are sampled based on the sampling clock internally. This feature further allows you to set sampling method based on your customization.

Example

If signal data is valid only when the clock is rising, you can:

  • Set Sequence by to Custom Rising
  • Select the Clock pin as the valid condition
  • Set conditions for other data lines using multi-level triggering

Note

Sequence by feature is only supported when sampling frequency is ≤ 250 MHz.

docs.title: Width Trigger
docs.text:
Trigger when a channel meets the trigger condition and the pulse width matches the specified length.

Width Trigger Settings

docs.title: Timeout Trigger
docs.text:
Trigger when a signal duration exceeds the set time value, without waiting for a complete pulse.

Timeout Trigger Settings

docs.title: External Trigger
docs.text: Use the device's Trig-In input pulse signal as the trigger condition.

docs.title: Manual Trigger (Force Trigger)
docs.text: During a capture process, click the Stop button to manually set the trigger point in the captured data.

docs.title: Protocol Trigger
docs.text:
We support triggering on protocol framing for many buses, which makes it easy to locate errors (complete reference docs are coming soon).

-->

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Protocol Analyzer mode captures and decodes bus protocol traffic in real-time, providing immediate visibility into protocol-level communication.

Protocol Analyzer mode focuses on protocol-level analysis rather than signal-level timing. It decodes bus transactions automatically and presents them in an easy-to-read report format.

Key differences from Logic Analyzer:

  • Real-time protocol decoding during capture
  • Report-focused view (optional waveform display)
  • Three operating modes for different use cases
  • Optimized for high-speed protocol capture

docs.title: Protocol Analyzer
docs.text:
Real-time capture with immediate display. Data is sent back to the PC for real-time display as it's captured.

Best for: Quick protocol debugging and interactive analysis

Learn more: Capture Modes

docs.title: Protocol Logger
docs.text:
Capture to disk without real-time processing. Data is saved as .LOG files and can be analyzed later.

Best for: Long captures and high-data-rate protocols

Learn more: Capture Modes

docs.title: Protocol Monitor
docs.text:
Capture to device memory with trigger-based retrieval. Data stays in the device until triggered or manually stopped.

Best for: Monitoring for specific events over extended periods

Learn more: Capture Modes

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Select protocol and configure channels
  2. Choose operating mode
  3. Configure memory settings
  4. Optional: Enable Show Waveforms for signal-level view
  5. Start capture (press Enter)
  6. Use Search to find specific transactions

docs.title: Protocol support
docs.text:
Supports dozens of protocols including:

  • I2C, SPI, UART
  • CAN, LIN, I3C
  • USB PD, eSPI, eMMC
  • And many more

docs.title: Analysis tools
docs.text:
• Real-time decode: See protocol data as it's captured
  • Search function: Find specific addresses, data, or patterns
  • Statistics: Analyze traffic patterns and error rates
  • Detail view: Inspect complex protocol transactions
  • Export: Save reports as .TXT or .CSV

docs.title: Integration
docs.text:
• Convert to Logic Analyzer: Switch modes for signal-level analysis
  • Stack Oscilloscope: Combine protocol and analog analysis (requires waveforms enabled)

docs.title: Documentation sections
docs.text:
• File Operations - Open, save, and export files
  • Keyboard Shortcuts - Quick key reference
  • Capture Modes - Analyzer, Logger, and Monitor modes
  • Protocol Settings - Configure protocol parameters
  • Operating Modes - Memory and stop conditions
  • Show Waveforms - Enable waveform display
  • Search - Find specific protocol data
  • Window Management - Reports and navigation
  • Detail & Statistics - Inspect and analyze data
  • Cursor - Cursor operations (requires waveforms)

docs.title: When to use Protocol Analyzer
docs.text:
Choose Protocol Analyzer mode when:

  • You need to see protocol transactions, not raw signal timing
  • Real-time decode is important
  • Working with complex multi-byte protocols
  • Debugging protocol-level issues (addressing, data errors, etc.)
  • Capturing high-speed protocol traffic

Choose Logic Analyzer mode when:

  • You need precise timing measurements
  • Signal integrity is a concern
  • Working with non-standard or custom protocols
  • Debugging electrical issues
  • Need advanced triggering on signal patterns

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
10BASE-T1S Protocol Analyzer settings (TravelLogic series)
  • Settings:
    • Preamble Count: Allowed preamble count range (Max–Min). Out of range may report Preamble Error. Main Default does not reset this field; UI often starts at Max 6, Min 1.
    • Sample Rate: Analysis sample rate (typical 200 MHz / 100 MHz). Too low may fail to decode. Default: 200 MHz.
    • Reference Point Adjust: Decode reference points (1st Position / 2nd Position, ns). A wrong setting can skew bit sampling. Default: 1st 20 ns, 2nd 60 ns.

  • Trigger settings:

    • Error triggers: Frame Error / Not In Table / Preamble Error / FCS Error. Default: all cleared.
    • Event Trigger: Trigger on Ethernet frame fields; when checked opens MII Trigger Settings (see popup notes). Use XXh for don't-care bytes. Default: cleared.
      • Destination / Source Address: 6-byte MACs; XXh = don't care per byte.
      • Ethertype/Length: 2 bytes (may be don't care) for type/length.
      • Data: Match payload by Data Type (e.g. Raw Data / IPv4); Offset, IPv4 addresses, or Raw Data Byte 1–8.
      • Default: Restore the dialog to don't-care / default conditions.
    • Basic triggers: 10BASE-T1S symbol/frame events such as BEACON(08h), SYNC/COMMIT(18h), SSD(04h), ESDHB(0Dh), ESDBRS(07h), ESDOK(07h), ESDERR(11h), ESDJAB(19h), Start of Frame, End of Frame. Default: all cleared. When Event Trigger is checked, open MII Trigger Settings to trigger on Ethernet frame fields (for example a MAC, Ethertype, or payload pattern):

  • Destination / Source Address: 6-byte MACs; XXh = don't care per byte.

  • Ethertype/Length: 2 bytes (may be don't care).
  • Data: Match by Data Type (e.g. Raw Data / IPv4); Offset, IPv4 addresses, or Raw Data Byte 1–8.
  • Default: Restore don't-care / default conditions.

Event Trigger — MII Trigger Settings

CAN 2.0B/FD Protocol Analyzer settings (TravelLogic series)
  • Settings:
    • Data Rate: CAN arbitration-phase bit rate in Kbps. A wrong setting can scramble decoding. Default: 500 Kbps.
    • CAN FD: Enable CAN FD decoding. When checked — ISO-CRC / Non ISO-CRC, Data phase (Kbps; 500–10000), Sample Point (70%–80%). Sub-fields are disabled (Disable) when cleared. Default: cleared; when enabled, defaults are ISO-CRC, Data phase 1000 Kbps, Sample Point 80%.

      • Non ISO-CRC: Original Bosch CAN FD 1.0 (no stuff-bit count). Incompatible with ISO-CRC — do not mix on the same bus.

docs.title: Capture modes
docs.text: Protocol Analyzer offers three distinct capture modes, each optimized for different analysis scenarios.

docs.title: Mode comparison
docs.text: Feature Protocol Analyzer Protocol Logger Protocol Monitor Real-time display Yes No No Data processing During capture After capture After capture Memory limit RAM + Device Hard disk Device only Best for Interactive debug Long captures Event monitoring PC performance High Medium-High Low

docs.title: Protocol Analyzer
docs.text: Real-time capture with immediate protocol decode and display.

docs.title: Functional description
docs.text: Captured data is sent back to the PC for real-time display. You can see the protocol data immediately as it's being captured.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
1. Immediate visibility: Data appears in real-time
  2. Small captures: No need to set memory limits for short tests
  3. Interactive: See results while capture is running

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
• Higher USB performance required: Data transfer and processing happen simultaneously
  • Computer performance: May slow down during capture if the PC can't keep up
  • Auto-stop on memory full: If the computer can't process data fast enough, the device may automatically stop

docs.title: Rules for repetitive captures
docs.text:
Repetitive times:

  • Disabled: Device stops after stop condition is matched
  • Enabled: After stop condition, device saves data and repeats capture for the specified number of times
  • Set to 0: Continuous repetitive capture

Stop conditions:

Two automatic stop conditions are available:

  1. Number of data lines: Stop when the stored data line count matches the setting
  2. Use when you need a specific number of protocol transactions
  3. Avoids unnecessarily long captures

  4. Default: OFF

  5. Maximum device memory limit: Stop when device memory reaches the set limit

  6. Prevents memory overflow
  7. Adjustable memory usage percentage

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use for quick protocol debugging
  • Monitor burst traffic patterns
  • Verify basic protocol functionality
  • Check for immediate errors or unexpected behavior

docs.title: Protocol Logger
docs.text: Capture to disk without real-time processing. Data is saved and analyzed later.

docs.title: Functional description
docs.text: Data is sent back to the PC for saving without being processed or displayed. Only after you press Stop will the data begin to be processed and displayed.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
1. Large captures: As long as the hard disk is big enough and fast enough, you can save vast amounts of data
  2. Deferred analysis: Logger files (.LOG) can be opened for analysis later
  3. No need to analyze immediately after capture
  4. Save captures for future reference
  5. Share captures with team members

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
• High USB and disk performance required: Continuous high-speed data streaming
  • Large data requirements:
  • Significant hard disk space needed
  • Long analysis time after capture
  • Processing may take time proportional to capture length

docs.title: Run data process after capture
docs.text:
Option: Run data process after logger capture stopped

  • Checked: Software analyzes data immediately after stopping
  • Unchecked: Software only saves the logger data without analysis
  • Faster capture termination
  • Analyze later by reloading the .LOG file

File format conversion:

When you analyze the data (immediately or later), the filename converts from .LOG to .TLW format.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use for long-duration captures (hours/days)
  • High-speed protocol analysis where real-time decode isn't possible
  • Capturing intermittent issues that occur over time
  • Production environment monitoring

Hard disk recommendations:

  • SSD for best performance
  • At least 10GB free space per hour of capture (varies by protocol speed)
  • Fast, dedicated disk if possible

docs.title: Protocol Monitor
docs.text: Capture to device memory with trigger-based or manual retrieval.

docs.title: Functional description
docs.text: Data is kept in the device and overwrites old data without returning to the PC. Capture can be stopped manually or by trigger condition. Then the device fills its memory and returns data to the PC for display.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
1. Reduced PC load: During capture, data doesn't return to the PC, minimizing performance requirements
  2. Fixed data size: Total data equals device memory capacity
  3. Long-term monitoring: Trigger conditions can monitor for extended periods
  4. Memory only fills when trigger conditions are met
  5. Efficient for rare events

docs.title: Considerations
docs.text:
Manual stop required if:

  • Trigger is not set, OR
  • Trigger is set but you want data before memory fills

Press Stop to send data back to the computer.

docs.title: Maximum device memory limit
docs.text:
• Unchecked: Uses maximum device memory
  • Checked: Adjustable memory usage ratio
  • Less memory = shorter subsequent processing time
  • Useful when you don't need full memory capacity

docs.title: Wait for stop
docs.text:
Data capture will continue until "Stop" is pressed

  • Data capture continues
  • When memory is full, new data replaces old data (circular buffer)
  • Press Stop when ready
  • Newest data is sent back to computer

Use case: Capturing the most recent activity before a known event

docs.title: Wait for trigger
docs.text:
Data capture will continue until the trigger condition is met

Without trigger condition:

  • No Pre/Post trigger relationship
  • Shows "Capturing..." until device memory is full

With trigger condition:

Configure post-trigger behavior:

  1. Fill the device memory then stop: Fill remaining memory according to trigger position, then stop
  2. Respects pre/post-trigger ratio

  3. Maximum data capture

  4. Stop immediately: Stop capturing immediately when triggered

  5. Fastest response
  6. Remaining memory is not filled

  7. Smaller data set

  8. Wait for seconds then stop: Continue capturing for specified time after trigger

  9. Configurable duration
  10. Stops early if memory fills first
  11. Balanced approach

Trigger position:

Data fills according to the set trigger position percentage. For example:

  • 20% trigger position = 20% pre-trigger data, 80% post-trigger data
  • 50% trigger position = 50% pre-trigger data, 50% post-trigger data

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Monitor systems for specific error conditions
  • Capture around trigger events efficiently
  • Reduce PC resource usage during long monitoring
  • Debug intermittent issues with trigger conditions

Typical workflow:

  1. Set up trigger for error condition or specific pattern
  2. Start capture and let it run
  3. Trigger occurs (or press Stop manually)
  4. Analyze captured data around the event

docs.title: Use Protocol Analyzer when:
docs.text:
• Debugging interactively
  • Need to see data in real-time
  • Captures are relatively short
  • PC performance is adequate
  • Immediate feedback is important

docs.title: Use Protocol Logger when:
docs.text:
• Capturing for extended periods
  • Protocol data rate exceeds real-time decode capability
  • Need to save captures for later analysis
  • Disk space is available
  • Archiving captures for documentation

docs.title: Use Protocol Monitor when:
docs.text:
• Waiting for specific trigger conditions
  • Monitoring over long periods with low PC load
  • Only need data around specific events
  • Device memory is sufficient for the event
  • Pre/post-trigger capture is important

docs.title: Cursor operations
docs.text: Use cursors for waveform measurements and searches in Protocol Analyzer mode.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Cursor functions are available in Protocol Analyzer mode, but only when the Show Waveforms feature is enabled.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Critical: The Show Waveforms function must be turned on before cursor operations become available.

If Show Waveforms is disabled:

  • Cursor buttons appear gray and are disabled
  • Waveform search is unavailable
  • Time measurements cannot be performed
  • Cursor keyboard shortcuts do not work

docs.title: Cursor functionality
docs.text: When Show Waveforms is enabled, cursor operations work identically to Logic Analyzer mode:

docs.title: Cursor features
docs.text:
• Place cursors: Add measurement cursors at specific time positions
  • Measure time intervals: Calculate time between cursors
  • Calculate frequency: Determine signal frequency from period
  • Search waveforms: Find edges, values, and patterns

docs.title: Special cursors
docs.text:
• T cursor: Trigger point marker (fixed position)
  • B cursor: Search-specific cursor
  • A-Z cursors: General-purpose measurement cursors (26 available)

docs.title: Adding cursors
docs.text:
Method 1: Mouse

Click the Add Cursor button and position cursor in waveform area.

Method 2: Keyboard

Press Shift + [A-Z letter] to add or move cursor to mouse position.

docs.title: Moving cursors
docs.text:
Drag:

  • Click and drag cursor sign or line
  • Reposition to desired time location

Keyboard:

  • Press A-Z key to jump to that cursor's position
  • Press Shift + A-Z to move cursor to mouse position

docs.title: Measurements
docs.text:
Cursor measurement bar shows:

  • Time interval: Between selected cursors
  • Frequency: 1 / interval
  • Sample count: Number of samples between cursors

docs.title: Waveform search
docs.text: Search for specific signal patterns using cursor positioning.

docs.title: Search modes
docs.text:
1. By Edge: Find rising/falling/either edges
  2. By Time: Move cursor by specified time offset
  3. By Value Match: Search for specific signal values
  4. Search Pulse Width: Find pulses matching width criteria

docs.title: Search workflow
docs.text:
1. Position starting cursor
  2. Configure search parameters
  3. Execute search
  4. Cursor moves to next match
  5. Repeat to find subsequent matches

docs.title: Timing verification
docs.text:
Measure protocol timing:

  1. Enable Show Waveforms
  2. Capture protocol data
  3. Place cursors at protocol events (START, STOP, ACK, etc.)
  4. Verify timing meets specification

Examples:

  • I2C setup and hold times
  • SPI clock period
  • UART bit timing
  • CAN bit periods

docs.title: Signal quality check
docs.text:
Inspect waveform quality:

  1. Enable Show Waveforms
  2. Capture suspect protocol
  3. Use cursors to measure:
  4. Rise/fall times
  5. Signal levels
  6. Noise or glitches
  7. Clock jitter

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text:
Correlate protocol with waveform:

  1. Click on protocol transaction in report
  2. Waveform view shows corresponding signals
  3. Use cursors to measure exact timing
  4. Verify signal integrity during transaction

docs.title: Transitioning to Logic Analyzer
docs.text:
If extensive cursor and waveform analysis is needed:

Recommended workflow:

  1. Capture in Protocol Analyzer with Show Waveforms
  2. Initial analysis using protocol report
  3. Click Convert to Logic Analyzer in File menu
  4. Continue with full Logic Analyzer cursor features

Why convert?

  • Full cursor measurement capabilities
  • Advanced waveform search
  • Detailed timing analysis tools
  • Signal-level triggering options
  • Complete waveform annotation

See: File Operations - Convert to Logic Analyzer

docs.title: Limitations in Protocol Analyzer mode
docs.text:
Compared to Logic Analyzer:

  • Fewer cursor analysis tools
  • Basic search functionality only
  • Limited waveform measurements
  • No advanced statistics on waveform
  • No cursor-based triggering

Recommendation: For extensive waveform analysis, convert to Logic Analyzer mode.

docs.title: When to use cursors in Protocol Analyzer
docs.text:
Use cursors here when:

  • Quick timing check needed
  • Verifying protocol meets timing spec
  • Simple signal quality inspection
  • Don't need full Logic Analyzer features

Convert to Logic Analyzer when:

  • Deep timing analysis required
  • Multiple complex measurements needed
  • Signal integrity is main concern
  • Advanced triggering required

docs.title: Efficient workflow
docs.text:
1. Start in Protocol Analyzer (without Show Waveforms)
  2. Pure protocol analysis

  3. Maximum capture capacity

  4. If issues found, enable Show Waveforms and recapture

  5. Add signal visibility

  6. Use cursors for basic timing checks

  7. If signal issues confirmed, convert to Logic Analyzer

  8. Full analysis capabilities
  9. Complete timing measurements

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
When Show Waveforms is enabled:

Function Key Move to cursor position A-Z Add/move cursor to mouse position Shift + A-Z Zoom in on waveform Number Pad + Zoom out on waveform Number Pad -

See: Keyboard Shortcuts

docs.title: Detail and statistics
docs.text: Inspect detailed protocol data and analyze traffic statistics.

docs.title: Detail window
docs.text: View complete details of protocol transactions with large amounts of data.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Many protocols contain extensive numerical data that isn't suitable for display in the main report window. The detail window provides expanded views of this data.

docs.title: Opening detail view
docs.text:
Method:

  1. Click on a row in the main report window
  2. Click on the Data column specifically
  3. The complete data is displayed in the detail window

What's displayed:

  • Full data payload
  • Formatted display (hex, decimal, ASCII, etc.)
  • Complete packet structure
  • Multi-byte data properly formatted
  • Any overflow data not shown in main report

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
Large data transfers:

  • I2C EEPROM reads with 256+ bytes
  • SPI flash page reads
  • UART data streams
  • CAN extended frames

Complex protocol structures:

  • Nested protocol data
  • Multi-level decode
  • Sub-protocol details
  • Payload interpretation

Data verification:

  • Confirm complete data transmission
  • Check for data corruption
  • Verify checksums or CRC
  • Compare against expected values

docs.title: Statistics window
docs.text: Analyze protocol traffic patterns and characteristics.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Statistics provide high-level analysis of protocol behavior across the entire capture. Different protocols offer different statistics based on their characteristics.

docs.title: Accessing statistics
docs.text:
Method:

  1. Click on Window menu
  2. Select Statistics
  3. Statistics window displays protocol-specific analysis

docs.title: Common statistics
docs.text:
Traffic analysis:

  • Total transaction count
  • Transactions per second
  • Read vs. write ratios
  • Address distribution

Error analysis:

  • NACK count
  • Timeout occurrences
  • CRC/checksum errors
  • Protocol violations

Timing statistics:

  • Average transaction duration
  • Maximum/minimum times
  • Idle time percentage
  • Bus utilization

Data analysis:

  • Data rate (bytes/second)
  • Average payload size
  • Data distribution patterns
  • Protocol command frequencies

docs.title: Identify issues
docs.text:
High-level problem identification:

  • Unusual error rates
  • Performance bottlenecks
  • Unexpected traffic patterns
  • Protocol violations

Example workflow:

  1. Open statistics window
  2. Notice high NACK rate on specific address
  3. Use search to find NACK transactions
  4. Bookmark problematic transactions
  5. Investigate with detail window

docs.title: Trace selection
docs.text:
Click on statistic trace:

  • Summarizes all records of the selected trace type
  • Displays in statistic list window
  • Shows detailed breakdown of that event type

Example:

  • Click on "Address 0x50" statistic trace
  • See all transactions to/from address 0x50
  • Analyze pattern for that specific device

docs.title: Protocol-specific statistics
docs.text:
Different protocols provide relevant statistics:

I2C:

  • Address usage distribution
  • Clock stretching occurrences
  • START/STOP condition count
  • ACK/NACK ratios per address

SPI:

  • Chip select assertion count
  • Data transfer sizes
  • Clock frequency distribution
  • CS idle time

UART:

  • Baud rate accuracy
  • Parity errors
  • Framing errors
  • Break conditions

CAN:

  • Message ID distribution
  • Error frame count
  • Bus load percentage
  • Retransmission statistics

docs.title: Hide Data window
docs.text: Filter the display to focus on relevant data.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Use the Hide Data function to temporarily remove data items from view, making it easier to focus on specific protocol activity.

docs.title: Hiding data
docs.text:
Method:

  1. Open Hide Data window
  2. Select data items to hide
  3. Apply filter
  4. Report display updates to show only non-hidden items

What can be hidden:

  • Specific addresses
  • Transaction types
  • Error conditions
  • Specific protocols (in multi-protocol captures)

docs.title: Restoring data
docs.text:
Method:

  1. Open Hide Data window
  2. Click Clear button
  3. All hidden data reappears in report

Important: Hide Data is a display filter only. Hidden data is still in the capture and can be unhidden at any time.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
Focus analysis:

  • Hide known-good traffic to see errors
  • Hide initialization sequence to focus on operational phase
  • Hide high-volume addresses to see low-traffic issues
  • Hide specific command types to analyze others

Example workflow:

  1. Capture shows heavy traffic from address 0x50
  2. Hide address 0x50 transactions
  3. Other addresses become visible
  4. Analyze low-traffic devices without distraction
  5. Clear hide filter to see complete picture again

docs.title: Saving reports
docs.text: Export detailed reports for documentation and further analysis.

docs.title: Save as text file
docs.text:
Contents of the report, detail, and statistics windows can be saved.

Supported formats:

  • .TXT - Plain text format
  • .CSV - Comma-separated values (import to Excel/spreadsheet)

docs.title: Save options
docs.text:
1. Save scope:
  2. Entire capture
  3. Selected rows only

  4. Specified row range

  5. Advanced reports:

  6. Enabled: Include detailed data from detail window

  7. Disabled: Main report data only

  8. Timestamp options:

  9. Combined: Timestamp and duration in one column

  10. Split: Separate timestamp and duration columns

  11. Byte limit:

  12. Maximum saving byte per column
  13. Prevents excessive column width in exports

docs.title: Export workflow
docs.text:
For documentation:

  1. Analyze capture, bookmark key events
  2. Hide irrelevant data
  3. Export visible data to CSV
  4. Open in spreadsheet for formatting
  5. Include in test report or documentation

For sharing:

  1. Capture and analyze data
  2. Export to CSV or TXT
  3. Share file with team members
  4. Recipients can import to their tools for analysis

docs.title: Detail window
docs.text:
• Keep detail window open during analysis
  • Use it to verify main report interpretations
  • Compare detail view with expected protocol format
  • Check for truncation in main report

docs.title: Statistics
docs.text:
• Review statistics first before diving into details
  • Use statistics to guide where to look closer
  • Export statistics for trend analysis across multiple captures
  • Compare statistics between captures to spot changes

docs.title: Hide Data
docs.text:
• Use hide data liberally - it's non-destructive
  • Try hiding different combinations to see patterns
  • Always clear hide filter before final export
  • Document what was hidden in analysis notes

docs.title: Saving reports
docs.text:
• Export regularly during long analysis sessions
  • Save with meaningful filenames (include date, test ID)
  • Consider CSV format for maximum flexibility
  • Include both summary and detail reports in documentation

DP Aux Protocol Analyzer settings (TravelLogic series)
  • Settings:
    • Data Rate: Aux channel data rate (UI unit: kHz). A wrong setting can shift decoding. Default: 1 MHz (1000 kHz).
    • DP version / eDP version: Choose DisplayPort or eDP version (affects available fields and decode meaning). Default: DP version, 1.4a (eDP list default 1.2). Main Default does not reset version (new protocol / version-dialog Default does).
    • DPCD 00108h: Channel coding 8b/10b / 128b/132b. With DP version, field enabled (Enable) only for DP 2.0+; with eDP version, only for eDP 1.5+; otherwise disabled (Disable) and forced to 8b/10b. Default: 8b/10b.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
eDP Protocol Analyzer settings (BusFinder / LA3000/LA4000 series)
  • Settings:
    • Startup Settings: DUT state at measurement start; required if AUX provides no parameters during capture.
      • Lane Number: Number of lanes in use (required). Default: 2 lanes.
      • Main-Link: Main-Link rate (UI shows Gbps/lane). Default about 2.97 Gbps/lane.
      • TPS Type / Control Symbol: Training pattern type and control-symbol mode. Default: TPS3 / Enhanced Mode.
      • DP version / eDP version: Aux Channel decode version.
      • Ignore Aux Channel Setting: Ignore AUX-provided settings. Default: cleared.
      • No Link Training / Disable Descramble / ASRE / Not Force Alignment: Wake without TPS, skip descramble, Alternate Scrambler Seed Reset, lane alignment options. Default: all cleared.
    • Probe Connection: Main Link probe vs Lane / P-N mapping; swap channel numbers and P/N as needed.
    • Filter: Drop commands or pixel data to reduce volume. Default: all filters cleared.
      • Filter Fill Start / Fill End
      • Filter Dummy Data
      • Filter TPS (TPS 1–4)
      • Specific Filter (Pixel Data): All or every Nth frame (max 128).
    • Option:
      • Fold TPS Symbols: Fold consecutive TPS in the report and show counts. Default: checked.
      • Show Idle Pattern. Default: cleared.
      • Ignore Unknown During TPS: Ignore Unknown between Sleep–TPS–Scrambler Reset while lanes are not yet aligned. Default: checked.
      • Detect TPS1: Enable TPS1 detection. Default: cleared.
  • Trigger settings:
    • Trigger On: Event Trigger or External Trigger In; Main-Link and Aux Channel tabs. When checked, the trigger tab is enabled (Enable). Default: cleared.
      • Main-Link: Lane, Simple Trigger (K-codes/events), Pattern Trigger (MSA/SDP, etc.). Pattern Default is often MSA; XX = don't care per nibble/byte.
      • Aux Channel:
        • Simple Trigger: Request Start/End, Reply Start/End, Timeout. Default: all cleared.
        • Pattern Trigger: Enable and open the Pattern Trigger dialog via the gear (see popup notes). Default: cleared.
          • Packet type (e.g. Request).
          • CMD: e.g. Any CMD.
          • DATA: Byte 0–15 (XX = don't care). Dialog Default: most bytes XX. Open this dialog from Trigger On → Aux Channel → Pattern Trigger via the gear. Choose the packet type (for example Request), CMD (for example Any CMD), and set a DATA pattern for Byte 0–15. Enter XX for don't-care bytes.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
eSPI Protocol Analyzer settings (TravelLogic series)
  • Settings:
    • Sample Rate: eSPI analysis sample rate (typical choices 1 GHz / 500 / 250 / 200 MHz). Too low may fail to decode. Default: 500 MHz.
    • Startup settings — I/O Mode: Bus I/O width (Single Mode / Dual Mode / Quad Mode). A wrong setting can shift decoding. Default: Single Mode.
    • Startup settings — Alert Mode: Alert source (From I/O[1] / From Alert#). Enabling extra CS (CS_B/C/D) forces From Alert# and disables (Disable) this field. Default: From Alert#.
    • Timing settings — tSHSL / tCLQV: Chip-select related timings in ns. Default: tSHSL 50 ns, tCLQV 25 ns.
    • Timing settings — Auto-select protocol timing: When checked, protocol timing is applied automatically and tCLQV is disabled (Disable); when cleared, tCLQV is enabled (Enable). Default: cleared.

  • Trigger settings:

    • Error triggers: Format Length error / OPCode error / Response error / Status error / CRC error. Default: all cleared.
    • eSPI Packet: Trigger on command/response content; when checked the gear is enabled (Enable) and opens eSPI Trigger Settings (see popup notes). First check often opens the dialog. Default: cleared.
      • Command / Response: Command and response match conditions (e.g. Any Command / Any Response). First open / Default is typically Any (OPCode shows XXh).
      • Data Dir: Command or Response.
      • Data Offset: Any Ofs or a fixed offset. Dialog Default: Any Ofs, offset 0.
      • Command / Response fields: e.g. OPCode, Response; XXh = don't care.
      • Default: Restore the dialog to Any / don't-care conditions. Open this dialog from the gear next to eSPI Packet to trigger on command/response content (for example a specific OPCode or a data pattern in one direction):

  • Command / Response: Match conditions (e.g. Any Command / Any Response). First open / Default is typically Any (OPCode shows XXh).

  • Data Dir: Command or Response.
  • Data Offset: Any Ofs or a fixed offset. Default: Any Ofs, offset 0.
  • Command / Response fields: e.g. OPCode, Response; XXh = don't care.
  • Default: Restore Any / don't-care conditions.

Switch from Protocol Analyzer to Logic Analyzer mode while preserving captured data.

Requirements:

What's transferred:

After conversion:

Continue using Logic Analyzer features:

Add oscilloscope measurements to Protocol Analyzer captures.

How it works:

  1. Enable Show Waveforms in Protocol Analyzer
  2. Capture data
  3. Click DSO icon to enter Logic Analyzer window

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
I2C Protocol Analyzer settings (TravelLogic series as representative)
  • Settings:
    • Options: Protocol analysis parameters.
      • Sample Rate: Choose a rate high enough for the I2C bus (typically ≥ 5–10× the bus clock).
      • Address Mode: Address display / decode mode.
        • 7-bit addressing: 7-bit address + 1-bit R/W.
        • 8-bit addressing (Include R/W in Address): Fold R/W into an 8-bit address.
        • 10-bit addressing: 10-bit address mode.
      • Clock Stretching: When checked, enable clock-stretch handling; open Clock Stretching Settings via the gear (shared with SMBus / PMBus); gear is disabled (Disable) when cleared. Default: cleared.
        • Clock stretching: Detect when a slave holds SCL low to stretch the clock. Default: cleared.
        • Timeout check (Range: 0 ns ~ 67 ms): Flag stretches longer than the limit. When checked, the value field is enabled (Enable) (enter ns); when cleared it is disabled (Disable). Default: cleared, value empty.
        • Violation check: Flag non-compliant clock stretching. Default: cleared.

Open this dialog from the gear next to Clock Stretching to configure how the analyzer detects or flags clock stretching (a slave holding SCL low so the master waits):

  • Clock stretching: Enable detection of clock stretching. Default: cleared.
  • Timeout check (Range: 0 ns ~ 67 ms): Flag a stretch that exceeds the allowed duration. When checked, the value field is enabled (Enable) — enter ns (about 0–67 ms); when cleared the value field is disabled (Disable). Default: cleared, value empty.
  • Violation check: Flag non-compliant clock stretching. Default: cleared.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text: Quick keyboard shortcuts for Protocol Analyzer operations.

docs.title: Available shortcuts
docs.text:
Function Key Move to cursor position A-Z Add a cursor to the mouse position Shift + A-Z Start capture Enter Stop capture ESC Search F3 or Ctrl+F Zoom in on waveform area Number Pad + Zoom out on waveform area Number Pad -

Note: Cursor shortcuts only work when Show Waveforms is enabled.

docs.title: Start capture
docs.text: Press Enter to begin data capture with the current settings.

docs.title: Stop capture
docs.text:
Press ESC to stop an ongoing capture operation.

This is particularly useful in Protocol Logger and Protocol Monitor modes where captures may run for extended periods.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
Press F3 or Ctrl+F to open the search dialog.

The search function works in all Protocol Analyzer modes and allows you to:

  • Find specific addresses
  • Locate data values
  • Search protocol fields
  • Filter by packet type

Learn more: Search operations

docs.title: Cursor operations
docs.text: Requirements: Show Waveforms must be enabled for cursor operations.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Press any letter key (A-Z) to quickly jump to the corresponding cursor position in the waveform area.

docs.title: Adding cursors
docs.text: Press Shift + any letter key (A-Z) to add a cursor at the current mouse position.

docs.title: Zoom operations
docs.text:
• Zoom in: Press Number Pad + to increase waveform magnification
  • Zoom out: Press Number Pad - to decrease waveform magnification

Alternatively, use the mouse wheel:

  • Scroll up to zoom in
  • Scroll down to zoom out

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• The Enter/ESC keys work from anywhere in the application window
  • Search (F3/Ctrl+F) is one of the most useful features for protocol analysis
  • If cursor shortcuts don't work, verify that Show Waveforms is enabled

MCTP over I3C Protocol Analyzer settings (TravelLogic series)

  • Settings:

    • Decode Address: Configure which bus addresses are treated as MCTP endpoints. Open Address Configuration to add/remove rows. If the list is empty, the decoder uses MCTP specification defaults.
      • Address Configuration: + Add / Remove rows of Address and Type. Types include Static I2C (no MCTP decode), MCTP (I3C), MCTP (I2C). New-row Default Type: MCTP (I3C).
    • SPDM Startup Setting: Fallback Signature / Hash / Ext counts used to parse SPDM bodies before algorithm negotiation latches sizes. Wrong values can mis-parse early SPDM messages.
      • Signature (S): Signature field length in bytes (0–512). Default: 256.
      • HashCnt (H): Hash count (1–15). Default: 2.
      • Ext-AsymCnt (A): Extended asymmetric count (0–15). Default: 1.
      • Ext-HashCnt (E): Extended hash count (0–15). Default: 1. Open Address Configuration under Decode Address to choose which bus addresses are decoded as MCTP endpoints:

  • + Add / Remove: Add or remove address rows. If the list is empty, the decoder uses MCTP specification defaults.

  • Address: Bus address for that row.
  • Type: Static I2C (no MCTP decode), MCTP (I3C), MCTP (I2C). New-row Default Type: MCTP (I3C).

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
MII Protocol Analyzer settings (TravelLogic series)
  • Settings:
    • Type: Select the interface (on many products MII / RMII; some also offer RGMII / GMII). A wrong choice misaligns channel pins and which trigger items are available. The main Default button does not reset this field.
    • Clock Latch: Rising / Falling data latch edge. A wrong setting can shift decoding. Field usually disabled (Disable) for RGMII. The main Default button does not reset this field.
    • RMII Clk Frequency: Field enabled (Enable) only when Type = RMII. Choose Normal Latch or Frequence Clk x10 (UI spelling); field disabled (Disable) for non-RMII types. Default: Normal Latch.

  • Trigger settings:

    • Trigger on: Select error/event triggers. Availability follows Type — items are field enabled (Enable) or field disabled (Disable) (for example Carrier Extend / Carrier Extend Error / False Indication are disabled (Disable) for MII/RMII and enabled (Enable) for RGMII/GMII). Default: all cleared.
      • Format Error / Frame Error / CRC Error: Trigger on format, frame-structure, or CRC errors. Default: cleared.
      • Rising Error Pin: Trigger on a rising Error pin (ER); field may be disabled (Disable) for some types such as RMII. Default: cleared.
      • Collision: Trigger on Collision (COL); field may be disabled (Disable) for some types. Default: cleared.
      • Carrier Extend / Carrier Extend Error / False Indication: Carrier-extend related events; typically available on RGMII/GMII. Default: cleared.
    • MII Packet: Trigger on Ethernet frame content; enable then open GMII Trigger Settings via the gear (see popup notes below). Use this to trigger on destination/source, Ethertype, or a payload pattern. Default: cleared.
      • Destination / Source Address: 6-byte MACs; XXh = don't care for that byte. Dialog Default: each byte XXh.
      • Ethertype/Length: 2 bytes (XXXXh = don't care) to lock a protocol type or length field. Dialog Default: XXh XXh (don't care).
      • Data (Byte 1–8): Payload pattern to match; enable Data Offset to start at a byte offset. Dialog Default: each byte XXh; Data Offset cleared, offset 0.
      • Default: Restore the dialog to all don't-care (addresses/Data = XXh, Ethertype don't care, Data Offset off). Open GMII Trigger Settings from the gear next to MII Packet to combine Ethernet frame fields (for example a specific destination, Ethertype, or payload pattern):

  • Destination / Source Address: 6-byte MACs; XXh means that byte is don't care. Default: each byte XXh.

  • Ethertype/Length: 2 bytes (XXXXh = don't care) to lock a protocol type or length field. Default: XXh XXh (don't care).
  • Data (Byte 1–8): Up to 8 hex bytes of payload pattern to match; XXh means that byte is don't care. Enable Data Offset to start matching at a byte offset. Default: each byte XXh; Data Offset cleared, offset 0.
  • Default: Restore the default (all don't-care) condition.

MII: GMII Trigger Settings (MII Packet)

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
MIPI CSI Protocol Analyzer settings (BusFinder / LA3000/LA4000 series)
  • Settings:
    • Lane Number: Number of lanes in use (e.g. 4 Lanes). Default: 4.
    • Probe Connection: Way Station mapping for D0–D3/CLK; swap lane numbers and P/N. Optional waveform capture for connection verification (Beta). Default: waveform capture cleared.
    • Filter Data >: When checked the slider is enabled (Enable); drop payload beyond the set length. Default: cleared (about 48 bytes step when enabled).
    • Timing Setup:
      • Clock Rate / T CLK-SETTLE: Clock and settle (Auto available).
      • Phase (D0–D3 / CLK): Per-lane phase; use Phase Adjustment for fine tuning. Default phase: 0.

  • Trigger settings:

    • Trigger on: ECC (single/multi-bit), CRC, External Trigger In, and CSI Packet (gear enabled (Enable) when checked; opens CSI Trigger Settings — see popup notes). Default: all cleared.
      • Transmission Type: Select the transmission type (e.g. HS or LP).
      • Direction: Host Sourced or Peripheral Sourced.
      • Data Type / DCS: Select the data type; DCS is field enabled (Enable) depending on Data Type.
      • Header: Set VC/DT, Data 0, Data 1, and ECC (XXh = don't care for that field).
      • Data: Payload pattern per byte (e.g. Byte 0–27); XXh = don't care per byte.
      • Default: Restore the dialog to default trigger conditions. Open this dialog from the gear next to Trigger on → CSI Packet to trigger on CSI packet fields:

  • Transmission Type / Direction / Data Type / DCS: Choose transfer type, direction, and data type; DCS availability depends on Data Type.

  • Header: VC/DT, Data 0, Data 1, ECC; XXh = don't care for that field.
  • Data: Payload pattern (e.g. Byte 0–27); XXh = don't care per byte.
  • Default: Restore the dialog to default trigger conditions.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
eMMC Protocol Analyzer settings (BusFinder / LA3000/LA4000 series)
  • Settings:
    • Sample Rate: Select the sample rate. If Secondary PA (NAND Flash) is enabled, use 1 GHz or below.
    • Primary Protocol Analyzer: Choose the probe type (eMMC Probe) or Custom eMMC wiring.
      • eMMC Probe: Click the exclamation icon to open Custom Channel Settings; view probe pins mapped to CLK, CMD, DAT0–DAT7, DS, and set Threshold.
      • Custom eMMC: Open Custom Channel Settings for custom wiring.
        • Signal source: Select eMMC Probe - Slot B, LA Probe - Slot A, or LA Probe - Slot B.
        • Pin mapping: Map pins to CLK, CMD, DAT0–DAT7, DS, and related signals.
        • Threshold / Quick Setup: Set the trigger threshold, or apply a quick setup.
        • Clear All / Default: Clear channel assignments, or restore defaults.
    • Secondary Protocol Analyzer or I/O: Run NAND Flash or I/O analysis on remaining pins. For I/O, open I/O Channel Settings.
      • Probe source: Select LA Probe - Slot A or LA/Protocol Probe - Slot B.
      • I/O0–I/O3: Enable each channel and assign a probe channel (e.g. B8–B11).
      • Threshold / Quick Setup: Set the trigger threshold, or apply a quick setup.
      • Select All / Deselect All / Default: Select all, clear all, or restore defaults.
    • Startup Settings: DUT mode at capture start; Tuning available.
      • Boot Settings: Boot-phase bus mode and width (e.g. SDR, 1-bit).
      • Bus Mode: Runtime speed/mode/width (e.g. High Speed, SDR, 4-bit).
      • Tuning Function: Open Tuning Settings for eMMC phase calibration.
        • Tuning mode: Select the calibration mode (e.g. Read data in HS200).
        • Tuning BUS width: Select the bus width (e.g. 8 bit).
        • Threshold: Set the calibration voltage threshold.
        • Accuracy (Count Times): Set the measurement count (e.g. 64 times).
        • Advance settings: Enable advanced settings.
        • Parameter list: Select, save, or delete a phase-parameter file.
        • Phase parameter: Set Response and the Read/Write phases for D0–D7; Fill in all fields applies one value to all lanes.
        • Current Status / Resume / Result: View calibration status, resume calibration, or view results.
      • Detect BOOTACK: Detect BOOTACK when the DUT is not powered on.
      • Retain settings after BOOT: Keep settings after boot.
    • Filter: Limit recorded payload to save memory.
      • Data Length >: Drop trailing data beyond the set byte length per Data Frame.
      • Number of blocks > 1 (SC > 1): Filter multi-block transfers.
    • Option:
      • Vendor CMD: Opens Vendor CMD settings (see Settings — Vendor CMD settings).
      • Timing: Opens eMMC Timing (see dialog below) to set Min/Max/Unit per Symbol (clock cycles or time).
        • Symbol / Min / Max / Unit: Set each symbol's minimum, maximum, and unit. Common clock-cycle Defaults: N_AC Min 2; N_CC/N_RC/N_SC Min 8; N_CD Min 56; N_CP Min 74; N_CR Min 2 / Max 64; N_ID Min/Max 5; N_WR Min 2; N_SB-A/B Min/Max 4; N_SB-C Min/Max 2. N_ST Min/Max is often 2 and disabled (Disable).
        • N_AC Max: Maximum can be calculated from TAAC, FOP, and NSAC (on-screen formula); enter TAAC/NSAC in hexadecimal. Default often TAAC 26h, NSAC 00h.
        • tBA / tBD: Units are ms and s. Default often tBA Max 50 ms, tBD Max 1 s.
        • Default: Restore default timing values.
      • 3 Pin mode (CMD, CLK, D0): Analyze command flow with CLK/CMD/D0 only. Default: cleared.
      • CLK Detect: Detect CLK activity; time condition enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared; time often 24 ns.
      • LBA Format: LBA display format. Default: Hex.
      • Voltage Detect: Enable VCC(A0) / VDD(A1) as voltage-detect channels (see Settings — Voltage Detect). Default: cleared.
  • Trigger settings:
    • Trigger on: Tabs General / Error / CRC Status / Timeout / VCC Drop. Children are enabled (Enable) when checked; CMD/RESP., Data, Timeout, and VCC/VDD Drop open matching dialogs (see Settings links). Default: Trigger on and error items cleared.
      • General:
        • CMD / RESP.: Opens Trigger Settings (see Settings — Trigger Settings).
        • No Response: Trigger when there is no response; the gear opens command conditions (button often shows No Resp.(Any CMD)).
        • Data: Opens Data Trigger (see Settings — Data Trigger).
      • Error: CRC7 error / CRC16 error / End bit error. Default: all cleared.
      • CRC Status: Set CRC Status Pattern (Positive / Negative).
      • Timeout: Opens Timeout Trigger (see Settings — Timeout Trigger).
      • VCC Drop / VDD Drop: Voltage-drop trigger; open Voltage Range Settings (see Settings — Voltage Range Settings). Default: cleared.

Open this dialog from the exclamation icon when Primary Protocol Analyzer is eMMC Probe, or when Custom eMMC is selected. Choose the signal source (eMMC Probe - Slot B / LA Probe - Slot A / LA Probe - Slot B), map pins to CLK, CMD, DAT0–DAT7, DS, and related signals, and set Threshold or use Quick Setup. Use Clear All to clear assignments, or Default to restore factory mapping.

eMMC: Custom Channel Settings

With Secondary Protocol Analyzer or I/O set to I/O, open this dialog to choose the probe source (LA Probe - Slot A / LA/Protocol Probe - Slot B), enable I/O0–I/O3 and assign channels, and set Threshold or use Quick Setup.

eMMC: I/O Channel Settings

Open this dialog from Startup Settings → Tuning Function. Configure Tuning mode, BUS width, Threshold, and Accuracy, and set Response plus Read/Write phases for D0–D7. Manage parameter files with Save/Delete, and use Resume/Result to continue or review calibration.

eMMC: Tuning Settings

Open this dialog from Option → Timing. Set Min/Max/Unit for each Symbol (clock cycles or time). N_AC Max can be calculated from TAAC, FOP, and NSAC (Default often TAAC 26h, NSAC 00h); tBA/tBD Default often Max 50 ms / 1 s. N_ST may be disabled (Disable). Use Default to restore factory values.

RS485 also offers Two-Wire / Four-Wire (default Two-Wire). Default: 1000 ms.

NAND Flash Protocol Analyzer settings (BusFinder / LA3000/LA4000 series)
  • Settings:
    • Sample Rate: Select the sample rate. If Secondary PA (SD 3.0 / eMMC) is enabled, use 1 GHz or below. Default: 2.4 GHz.
    • Primary Protocol Analyzer: Choose NAND Probe or Custom NAND wiring.
    • Secondary Protocol Analyzer or I/O: Run SD 3.0, eMMC, or I/O on remaining pins.

    • Filter: When checked, Data Length > is enabled (Enable) — drop data beyond the set byte length per Data Frame. Default: cleared.
    • Option:
      • Invert RE# (W/R#) / Invert DQS: When probing inverted differential RE/DQS in DDR mode. Default: cleared.
      • Don't care R/B: Ignore R/B (R/B wiring optional). May disable (Disable) Busy-time items. Default: cleared.
      • Single R/B#: In Multi-CE, use Read Status Ready for Busy time when checked; otherwise use R/B. Default: cleared.
      • Remove READ STATUS Command (Busy State): Remove repeated Not Ready Polling Read Status. Default: checked.
      • Set Row Addressing: Split Row Address into Page / Word Line / Plane / Block / LUN, etc.; Set button enabled (Enable) when checked, opening the Set Row Addressing dialog (see below). Defaults come from the NAND Command Set. Default: cleared.
  • Trigger settings:
    • Trigger on: When checked, configure CMD/ADDR/DATA, Busy time check, VCC1(A0)/VCC2(A1) Drop; gears are enabled (Enable) per child and first check often opens a dialog. Dialog Default: CMD XXh, Row XXXXXXh, Data XXh/XXXXh; Busy about 250 ms. Default: Trigger on and children cleared.
      • VCC1(A0) Drop / VCC2(A1) Drop: Voltage-drop trigger; open Voltage Range Settings (see Settings — Voltage Range Settings). Typical VDD1 about 2.70–3.60 V, VDD2 about 1.70–1.95 V.

Optionally enable Show Row Addressing in the Report. Use Default / Reset to restore or clear.

docs.title: Operating modes
docs.text: Configure memory usage, stop conditions, and repetitive capture behavior.

docs.title: Memory settings
docs.text: Control how much memory is used for capturing protocol data.

docs.title: Device memory usage
docs.text:
Maximum device memory limit:

  • Unchecked: Uses the maximum available device memory
  • Checked: Adjustable memory usage ratio
  • Allows limiting memory to speed up post-processing
  • Useful when full memory isn't needed

Considerations:

  • More memory = longer captures
  • More memory = longer processing time after capture
  • Less memory = faster to process and display

docs.title: Trigger position
docs.text:
Set the percentage of memory used for pre-trigger vs. post-trigger data.

Examples:

  • 0%: All memory for post-trigger data (no pre-trigger)
  • 20%: 20% pre-trigger, 80% post-trigger
  • 50%: Equal pre and post-trigger data
  • 80%: 80% pre-trigger, 20% post-trigger
  • 100%: All memory for pre-trigger data (trigger at end)

Use cases:

  • 0-20%: Capturing what happens after a trigger event
  • 50%: Balanced view of activity before and after trigger
  • 80-100%: Capturing what led up to a trigger event

docs.title: Stop conditions
docs.text: Configure when the capture automatically stops.

docs.title: Number of data lines
docs.text:
Stop capture when the stored data line count reaches the specified number.

Configuration:

  • Enabled: Set target number of protocol transactions/packets
  • Disabled: (Default) Capture until memory full or manual stop

Use cases:

  • Need specific number of transactions (e.g., 1000 I2C packets)
  • Avoid unnecessarily long captures
  • Consistent test data size across multiple runs
  • Automated testing with fixed packet counts

Benefits:

  • Faster captures when you know how much data you need
  • Prevents wasting time capturing more than necessary
  • Simplifies post-processing when data size is predictable

docs.title: Maximum device memory limit
docs.text:
Stop capture when device memory fills to the specified limit.

Default behavior: Enabled in all modes

Effect by capture mode:

  • Protocol Analyzer: Device stops when memory is full
  • Protocol Logger: Stops when disk space limit is reached
  • Protocol Monitor: Stops when device memory is full (or trigger condition met)

docs.title: Repetitive capture
docs.text: Automatically repeat captures multiple times.

docs.title: Repetitive times setting
docs.text:
Disabled (default):

  • Device stops after stop condition is met once
  • Single capture per Start command

Enabled:

  1. Device captures until stop condition is met
  2. Saves captured data
  3. Automatically starts next capture
  4. Repeats for the specified number of times

Set to 0: Continuous repetitive capture (infinite loop)

  • Captures continuously until manually stopped
  • Each capture is saved separately
  • Useful for long-term monitoring

docs.title: Repeat acquisition behavior
docs.text:
Control waveform decoding during repetitive captures.

Options:

  1. Don't display decoding: Faster acquisition, analyze later
  2. Display with intervals: Choose display time
  3. 1 second
  4. 2 seconds
  5. 5 seconds

Trade-off:

  • No display = Fastest capture rate
  • Display = Slower but provides real-time feedback

docs.title: Protocol Analyzer mode
docs.text:
Memory considerations:

  • Limited by RAM and device memory
  • Real-time processing uses more resources
  • Computer performance affects capture reliability

Stop behavior:

  • May auto-stop if computer can't keep up with data rate
  • Monitor memory usage during capture
  • Reduce sample rate if auto-stopping occurs

docs.title: Protocol Logger mode
docs.text:
Memory considerations:

  • Limited by hard disk space
  • Can capture for very long durations
  • Processing time proportional to capture size

Additional option:

Run data process after capture stopped:

  • Checked: Automatically process .LOG file after stopping
  • Immediate analysis

  • Longer stop time

  • Unchecked: Save .LOG file only

  • Faster stop
  • Analyze later by manually opening the .LOG file
  • Better for very large captures

docs.title: Protocol Monitor mode
docs.text:
Memory considerations:

  • Limited to device memory only
  • Circular buffer in some configurations
  • Fixed maximum data size

Wait modes:

docs.title: Wait for stop
docs.text:
Data capture continues until "Stop" is pressed

  • Memory fills with latest data
  • When memory is full, old data is overwritten (circular buffer)
  • Press Stop when ready to retrieve data
  • Always get the most recent activity

Use case: Capturing the moments before a system failure or user action

docs.title: Wait for trigger
docs.text:
Data capture continues until trigger condition is met

Without trigger condition set:

  • No Pre/Post trigger relationship
  • Captures until memory is full
  • Essentially same as "Wait for stop" without circular buffer

With trigger condition set:

Three post-trigger options:

  1. Fill the device memory then stop
  2. Respects trigger position percentage
  3. Maximizes data capture

  4. Fills all available memory

  5. Stop immediately

  6. Stops as soon as trigger occurs
  7. Fastest response
  8. Smaller data set

  9. Useful when you only care about pre-trigger data

  10. Wait for seconds then stop

  11. Configurable time duration after trigger
  12. Balance between immediacy and data completeness
  13. Stops early if memory fills first

docs.title: Choosing memory settings
docs.text:
Use full memory when:

  • You don't know how much data you need
  • Capturing intermittent issues
  • Maximum data is desired

Limit memory when:

  • You know exactly how much data is needed
  • Fast post-processing is important
  • Multiple repetitive captures are planned

docs.title: Repetitive capture strategies
docs.text:
Use repetitive capture for:

  • Stress testing (capture same scenario multiple times)
  • Detecting intermittent issues (capture until problem appears)
  • Statistical analysis (collect multiple samples for averaging)
  • Long-term monitoring (continuous overnight captures)

Workflow example:

  1. Set repetitive times to 100
  2. Set stop condition to 1000 packets
  3. Start capture
  4. System automatically captures 100 × 1000 packet sets
  5. Analyze all captures for anomalies

docs.title: Stop condition combinations
docs.text:
Fast known-size captures:

  • Enable "Number of data lines"
  • Set to required packet count
  • Disable memory limit (or set high)
  • Result: Captures exactly what you need, stops quickly

Long monitoring:

  • Disable "Number of data lines"
  • Use Protocol Monitor "Wait for trigger"
  • Set appropriate trigger condition
  • Result: Efficient long-term monitoring with triggered capture

  • Timeout check (Range: 0 ns ~ 67 ms): Flag a stretch that exceeds the allowed duration. When checked, the value field is enabled (Enable) — enter ns (about 0–67 ms); when cleared the value field is disabled (Disable). Default: cleared, value empty.
  • Violation check: Flag non-compliant clock stretching. Default: cleared.

docs.title: Protocol settings
docs.text: Configure protocol type, channels, and decode parameters for capture.

docs.title: Protocol configuration styles
docs.text: Protocols use one of two configuration styles based on their complexity.

docs.title: Style 1: Easy setting protocols
docs.text: For protocols with straightforward configuration.

docs.title: Configuration steps
docs.text:
1. Select the protocol: Choose from the protocol dropdown list
  2. Channel setting: Assign device channels to protocol signals
  3. Waveform preview: The software automatically detects signal waveform and frequency
  4. Options: Set capture and decoding parameters specific to the protocol
  5. Threshold: Set voltage levels according to the signal specifications

Protocols using Style 1:

  • Simple protocols with automatic signal detection
  • Protocols with minimal configuration options
  • Self-clocked protocols

docs.title: Style 2: Advanced setting protocols
docs.text: For protocols requiring more detailed configuration.

docs.title: Configuration steps
docs.text:
1. Select the protocol: Choose from the protocol dropdown list
  2. Set the sample rate: Specify sampling frequency based on protocol speed
  3. Channel setting: Assign device channels to protocol signals
  4. Trigger on: Configure trigger conditions for protocol events
  5. Options: Set capture and decoding parameters specific to the protocol
  6. Threshold: Set voltage levels according to the signal specifications

Protocols using Style 2:

  • High-speed protocols requiring precise sample rates
  • Protocols with complex triggering requirements
  • Protocols with multiple clock domains

docs.title: Channel setting
docs.text: Assign physical channels to protocol signal lines.

docs.title: Common protocol signals
docs.text:
For I2C:

  • SDA (Serial Data)
  • SCL (Serial Clock)

For SPI:

  • MOSI (Master Out Slave In)
  • MISO (Master In Slave Out)
  • SCK (Serial Clock)
  • CS (Chip Select)

For UART:

  • TX (Transmit)
  • RX (Receive)

For CAN:

  • CAN_H (CAN High)
  • CAN_L (CAN Low)

docs.title: Channel assignment
docs.text:
1. Select the protocol signal from the dropdown
  2. Choose the corresponding device channel
  3. Repeat for all required signals
  4. Optional signals can be left unassigned if not used

docs.title: Sample rate configuration
docs.text: Set the sampling frequency appropriate for the protocol speed.

docs.title: Guidelines
docs.text:
Minimum sampling rate: 4× the protocol clock frequency

Recommended sampling rate: 10× the protocol clock frequency

Examples:

  • I2C at 400 kHz → Use at least 4 MHz (recommended: 10 MHz)
  • SPI at 10 MHz → Use at least 40 MHz (recommended: 100 MHz)
  • UART at 115200 baud → Use at least 460 kHz (recommended: 1.15 MHz)

docs.title: Auto-configuration
docs.text: For Style 1 protocols, the software automatically sets an appropriate sample rate based on the detected signal frequency.

docs.title: Waveform preview
docs.text:
Available in Style 1 protocols.

Features:

  • Automatic signal detection
  • Frequency measurement
  • Signal quality indication
  • Waveform visualization

What it shows:

  • Detected clock frequency
  • Signal levels
  • Edge transitions
  • Signal integrity indicators

docs.title: Options (Protocol-specific settings)
docs.text: Each protocol has specific decode and capture options.

docs.title: Common options
docs.text:
Decode parameters:

  • Address format (7-bit, 10-bit, etc.)
  • Data format (hex, decimal, binary, ASCII)
  • Endianness (big-endian, little-endian)
  • Error detection (parity, CRC, etc.)

Capture parameters:

  • Decode on-the-fly vs. post-capture
  • Filter settings
  • Packet size limits
  • Buffer settings

Display options:

  • Show/hide specific packet types
  • Color coding
  • Report format preferences

docs.title: Threshold settings
docs.text: Configure voltage thresholds for logic level detection.

docs.title: Single threshold
docs.text:
Set one threshold voltage:

  • Signal above threshold = Logic High (1)
  • Signal below threshold = Logic Low (0)

Recommendation: Set threshold to half the signal voltage level.

Examples:

  • 3.3V logic → Threshold: 1.65V
  • 5V logic → Threshold: 2.5V
  • 1.8V logic → Threshold: 0.9V

docs.title: Per-channel threshold
docs.text:
Different channels can have different thresholds if needed.

Use cases:

  • Mixed voltage systems
  • Level-shifted signals
  • Different logic families on same bus

docs.title: Quick presets
docs.text:
Common threshold presets:

  • TTL (5V): 2.5V
  • CMOS 3.3V: 1.65V
  • CMOS 2.5V: 1.25V
  • CMOS 1.8V: 0.9V
  • Custom: Manual entry

docs.title: Trigger configuration
docs.text: Available in Style 2 protocols.

docs.title: Trigger options
docs.text:
Trigger on protocol events:

  • Start condition
  • Stop condition
  • Specific address
  • Data pattern
  • Error conditions

Trigger on signal events:

  • Edge transitions
  • Pulse width
  • Timeout
  • External trigger

docs.title: Trigger position
docs.text:
Set the percentage of memory for pre-trigger vs. post-trigger data:

  • 0%: All post-trigger data
  • 50%: Equal pre and post-trigger
  • 100%: All pre-trigger data

docs.title: I2C
docs.text:
• Address format: 7-bit or 10-bit
  • Speed modes: Standard (100 kHz), Fast (400 kHz), Fast-plus (1 MHz), High-speed (3.4 MHz)
  • Watch for clock stretching

docs.title: SPI
docs.text:
• Clock polarity (CPOL): 0 or 1
  • Clock phase (CPHA): 0 or 1
  • Bit order: MSB-first or LSB-first
  • Word size: 8, 16, 24, or 32 bits

docs.title: UART
docs.text:
• Baud rate: Common rates from 300 to 921600
  • Data bits: 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9
  • Parity: None, odd, even, mark, space
  • Stop bits: 1, 1.5, or 2

docs.title: CAN
docs.text:
• Baud rate: Typical 125, 250, 500 kbps, 1 Mbps
  • Frame format: Standard (11-bit ID) or Extended (29-bit ID)
  • CAN FD support: If available

docs.title: Getting good captures
docs.text:
1. Choose appropriate sample rate: Higher is better, but not excessive
  2. Set accurate thresholds: Use multimeter to measure actual signal levels
  3. Test with known-good signals: Verify configuration before debugging

docs.title: Troubleshooting decode errors
docs.text:
If decode fails or shows errors:

  • Check channel assignments
  • Verify threshold levels
  • Increase sample rate
  • Check signal quality with Logic Analyzer mode
  • Verify protocol-specific settings (baud rate, clock polarity, etc.)

    • Filter:
      • Data Length >: When checked, field enabled (Enable); drop data beyond the set byte length. Default: cleared.
      • Number of blocks > 1 (SC > 1): Filter multi-block transfers. Default: cleared.
    • Option:
      • 3 Pin mode (CMD, CLK, D0): Command-flow analysis with three pins only. Default: cleared.
      • BUS mode settings at startup: Mode at capture start (e.g. DDR) and bus width. Default bus width 4 bit, DDR cleared.
      • Tuning settings: Opens Tuning Settings (see dialog below); set Tuning mode, Threshold, and Accuracy, and adjust Response / Read / Write (D0–D3) phase. Manage parameter files with Save / Delete.
      • Vendor CMD: Opens Vendor CMD settings (see Settings — Vendor CMD settings).
      • SDIO Block Size / Enable SDIO Read Wait: Opens SDIO Fn Block Size Setting (see below) for Fn0–Fn7 block sizes; optionally enable SDIO Read Wait. Block Size Default for each Fn is 256 bytes; Read Wait Default cleared.
      • CLK Detect: Detect CLK activity; time condition enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Trigger settings:
    • Trigger on: CMD/Resp/Data, End-bit/CRC7/CRC16/CRC status (with timeout), VDD Drop, etc. Children are enabled (Enable) when checked; CMD/Data open matching dialogs (see Settings links). Default: Trigger on and error items cleared.
      • Command / Response: Opens Trigger Settings (see Settings — Trigger Settings).
      • Data: Opens Data Trigger (see Settings — Data Trigger).
      • VDD Drop: Voltage-drop trigger; open Voltage Range Settings (see Settings — Voltage Range Settings).

Open this dialog from Option → Tuning settings. Set Tuning mode, Threshold, and Accuracy, and adjust Response and Read / Write (D0–D3) phase. Manage parameter files with Save / Delete; use Resume / Result to continue calibration or view results.

SD 3.0: Tuning Settings

Open this dialog from Option → SDIO Block Size. Set Block Size for CCCR Fn0 and FBR Fn1–Fn7 (Default 256 bytes each).

SD 3.0: SDIO Fn Block Size Setting

docs.title: Search
docs.text: Search for specific protocol data, addresses, or patterns in the report window.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The search function helps you quickly locate specific protocol transactions in captured data. This is particularly useful when analyzing large captures or looking for specific events.

docs.title: Search interface
docs.text:
Access the search function using:

  • Menu: Click Search in the toolbar
  • Keyboard: Press F3 or Ctrl+F

docs.title: 1. Enter search text
docs.text:
Type the text, value, or pattern you're looking for.

Search supports:

  • Text strings (for ASCII decode)
  • Hexadecimal values (0x prefix or without)
  • Decimal values
  • Binary patterns
  • Protocol-specific fields

Examples:

  • Search for address: 0x50 or 50
  • Search for ASCII text: ERROR
  • Search for specific data: FF or 255

docs.title: 2. Navigate results
docs.text:
Use navigation buttons to move through search results:

  • Next: Find the next matching item
  • Previous: Find the previous matching item

Keyboard shortcuts:

  • F3: Find next
  • Shift + F3: Find previous (in some implementations)

docs.title: 3. Field specification
docs.text:
Narrow your search to specific fields for faster results.

Search scope options:

  • All fields: Search across all columns in the report
  • Target fields: Search only specific columns

Available target fields (protocol-dependent):

  • Address column
  • Data column
  • Command/Type column
  • Status column
  • Custom decode fields

Why specify fields?

  • Faster search: Reduced search range
  • More precise: Avoid false matches in irrelevant fields
  • Better performance: Especially important for large captures

docs.title: Visual feedback
docs.text:
Match found:

  • Matching data shown with green background color
  • Total number of packets found is displayed
  • Current match is highlighted

No match found:

  • Search result shown in orange background color
  • "No results found" message
  • Verify search term and try again

docs.title: Result navigation
docs.text:
Current match indicator:

  • Shows which match you're viewing (e.g., "3 of 15")
  • Updates as you navigate with Next/Previous
  • Report automatically scrolls to show current match

docs.title: Partial matching
docs.text:
The search typically supports partial string matching.

Examples:

  • Search AB finds ABCD, CAB, FFAB00
  • Search ERR finds ERROR, PERROR, ERR_CODE

docs.title: Case sensitivity
docs.text:
Check search dialog for case-sensitive option if available.

  • Case-insensitive (default): error matches Error, ERROR, error
  • Case-sensitive: error matches only error

docs.title: Multiple criteria
docs.text:
For complex searches:

  1. Perform first search
  2. Note results
  3. Refine search term
  4. Search again

Tip: Export to CSV and use spreadsheet tools for complex multi-criteria searches.

docs.title: Find specific addresses
docs.text:
I2C address search:

Search: 0x50
Field: Address
Result: All transactions to/from device 0x50

docs.title: Locate error conditions
docs.text:
Search: NACK
Field: Status
Result: All transactions with NACK (Not Acknowledged)

docs.title: Find data patterns
docs.text:
Search: FF
Field: Data
Result: All transactions containing 0xFF

docs.title: Debug specific commands
docs.text:
SPI command search:

Search: 0x03
Field: Command
Result: All READ operations (command 0x03)

docs.title: Trace register access
docs.text:
Search: 0x1A
Field: Address
Result: All accesses to register 0x1A

docs.title: For large captures
docs.text:
Speed up searches:

  1. Use field specification: Don't search all fields if you know which field contains your data
  2. Be specific: More specific search terms = fewer false matches
  3. Close unused windows: Reduce system load
  4. Consider filtering: Use Hide Data to filter before searching

docs.title: For repeated searches
docs.text:
Workflow:

  1. Perform common searches
  2. Note the row numbers
  3. Use bookmarks (Window Management) to mark important results
  4. Return to bookmarks instead of re-searching

docs.title: Troubleshooting communication failures
docs.text:
Find failed transactions:

  1. Search for error indicators: NACK, ERR, FAIL
  2. Check address field for problem device
  3. Use Previous to find the last successful transaction before failure

docs.title: Verifying protocol compliance
docs.text:
Check for specific sequences:

  1. Search for initialization commands
  2. Verify proper ordering
  3. Check response codes

docs.title: Data validation
docs.text:
Find specific data values:

  1. Search for expected data pattern
  2. Verify correct transmission
  3. Check for corruption or errors

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Search operates on displayed/decoded data only
  • Raw waveform data is not searchable (use Logic Analyzer search for signal-level search)
  • Very large captures may take time to search
  • Search is sequential (not indexed)

docs.title: SGMII (Serial Gigabit Media Independent Interface)
docs.text:
SGMII Protocol Analyzer settings. SGMII analysis shows two layers: line-side PCS (Physical Coding Sublayer / PHY) and MAC-side GMII (Gigabit Media Independent Interface). Decide which layer you need before setting triggers.

For application notes, probe connection, and measurement details, see Protocol Solution — SGMII.

docs.title: BusFinder
docs.text: BF6000 is supported only on B series, all BF7000 models are supported. This feature requires purchasing an additional option.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
SGMII Protocol Analyzer settings (BusFinder / LA3000/LA4000 series)
  • Settings:
    • SGMII probe settings: Shows the Acute SGMII Way Station pinout (e.g. TX0p/TX0n, RX0p/RX0n, RefClk). Swap Lane p/n to match differential wiring. SGMII uses 8b/10b, so the analyzer can usually recover the clock from the differential data and a Reference clock (RefClk) is optional. If the DUT provides RefClk and you want the analyzer to use that external reference, wire it to the Way Station RefClk port and enable Ref. Clock. Default: Ref. Clock cleared.
    • Startup Settings — Packet Speed: Sets the initial packet speed (1000/100/10 Mbps). A wrong setting can inflate decoded data volume by about 10×/100×. If a Speed Config packet appears during capture, the speed follows that Config afterward. Default: 1000 Mbps.
    • Filter: Drop unneeded traffic to save memory.
      • Data filter > N bytes: Truncate long packet payloads (about 14–1475 bytes). CRC is unavailable while enabled; keep Address and Ethertype. Default: cleared, N = 14.
      • Idle filter: Drop Idle symbols so idle traffic does not fill memory. Default: cleared.

  • Trigger settings:

    • Trigger On: When enabled, trigger by Direction (e.g. TX Only / RX Only). SGMII analysis shows two layers: line-side PCS and MAC-side GMII. Trigger on events/errors at either layer, or use Data Trigger for detailed pattern matching. Default: Trigger On cleared; Direction TX Only; all PCS/GMII event and error items cleared.
      • PCS (Physical Coding Sublayer, PHY side): Handles 8b/10b coding, K codes, and link-control symbols on the serial wire. Typical triggers: Start/End of Packet, Carrier Extend, Propagation Error, Disparity Error, Not in Table (illegal code group), and Configuration (ordered sets used for link/speed setup). Default: all items cleared.
      • GMII (Gigabit Media Independent Interface, MAC side): Frame data between MAC and PHY. Typical triggers: Frame Error and CRC Error. Default: all items cleared.
      • Data Trigger: Opens SGMII Data Trigger Settings. Choose PCS Configuration to catch link-setup traffic, or GMII Data to match Ethernet frame content (see the dialog notes below). Default: cleared; when opened, PCS Configuration is selected.
        • Direction for Data: Choose which direction to match (e.g. TX Only). Default: TX Only.
        • PCS Configuration Register: Trigger on PCS Configuration values (PCS control information for link/speed negotiation), not ordinary data packets. XXXXh means don't care. Default: XXXXh.
        • GMII Data: The gear opens GMII Trigger Settings to match MAC frame fields (addresses / Ethertype / data). Dialog Default: address/Data bytes XXh, Ethertype XXXXh, Data Offset cleared (offset 0). Open SGMII Data Trigger Settings from Trigger On → Data Trigger when you need a detailed match on a chosen direction, not only a general PCS/GMII event:

  • Direction for Data: Choose which direction to match (e.g. TX Only). Default: TX Only.

  • PCS Configuration Register: Trigger on PCS Configuration values — PCS/PHY-side control information used for link negotiation and speed setup, not ordinary user data packets. XXXXh means don't care. Default: XXXXh. Use this when you want to catch how the link/speed is being configured.
  • GMII Data: Match GMII/MAC-side Ethernet frame content (addresses, Ethertype, payload) instead; use the gear for the next dialog. Use this when you want a specific device or protocol frame.

SGMII: SGMII Data Trigger Settings (Data Trigger)

Open GMII Trigger Settings from the gear next to GMII Data to combine Ethernet frame fields (for example a specific destination, Ethertype, or payload pattern):

  • Destination / Source Address: 6-byte MACs; XXh means that byte is don't care. Default: each byte XXh.
  • Ethertype/Length: 2 bytes (XXXXh = don't care) to lock a protocol type or length field. Default: XXXXh.
  • Data (Byte 1–8): Up to 8 hex bytes of payload pattern to match (for example AAh 55h …); XXh means that byte is don't care. Enable Data Offset to start matching at a byte offset when the target data is not at the start of the payload. Default: each byte XXh; Data Offset cleared, offset 0.
  • Default: Restore the default (all don't-care) condition.

SGMII: GMII Trigger Settings (GMII Data)
