docs.title: Show waveforms
docs.text: Enable waveform display alongside protocol decode for signal-level visibility.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: By default, Protocol Analyzer shows only the decoded protocol report. Enabling Show Waveforms adds a waveform view, allowing you to see the actual signal transitions alongside the protocol decode.

docs.title: Enabling Show Waveforms
docs.text:
Select the Show Waveforms option before starting capture.

Memory impact:

  • Requires additional device memory to store waveform data
  • Reduces the total number of protocol transactions that can be captured
  • Memory is divided between decode data and waveform data

docs.title: Available features
docs.text: When Show Waveforms is enabled, the waveform area provides additional functions:

docs.title: 1. Bus decode button
docs.text:
Refresh bus decode

Manually refresh or update the bus decode after capture completes.

Use cases:

  • Reprocess decode with different parameters
  • Update decode after changing settings
  • Verify decode accuracy

docs.title: 2. Stop bus decode button
docs.text:
Stop the bus decode process immediately.

Use cases:

  • Lengthy decode is taking too long
  • Want to start analysis before decode completes
  • Decode parameters need changing

docs.title: 3. Add user notes
docs.text:
Add annotations and comments directly in the waveform area.

Features:

  • Text notes at specific time positions
  • Visual markers for important events
  • Documentation for later review

Use cases:

  • Mark interesting protocol transactions
  • Note signal anomalies
  • Document test conditions

docs.title: 4. Waveform zoom
docs.text:
Scale waveforms in and out for detailed inspection.

Methods:

  • Toolbar button: Click zoom in/out buttons
  • Mouse wheel (recommended): Scroll to zoom smoothly
  • Keyboard: Number Pad + / Number Pad -

Tips:

  • Mouse wheel zoom is most convenient
  • Zoom focuses on cursor or mouse position
  • Combine zoom with panning for efficient navigation

docs.title: Convert to Logic Analyzer
docs.text:
Requirement: Show Waveforms must be enabled

After capturing protocol data with waveforms:

  1. Click Convert to Logic Analyzer in the File menu
  2. Waveform data and settings transfer to Logic Analyzer window
  3. Continue using full Logic Analyzer capabilities

What transfers:

  • Captured waveform data
  • Channel assignments
  • Threshold settings
  • Trigger position

Benefits:

  • Seamless transition between protocol and signal analysis
  • No need to recapture data
  • Preserve existing decode results

See: File Operations - Convert to Logic Analyzer

docs.title: Stack Oscilloscope
docs.text:
Requirements:

  • Show Waveforms must be enabled
  • Capture protocol data with waveforms
  • Supported oscilloscope connected

Workflow:

  1. Enable Show Waveforms in Protocol Analyzer
  2. Configure and start capture
  3. After capture, click the DSO icon
  4. System enters Logic Analyzer window
  5. Configure oscilloscope stack connection
  6. View protocol decode with analog waveforms

See: File Operations - Stack Oscilloscope

docs.title: Cursor operations
docs.text:
Requirement: Show Waveforms must be enabled

When waveforms are displayed, cursor functions become available:

  • Place cursors: Measure time intervals
  • Cursor navigation: Jump between interesting points
  • Waveform search: Find edges, values, or patterns

See: Cursor

docs.title: Protocol Report (default)
docs.text:
Advantages:

  • Uses less memory
  • Captures more protocol transactions
  • Faster post-processing
  • Focuses on protocol-level issues

Best for:

  • Protocol-level debugging
  • High-speed protocol capture
  • Long-duration captures
  • When timing isn't critical

docs.title: Waveforms enabled
docs.text:
Advantages:

  • See signal quality and timing
  • Measure precise timing relationships
  • Detect signal integrity issues
  • Convert to Logic Analyzer for detailed analysis

Best for:

  • Signal integrity analysis
  • Mixed protocol/signal debugging
  • Understanding timing issues
  • When you might need signal-level detail

docs.title: Memory usage
docs.text:
With Show Waveforms:

  • ~50-70% reduction in protocol transaction capacity
  • Depends on sample rate and channel count
  • Higher sample rates use more memory

Without Show Waveforms:

  • Maximum protocol transaction capacity
  • Memory used only for decode data
  • Optimal for pure protocol analysis

docs.title: Processing time
docs.text:
With Show Waveforms:

  • Longer post-processing time
  • Waveform rendering overhead
  • Decode + waveform display

Without Show Waveforms:

  • Faster post-processing
  • Decode-only processing
  • Faster display updates

docs.title: Enable Show Waveforms when:
docs.text:
• You might need signal-level detail
  • Debugging both protocol and signal issues
  • Want option to convert to Logic Analyzer
  • Planning to use Stack Oscilloscope
  • Signal timing is important
  • Unknown issue - might need multiple analysis approaches

docs.title: Disable Show Waveforms when:
docs.text:
• Pure protocol analysis
  • Need maximum transaction capture
  • Long-duration captures
  • High-speed protocols
  • Memory is limited
  • Faster processing is priority
  • Signal quality is known good

docs.title: Decision workflow
docs.text:
Ask yourself:

  1. Do I need signal timing information? → Enable
  2. Might I need to use Logic Analyzer features? → Enable
  3. Do I need maximum protocol transaction capture? → Disable
  4. Is this a quick protocol debug session? → Disable

docs.title: Hybrid approach
docs.text:
First capture: Disable Show Waveforms for quick protocol analysis

If issues found: Enable Show Waveforms and recapture to investigate signal-level details

This two-stage approach maximizes efficiency while maintaining flexibility.

SMBus Protocol Analyzer settings (TravelLogic series)

  • Clock stretching: Enable detection of clock stretching. Default: cleared.

  • Timeout check (Range: 0 ns ~ 67 ms): Flag a stretch that exceeds the allowed duration. When checked, the value field is enabled (Enable) — enter ns (about 0–67 ms); when cleared the value field is disabled (Disable). Default: cleared, value empty.

SPI Protocol Analyzer settings (TravelLogic series)

    • Clock Latch: Rising / Falling data latch edge. A wrong setting can shift decoding. Default: Rising.
    • Chip Select: Active Low / Active High. Default: Active Low.
    • Data Bits: Data bits per character (4–8). Default: 8.

    • Word Wrap: How decoded results wrap/segment. 8 data wraps every 8 data words; All block data shows a whole transfer block (e.g. one CS-active period). Default: 8 data.

docs.text:
UART Protocol Analyzer settings (TravelLogic series)
  • Settings:
    • Baud Rate: Bit rate in bps. A wrong setting can scramble decoding; choose from the list (some UIs also offer waveform-assisted baud detection). Default: 9600.
    • Data Bits: Data bits per character (4–16). Default: 8.
    • Parity: None / Odd / Even / Mark / Space. A wrong setting can produce parity errors or wrong characters. Default: None.
    • Stop Bits: Stop-bit count (1–4.5, including 1.5 / 2.5, etc.). Default: 1.
    • Polarity: Voltage level when Idle. Idle High is a common setting; Idle Low is for inverted signaling. A wrong setting inverts Start/Stop detection. Default: Idle High.
    • Line Wrap: Controls how decoded results wrap/segment in the report (not a hardware trigger).
      • Data Length > N bytes: Wrap when consecutive data exceeds N bytes (slider range about 1–128). Default: 2 bytes.
      • Idle, Break: Wrap on Idle or Break so one burst is separated from the next. Default: checked.
      • Data pattern: Wrap on a data pattern. Enable and set 1st […] h; optionally enable 2nd […] h to wrap on the 1st→2nd sequence. Default: cleared (1st/2nd = 00h).

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
UFS Protocol Analyzer settings (BusFinder)
  • Settings:
    • Connection: Select how BF7264B+ / Pro connects to the DUT (for example UFS Fixture).
    • Startup: Startup conditions of the DUT at capture time.
      • Mode: Startup mode (for example PWM). Default: PWM.
      • Lane: Number of lanes (for example 1 Lane / 2 Lane). Default: 1 Lane.
      • Gear: Gear for the selected mode (for example PWM-Gear1). Default: PWM-Gear1.
      • Reference Clock: Reference clock frequency (19.2 / 26 / 38.4 / 52 MHz). This value must be set correctly even if RefClk is not connected; otherwise analysis may fail.
    • UFS Probe Settings: Probe / lane wiring settings.
      • Way Station pinout for each lane (TX/RX p, n, RefClk, etc.); swap p/n per lane as wired.
      • Show RefClk: Show RefClk measurement data in the result. Default: cleared.
      • UFS-tip Settings: Open the UFS-tip Settings dialog (see below) for tip pin options. Default: all items cleared.
        • Reset pin (CH4): Enable UFS Reset pin detection. Reset must connect to UFS probe LA tip CH4; when Reset is seen, Power mode is reset to PWM mode.
        • Show Volt. Detect Ch — VCC(A0) / VCCQ2(A1): Show tip voltage-detect channels A0 / A1 (VCC / VCCQ2; used with voltage-drop trigger — see Settings — Voltage Range Settings).
    • Filter: With Data Filter enabled, the length field is enabled (Enable); drop trailing payload beyond the set byte length. Default: cleared (about 256 bytes when enabled).
    • Option:
      • Force Off Descramble: Skip descramble and show scrambled data only. Default: cleared.
      • Ignore Error when 'Data Frame TC0' Size > 'UPIU' Size: Ignore that size mismatch error when checked. Default: checked.
    • Detail Report Display: Detail report presentation. Default: Table only.
      • Table + Text: Table plus textual decode.
      • Table only: Table only.
  • Trigger settings:
    • Trigger On: Up to 8 trigger conditions. Main Default does not reset the trigger list.
      • Unipro / UFS packets, SCSI Command items (for example Any UFS packets or a specific SCSI command).
      • Unknown Packet / CRC Error: Trigger on unknown packets or CRC errors.
      • VCC(A0) Drop / VCCQ2(A1) Drop: Voltage-drop trigger; open Voltage Range Settings (see Settings — Voltage Range Settings). Typical VCC about 2.70–3.60 V, VCCQ2 about 1.70–1.95 V.
      • Clear All: Clear configured triggers.

Open this dialog from UFS Probe Settings → UFS-tip Settings. The left side shows the tip pinout (including CH4 / A0 / A1). Enable Reset pin (CH4) and, under Show Volt. Detect Ch, VCC(A0) / VCCQ2(A1) as needed. Dialog Default: all items cleared.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
SD 4.0 (UHS-II) Protocol Analyzer settings (BusFinder / LA3000/LA4000 series)
  • Settings:
    • Sample Rate: Select the sample rate. Default: 2 GHz.
    • Primary Protocol Analyzer: SD 4 Probe for SD 4.0 (UHS-II).
    • Secondary Protocol Analyzer or I/O: NAND Flash or I/O on remaining pins.
    • Log Filter: Filter by packet type (SYN, BSYN, DIR, LIDL, DIDL, EIDL, …). When length filtering is checked, Data Length > is enabled (Enable). Default: packet types cleared, length filter cleared.
    • VDD Detect: When checked, show VDD voltage in the report. Display only — no trigger capability (unlike Trigger On VDD1/VDD2 Drop). Default: checked. See also Settings — Voltage Detect.
  • Trigger settings:
    • Trigger On: When checked, child items are enabled (Enable); first check often opens the matching dialog (see dialogs below). Default: Trigger On and all children cleared.
      • CM TRAN: CCMD / DCMD / MSG / RES triggers.
        • CCMD: Opens Trigger On CM-TRAN (CCMD). Default: Read Only; I/O Address XXXh; Payload cleared (field disabled (Disable), typically XXXXXXXXh).
        • DCMD: Opens Trigger On CM-TRAN (DCMD). Default: Read Only; TMode Xh; Data Address cleared (field disabled (Disable), typically XXXXXXXXh).
        • MSG: Opens Trigger On Message Packet (MSG). Default: packet type All; Check Direction Any.
        • RES: Opens Trigger On CM-TRAN (RES). Default: NACK = 1 (I/O Address / Payload then disabled (Disable)).
      • SD TRAN: CCMD/DCMD and RES (NACK / No RES); command/response setup opens Legacy SD Trigger Settings. Choosing NACK may disable (Disable) the RES setup button. Default: No RES.
      • Error / Busy / Voltage: CRC16, Packet Type Error, CMD25/18/38 Busy Period, VDD1/VDD2 Drop. Busy Period dialog Default about 10 ms. Default: all cleared.
        • VDD1 Drop / VDD2 Drop: Voltage-drop trigger; open Voltage Range Settings (see Settings — Voltage Range Settings). Typical VDD1 about 2.70–3.60 V, VDD2 about 1.70–1.95 V.

Open this dialog from Trigger On → CM TRAN → CCMD. Choose Read Only / Write Only / Read or Write, and set I/O Address (12 bits). When Payload is checked, the 32-bit field is enabled (Enable). XXXh / XXXXXXXXh means don't care for that field.

SD 4.0 (UHS-II): Trigger On CM-TRAN (CCMD)

Open this dialog from Trigger On → CM TRAN → DCMD. Choose Read / Write, set TMode (4 bits), and optionally enable Data Address (32 bits). Xh / XXXXXXXXh means don't care for that field.

SD 4.0 (UHS-II): Trigger On CM-TRAN (DCMD)

Open this dialog from Trigger On → CM TRAN → MSG. Select a Message Packet type (All, FCREQ/FCRDY Unrecoverable, AMSG Memory, STAT, …) and filter by Check Direction (Any / From Host / From Card).

SD 4.0 (UHS-II): Trigger On Message Packet (MSG)

Open this dialog from Trigger On → CM TRAN → RES. Choose NACK = 1 or NACK = 0. With NACK = 1, I/O Address / Payload are disabled (Disable).

SD 4.0 (UHS-II): Trigger On CM-TRAN (RES)

Open Legacy SD Trigger Settings when configuring an SD TRAN command. Choose Any Command (or a specific command) and combine r / A / Command / Stuff Bits fields. X / XXh means don't care for that field.

SD 4.0 (UHS-II): Legacy SD Trigger Settings (Any Command)

Open the same dialog for an SD TRAN response (for example SD R1). Combine R1 status bits and CUR_STATE. X / Xh / XXh means don't care for that field.

SD 4.0 (UHS-II): Legacy SD Trigger Settings (SD R1)

Open this dialog from Trigger On when CMD25 Busy Period is selected. The diagram shows the Write Multiple Block busy period; set Check on Busy Period > (Default about 10 ms).

SD 4.0 (UHS-II): Busy Period Settings (CMD25)

Open this dialog from Trigger On when CMD18 Busy Period is selected. The diagram shows the Read Multiple Block busy period; set Check on Busy Period > (Default about 10 ms).

SD 4.0 (UHS-II): Busy Period Settings (CMD18)

Open this dialog from Trigger On when CMD38 Busy Period is selected. The diagram shows the Erase busy period; set Check on Busy Period > (Default about 10 ms).

SD 4.0 (UHS-II): Busy Period Settings (CMD38)

docs.title: Window management
docs.text: Manage report views, bookmarks, and navigation tools for efficient analysis.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Window management features help you navigate large protocol captures and organize data for analysis.

docs.title: Report lists
docs.text: Select which report views to display.

docs.title: Available report lists
docs.text:
Options:

  • Report List: Standard decode report
  • Show Both Report: Display multiple report types simultaneously
  • Transition Report: Show signal transition data (requires Show Waveforms)
  • Statistics: Protocol-specific statistics
  • Custom views: Protocol-dependent additional views

docs.title: Position controls
docs.text:
Use control buttons to navigate the report:

Functions:

  • First: Jump to the first row
  • Previous: Move to previous row
  • Next: Move to next row
  • Last: Jump to the last row
  • Go to row: Input row number to jump directly to that position

Keyboard alternatives:

  • Home: Jump to first row
  • End: Jump to last row
  • Arrow keys: Move up/down one row
  • Page Up/Down: Scroll by page

docs.title: To bottom button
docs.text:
Move directly to the end of captured data.

Static data: Jumps to the last line

During capture: Displays the most up-to-date data in real-time

Use cases:

  • Monitor live capture progress
  • Check most recent protocol activity
  • Verify capture is still running
  • Jump to end of large capture

docs.title: Bookmark list
docs.text: Mark important rows for quick reference.

docs.title: Adding bookmarks
docs.text:
Methods:

  1. Select a row in the report
  2. Click Add to Bookmark List button
  3. The row is added to the bookmark list with its row number and key information

Keyboard shortcut: Check for available shortcut in your software version

docs.title: Using bookmarks
docs.text:
Bookmark list displays:

  • Row number
  • Key protocol information (address, data, status)
  • Timestamp
  • Any custom notes (if supported)

Navigate to bookmarks:

  • Click on a bookmark entry
  • Report jumps to that row
  • Highlighted for easy identification

docs.title: Removing bookmarks
docs.text:
Methods:

  1. Select bookmark in the bookmark list
  2. Click Remove from Bookmark List button
  3. Bookmark is deleted (captured data remains unchanged)

docs.title: Managing bookmarks
docs.text:
Tips:

  • Add bookmarks as you analyze
  • Use bookmarks to mark errors, interesting transactions, or key events
  • Bookmarks persist when you save the file
  • Review bookmark list to see overview of important events

docs.title: Report list advanced features
docs.text: Detailed report list functionality for in-depth analysis.

docs.title: Display configuration
docs.text:
Configure display:

  1. Select display list: Choose which report type to show
  2. Column selection: Enable/disable specific columns
  3. Row filtering: Show/hide specific transaction types
  4. Sorting: Sort by column (if supported)

docs.title: Position tracking
docs.text:
Row number display:

Enable "Display row number in LA Decode Report" in system environment settings to show row numbers on the left side of the report area.

Benefits:

  • Easy reference to specific transactions
  • Better communication when discussing results ("see row 1523")
  • Simpler bookmark management
  • Easier navigation in large captures

docs.title: Search integration
docs.text:
The report list integrates with Search functionality:

Workflow:

  1. Perform search
  2. Search highlights matches in report list
  3. Use search navigation to move between matches
  4. Bookmark important search results for later reference
  5. Clear search to return to normal view

docs.title: Statistics window integration
docs.text:
Access detailed statistics through the window management interface.

Statistics features:

  • Protocol-specific traffic analysis
  • Error rate calculation
  • Transaction counts
  • Timing statistics

Click on statistic trace:

  • Summarizes all records of the selected trace
  • Displays in statistic list window
  • Allows detailed analysis of specific event types

See: Detail & Statistics

docs.title: Working with multiple reports
docs.text:
Common setup:

  1. Main report: Full decode report
  2. Bookmark list: Important events
  3. Statistics window: Traffic analysis
  4. Detail window: Inspect specific transactions

Layout tips:

  • Arrange windows for your workflow
  • Use multiple monitors if available
  • Save layout preferences (if supported)

docs.title: Cross-referencing
docs.text:
Efficient analysis:

  1. Use statistics to identify issues
  2. Bookmark interesting transactions
  3. Navigate between bookmarks
  4. Use search to find related transactions
  5. Export relevant data for documentation

docs.title: Bookmark strategy
docs.text:
During capture analysis:

  • Bookmark first error
  • Bookmark pattern changes
  • Bookmark unexpected events
  • Bookmark known-good transactions for comparison

Review workflow:

  1. Scan statistics for anomalies
  2. Bookmark anomalies
  3. Use detail window to investigate
  4. Search for related transactions
  5. Document findings using notes or export

docs.title: Navigation efficiency
docs.text:
For large captures:

  • Use "Go to row" for quick jumps
  • Bookmarks for key positions
  • Search for specific data
  • To bottom for latest activity
  • Statistics for overview before diving into detail

docs.title: Organization
docs.text:
Keep captures organized:

  • Use meaningful bookmark names/notes
  • Export bookmark lists with captures
  • Document important row numbers in external notes
  • Save captures with bookmarks for future reference

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Protocol Analyzer settings. Review the common rules and product-family UI differences below, then select a protocol from the left menu for parameter details.

docs.title: Protocol select (common)
docs.text:
After you select a protocol, the settings dialog typically includes:

Protocol select / settings dialog (TravelBus I2C example)

1. Channel: Assign protocol signals to channels or interfaces (UI differs by product family; see below).

2. Waveform preview: The software can automatically detect and show the signal waveform and maximum frequency. The preview bar shows the selected clock channel and the measured bus frequency (KHz). It displays --- KHz when no signal is detected.

3. Options: Protocol packet format or analysis parameters.

4. Trigger Level / Threshold: Set the trigger voltage for the signal level. A common recommendation is about half the DUT operating voltage. Adjust with the slider or by entering a value, or use Quick Setup to apply a preset for common Vcc levels, for example:

  • Vcc 5 V → Threshold 2.5 V
  • Vcc 3.3 V → Threshold 1.6 V
  • Vcc 1.8 V → Threshold 0.9 V

This works the same across product families and is not repeated on each protocol page.

docs.title: Product-family UI differences
docs.text:
Protocol Analyzer settings differ mainly in the Channel area by product family. The following examples use I2C.

  • BusFinder 6000/7000 series, LA3000/LA4000 series These instruments have Slot A and B (some models also have Slot C and D). Channel numbers are shown as “slot letter + channel index”; for example A0 means channel 0 on Slot A, and B31 means channel 31 on Slot B.

Channel UI example (BusFinder 6000/7000, LA3000/LA4000) — I2C (example: SCK = A0, SDA = A1)
  • MSO2000/3000 series, TravelScope 3000 series, TravelLogic 3000/4000 series Assign signals by logic channel number. For Voltage Detect on supported TravelLogic models, see Voltage Detect at the end of this page.

Channel UI example (MSO2000/3000, TravelScope 3000, TravelLogic 3000/4000) — I2C
  • TravelBus 1000/2000/3000 series Choose the dedicated I2C interface or the general LA interface. The I2C interface shows the instrument pin map; the LA interface uses general logic channels numbered on the cable.

Channel UI example (TravelBus 1000/2000/3000) — I2C
  • PX2000 series First select the device / Pod (for example PX POD), then assign PX channels (for example PX-00, PX-01).

Channel UI example (PX2000) — I2C

On each protocol page:

  • Protocols available on all product lines use a TravelLogic screenshot as the representative UI.
  • Protocols limited to a specific line (for example BusFinder only) use that product's screenshot.
  • Channel differences, waveform preview, Trigger Level, Voltage Detect, and Voltage Range Settings (voltage-drop trigger) are covered in the common sections above.
  • Dialogs used only by SD 3.0 / eMMC (but shared between them)—Vendor CMD, Trigger Settings, Data Trigger, Timeout Trigger—are under Shared SD / eMMC dialogs below and are not repeated on each protocol page.

docs.title: Voltage Detect
docs.text: Voltage Detect (VCC(A0), VDD(A1))

docs.title: Supported models
docs.text: Voltage Detect is available only on TravelLogic and LA3000 / LA4000 / BusFinder.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
The cable marks these pins with A0 and A1 stickers. Some protocols expose Voltage Detect in Options, with checkboxes such as VCC(A0) and VDD(A1) to enable those pins as voltage-detect channels.

In the Protocol Analyzer report window, the software shows the voltage measured on those pins. The sampling interval is about 1 µs.

Use it to monitor the supply state of an external circuit—for example, when the DUT suddenly loses power, the drop can be detected and shown on screen.

docs.title: Voltage Range Settings (voltage-drop trigger)
docs.text:
Some protocols offer voltage-drop triggers under Trigger on / Trigger On (for example VCC Drop, VDD Drop, VCC(A0) Drop, VDD1 Drop). Selecting one opens Voltage Range Settings.

Set the voltage check range graphically (e.g. 2.7 V < VDD1 < 3.6 V). Out-of-range zones are shown with red hatching. Use Default to restore the factory range. Default limits may differ by protocol—follow that protocol’s dialog or Default.

Voltage Range Settings (voltage-drop trigger)

docs.title: Shared SD / eMMC dialogs
docs.text: The following dialogs appear only for SD 3.0, eMMC, and related timeout settings. The UI and workflow are shared; protocol pages link here instead of repeating the details.

docs.title: Vendor CMD settings
docs.text:
Open from Option → Vendor CMD. Customize Vendor CMD name, Response, Read/Write, and Data Size from Original CMD. Manage the list with ADD / DEL / Del All.

Default is often Original/Vendor CMD00 GO_IDLE_STATE, Response NO_RESP, Read/Write Read, Data Size No data.

Vendor CMD settings

docs.title: Trigger Settings (Command / Response)
docs.text:
Open from Trigger on when Command/Response (or eMMC CMD / RESP.) is selected. Choose Any Command (or a specific command) and combine S/T/Command/Stuff Bits/CRC/E fields. XXh means don't care. S/T/E are often fixed (S=0, T=1, E=1); Description appears on the right.

Trigger Settings (Any Command)

docs.title: Data Trigger
docs.text:
Open from Trigger on when Data is selected. Optionally start after READ (CMD17/18), WRITE (CMD24/25), or a custom command, then set match / NOT match, Pattern Size, and byte patterns. XXh means don't care for that byte.

Default: start conditions cleared; Trigger when pattern(s) match; Pattern Size often 8 bytes; bytes mostly XXh.

Data Trigger

docs.title: Timeout Trigger
docs.text:
Open from Trigger on → Timeout (mainly eMMC; related SD/MMC timeout settings are the same). Choose Data timeout after CMD/DATA, Data IDLE timeout before CRC status, Busy timeout after CRC Status, or Busy timeout After CMD, and set the time threshold and unit.

Default is often Data timeout after CMD/DATA with > 5 ns; Command filter Default often Cmd 17 / 18 / 24 / 25.

Timeout Trigger

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Protocol Exerciser mode allows you to generate, send, and receive protocol traffic for testing and debugging bus communications.

Protocol Exerciser transforms your TravelLogic device into a protocol generator and receiver. You can act as a controller, target, or both simultaneously, making it ideal for:

  • Testing protocol implementations without full system
  • Debugging communication issues
  • Validating device responses
  • Simulating missing components
  • Automated protocol testing

docs.title: Device and protocol selection
docs.text:
Select which protocol to use from the dropdown list. You can only use one protocol at a time.

Supported protocols:

  • I2C
  • MIPI I3C
  • UART

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Opens the topology dialog for the current protocol. Configure bus topology, nodes, addresses, and communication parameters.

See protocol-specific documentation for detailed configuration:

  • I2C Configuration
  • MIPI I3C Configuration
  • UART Configuration

docs.title: Power supply
docs.text:
Control and monitor the DC power output while using Protocol Exerciser.

Controls:

  1. Set voltage value: Adjust output voltage for your device
  2. Auto-off on close: When checked, DC output turns off automatically when the dialog is closed
  3. DC output on/off: Enable or disable the DC output
  4. Monitoring on/off: Enable or disable voltage and current monitoring
  5. Monitoring time interval: Set how frequently to update measurements
  6. Monitor window: Displays real-time voltage and current readings

Features:

  • Independent display window that can remain visible during operation
  • Real-time monitoring of voltage and current
  • Ensures proper power delivery to devices under test

docs.title: Start/Stop capture
docs.text:
Start or stop Logic Analyzer and Protocol Analyzer capture operations.

Use this to:

  • Capture traffic generated by Protocol Exerciser
  • Record bus activity during testing
  • Verify protocol transactions
  • Debug communication issues

docs.title: Wizard
docs.text:
Opens the protocol wizard dialog for sending packets on the current protocol.

Each protocol has a specific wizard interface tailored to its features:

  • I2C Wizard - Send READ/WRITE transactions
  • I3C Wizard - Send CCC commands and transfers
  • UART Wizard - Transmit UART data

docs.title: Loop
docs.text:
You can set a loop count to send the packets repeatedly.

The following uses I3C as an example.

Set this value to loop all the packets (every black block).

Or loop just one group of packets (inside a single black block).

You can also loop a single frame.

docs.title: Supported protocols
docs.text: Protocol Exerciser currently supports the following protocols. Click each link for detailed documentation:

docs.title: I2C
docs.text:
• Controller and Target modes
  • 7-bit and 10-bit addressing
  • Internal node simulation
  • Quick send wizard
  • Packet constructor

docs.title: MIPI I3C
docs.text:
• Controller and Target modes
  • Dynamic address assignment
  • CCC (Common Command Codes)
  • Broadcast and direct commands
  • Advanced timing configuration

docs.title: UART
docs.text: Note: UART protocol documentation is in development.

docs.title: Quick start workflow
docs.text:
1. Select protocol: Choose from the Device and Protocol dropdown
  2. Configure topology: Click Settings to set up bus configuration
  3. Optional - Enable power: Use Power Supply to power your device
  4. Start capture: Click Start Capture to begin recording
  5. Send packets: Use Wizard to generate protocol traffic
  6. Analyze: Review captured data in Logic Analyzer or Protocol Analyzer

docs.title: Protocol selection
docs.text:
• Choose the protocol that matches your device under test
  • Configure all settings before starting capture
  • Test with known-good devices first to verify configuration

docs.title: Power supply
docs.text:
• Always verify voltage requirements before enabling output
  • Monitor current draw to detect shorts or connection issues
  • Use auto-off feature to prevent accidental voltage application

docs.title: Capture integration
docs.text:
• Start capture before sending packets to record complete transactions
  • Use Protocol Analyzer for protocol-level decode
  • Use Logic Analyzer for signal timing analysis

docs.title: Add internal node
docs.text: Create virtual I2C target devices to simulate multi-device scenarios.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Internal nodes are virtual I2C devices that respond to bus transactions. They allow you to test controller behavior without connecting physical devices.

After configuration: Press the Assign button to activate the internal node on the bus.

docs.title: 1. Name
docs.text:
Set a descriptive name for this internal node for easy identification.

Examples:

  • "EEPROM_1"
  • "Temperature_Sensor"
  • "RTC"
  • "Test_Device_0x50"

docs.title: 2. Address type
docs.text:
Select the addressing mode for this node.

Current support: 7-bit addressing mode only

Future versions may support:

  • 10-bit addressing
  • Additional I2C extensions

docs.title: 3. Address settings
docs.text: Choose the addressing range for this internal node:

docs.title: I2C standard address
docs.text:
Restricts address to the standard I2C device range: 0x08 to 0x77

Use this mode to:

  • Follow I2C specification
  • Avoid reserved addresses
  • Ensure compatibility with all controllers

docs.title: I2C address (include reserved address)
docs.text:
Allows the full address range: 0x00 to 0x7F

Reserved addresses to note:

  • 0x00: General call address
  • 0x01-0x07: CBUS, different bus format, reserved
  • 0x78-0x7F: 10-bit addressing, reserved

Use this mode to:

  • Test reserved address handling
  • Use general call functionality
  • Advanced protocol testing

docs.title: 4. Address value
docs.text:
Enter the specific I2C address for this internal node.

Guidelines:

  • Must be unique among all nodes on the bus
  • Must fall within the selected address range
  • Avoid conflicts with external devices

docs.title: Register settings
docs.text: Configure the internal node's register behavior.

docs.title: 1. Register type
docs.text:
Set the register depth for the internal node.

Current support: 32-bit register only

What this means: The internal node simulates a device with 32-bit register storage.

docs.title: 2. Sub-address type
docs.text: Configure whether the internal node uses sub-addressing (register addressing).

docs.title: Without sub-address
docs.text:
Internal node does not use sub-addressing.

Behavior:

  • Simpler protocol
  • Direct data READ/WRITE without register selection
  • Suitable for simple I2C devices

docs.title: 8-bit sub-address
docs.text:
Internal node uses 8-bit sub-addressing for register access.

Current support: 8-bit sub-address only

Behavior:

  • First byte after address is the sub-address (register address)
  • Subsequent bytes are data for that register
  • Matches common EEPROM and sensor behavior

docs.title: 3. Sub-address data format
docs.text:
Configure how the internal node handles sub-addresses during multi-byte transactions.

Availability: Only when 8-bit Sub-Address is selected

docs.title: Repeat sub-address
docs.text:
Sub-address remains the same for all bytes in the transaction.

Use case: Reading or writing multiple bytes to/from the same register

Example: Write 4 bytes to register 0x10 - Byte 1 → Register 0x10 - Byte 2 → Register 0x10 - Byte 3 → Register 0x10 - Byte 4 → Register 0x10

docs.title: Increment sub-address
docs.text:
Sub-address increments by 1 for each byte in the transaction.

Use case: Sequential register access (common in EEPROMs)

Example: Write 4 bytes starting at register 0x10 - Byte 1 → Register 0x10 - Byte 2 → Register 0x11 - Byte 3 → Register 0x12 - Byte 4 → Register 0x13

docs.title: Increment loop sub-address
docs.text:
Sub-address increments and wraps around at register boundary.

Use case: Circular buffer access or page-based EEPROMs

Example: Write 4 bytes starting at register 0xFE (assuming 8-bit register space) - Byte 1 → Register 0xFE - Byte 2 → Register 0xFF - Byte 3 → Register 0x00 (wraps around) - Byte 4 → Register 0x01

docs.title: Ignore sub-address
docs.text:
Sub-address byte is acknowledged but ignored. All data goes to the same location.

Use case: Testing controller behavior when target doesn't implement sub-addressing properly

docs.title: Choosing address format
docs.text:
• Use Standard address range for normal testing
  • Use Include reserved range only when testing edge cases or protocol extensions

docs.title: Sub-addressing
docs.text:
• Increment mode is most common (EEPROMs, flash)
  • Repeat mode for FIFO-like devices
  • Loop mode for circular buffers
  • Ignore mode for troubleshooting and edge testing

docs.title: Multiple internal nodes
docs.text:
Create multiple internal nodes to:

  • Simulate complete systems
  • Test controller multi-device handling
  • Verify address arbitration
  • Check for address conflicts

Remember: Total controllers + internal nodes must not exceed 4

docs.title: Bus select
docs.text: Choose which bus to use for I2C Protocol Exerciser operations.

docs.title: Available buses
docs.text:
Four buses are available for configuration. Each bus can be set to a different mode by clicking on it.

Example multi-bus configuration:

  • Bus 1: Controller mode
  • Bus 3: Another controller (simultaneous operation)
  • Bus 2, 4: Disabled or Target mode

docs.title: Channel assignments
docs.text: Channel assignments for each bus are fixed and cannot be adjusted manually. The device automatically assigns channels based on the bus number you select.

docs.title: Current limitation
docs.text:
Important: Currently, only ONE bus is supported for user operation.

Multiple bus support may be available in future software versions.

docs.title: Selecting a bus
docs.text:
1. Click on the desired bus in the topology diagram
  2. The selected bus is highlighted
  3. Configure the bus using Px Pair Settings

docs.title: Controller mode
docs.text: Configure I2C controller settings, timing parameters, and send transactions to target devices.

docs.title: Timing settings
docs.text: Adjust I2C timing parameters to match your device requirements or test edge cases.

docs.title: 1. Clock frequency
docs.text:
Set the I2C clock (SCL) frequency.

Range: 1 kHz to 1000 kHz (1 MHz)

Standard I2C speeds:

  • Standard mode: 100 kHz
  • Fast mode: 400 kHz
  • Fast-mode Plus: 1000 kHz (1 MHz)

docs.title: 2. Timing components
docs.text:
Adjust individual timing components for precise control.

Adjustable range: 5 ns to 20 μs per component

Components:

  • Setup time (SDA before SCL)
  • Hold time (SDA after SCL)
  • Clock high time
  • Clock low time
  • START/STOP conditions timing

Interactive adjustment:

Drag the slider bar to adjust the setup and hold time of data signals dynamically.

docs.title: Assign
docs.text:
Upload the configured topology to the exerciser device.

What's uploaded:

  • Number of controllers
  • Internal node configurations
  • Device addresses
  • Internal node types and register settings

Purpose: The device needs this information to properly send commands and respond to bus transactions.

When to use: After making any changes to:

  • Internal nodes
  • Addresses
  • Mode settings
  • Bus configuration

docs.title: Reload
docs.text:
Reload the topology from the exerciser device and display it in the software.

Use cases:

  • Verify what's currently loaded on the device
  • Synchronize after external changes
  • Refresh after programmatic configuration (e.g., via Python API)

docs.title: Scan external node
docs.text:
Scan all available addresses from 0x08 to 0x77 to detect connected devices.

How it works:

  • Controller sends transactions to each address
  • If a device responds with ACK, it appears in the topology
  • Non-responsive addresses are skipped

Benefits:

  • Automatically discover connected devices
  • Verify device addresses
  • Check for address conflicts
  • Confirm device connectivity

Time: Scanning all addresses takes a few seconds.

docs.title: Decode settings
docs.text:
Configure Logic Analyzer parameters for I2C signal decoding.

Settings include:

  • SCL (clock) channel assignment
  • SDA (data) channel assignment
  • Decode display options
  • Color coding

Purpose: Proper decode settings ensure the Logic Analyzer correctly interprets I2C signals captured during exerciser operations.

docs.title: Send packets
docs.text:
To open the wizard, see Wizard in the toolbar.

The I2C wizard provides two methods for sending packets: Quick Send and Packet Constructor.

docs.title: Quick send
docs.text:
Send simple I2C transactions quickly with a streamlined interface.

Configuration:

  1. Bus selection: Choose which bus to send the packet from
  2. Address mode: Select 7-bit, 8-bit, or 10-bit addressing
  3. This documentation uses 7-bit mode as the example
  4. Packet details:
  5. R/W: Select WRITE or READ operation
  6. Address: Set the target device address
  7. Sub-address: Set the register address (if sub-addressing is enabled)
  8. Write data: Enter data bytes to write
  9. Read byte count: Specify number of bytes to read (for READ operations)
  10. Address table: Displays information about internal and external nodes
  11. Send button: Transmit the configured packet
  12. Reload button: Refresh the address table

docs.title: Packet constructor
docs.text:
Build complex I2C transaction sequences with multiple packets.

How to use:

  1. Switch to the Bus tab
  2. Click the Add button (bottom right)
  3. Add 7-bit, 8-bit, or 10-bit WRITE or READ packets
  4. Configure packet details
  5. Click Execute to send all packets in sequence

This documentation uses 7-bit mode as the example.

docs.title: Edit packet
docs.text:
Manage and sequence multiple I2C packets.

Functions:

  1. Reorder packets: Use arrow buttons to adjust packet execution order
  2. Edit packet details: Click to open the detailed editing dialog (see below)
  3. Delete packet: Remove packet from the sequence
  4. Packet list: View all configured packets

docs.title: Packet sequence editor
docs.text:
Configure a sequence of WRITE and READ operations.

Operations:

  1. Add packet: Insert new WRITE or READ packet into the sequence
  2. Edit packet: Configure packet details (opens detail editor)
  3. Delete packet: Remove selected packet from sequence
  4. Reorder: Adjust execution order of packets

docs.title: Detail packet editor
docs.text:
Configure individual packet parameters.

Fields:

  1. Address: Set device address and choose WRITE or READ operation
  2. Sub-address: Set register address (if this function is enabled for the target)
  3. Data:
  4. WRITE operation: Enter data bytes to transmit
  5. READ operation: Set the number of bytes to read
  6. Next packet: Choose the condition between this packet and the next:
  7. START: New I2C transaction (STOP then START)
  8. REPEAT START: Continue transaction (no STOP condition)

docs.title: Timing configuration
docs.text:
• Start with standard frequencies (100 kHz or 400 kHz)
  • Adjust timing only if testing edge cases or specific requirements
  • Verify timing meets I2C specification for your target devices

docs.title: Quick send vs. Packet constructor
docs.text:
Use Quick Send for:

  • Single transactions
  • Quick testing
  • Simple READ/WRITE operations

Use Packet Constructor for:

  • Complex sequences
  • Multiple operations
  • Testing specific protocol scenarios
  • Automated test sequences

docs.title: Transaction sequences
docs.text:
Common patterns:

EEPROM write: 1. START 2. Address + WRITE 3. Register address 4. Data byte(s) 5. STOP

EEPROM read: 1. START 2. Address + WRITE 3. Register address 4. REPEAT START 5. Address + READ 6. Data byte(s) 7. STOP

Use Repeat Start for read operations to maintain bus control and specify the starting register address.

docs.title: I2C Protocol Exerciser
docs.text: The I2C Protocol Exerciser allows you to generate and respond to I2C bus traffic, supporting controller and target modes with internal node simulation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Use I2C Protocol Exerciser to:

  • Act as an I2C controller to test target devices
  • Simulate I2C target devices
  • Create virtual internal nodes for multi-device testing
  • Test I2C communication without a full system

Supported addressing modes:

  • 7-bit addressing
  • 10-bit addressing (limited support)

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Follow the Quick Start guide for step-by-step setup instructions.

docs.title: Documentation sections
docs.text:
• Quick Start - Step-by-step setup guide
  • Bus Select - Choose which bus to use
  • Px Pair Settings - Configure mode, voltage, and pull-up resistors
  • Add Internal Node - Create virtual I2C devices
  • Controller Mode - Send I2C transactions
  • Target Mode - Respond to I2C transactions

docs.title: PX pair settings
docs.text: Configure operating mode, voltage levels, and pull-up resistors for the I2C bus.

docs.title: Accessing settings
docs.text: Click the button on the left side of the topology dialog (highlighted in red box) to open the PX Pair Settings dialog.

docs.title: Mode settings
docs.text:
Choose the operating mode for the exerciser on this bus:

  1. Controller mode: Exerciser acts as an I2C controller on this bus
  2. Target mode: Exerciser acts as an I2C target device on this bus
  3. Disable: Bus is inactive

docs.title: Internal nodes
docs.text:
In both Controller and Target modes, you can create virtual internal nodes to simulate multiple target devices on the bus.

Limitation: The total number of controllers and internal nodes combined must not exceed 4.

docs.title: Voltage settings
docs.text:
Configure voltage levels for proper I2C operation and signal decoding.

All voltage values are in millivolts (mV).

docs.title: 1. Vdd
docs.text:
Set the working voltage for the I2C bus.

Typical values:

  • 3300 mV (3.3V) - Common for modern devices
  • 5000 mV (5.0V) - Legacy and some automotive applications
  • 1800 mV (1.8V) - Low-power devices

docs.title: 2. Logic Analyzer threshold
docs.text:
Set the threshold voltage for the Logic Analyzer to properly decode I2C signals.

Recommendation: Set to approximately Vdd/2 for optimal signal detection.

Examples:

  • Vdd = 3300 mV → Threshold = 1650 mV
  • Vdd = 5000 mV → Threshold = 2500 mV
  • Vdd = 1800 mV → Threshold = 900 mV

docs.title: 3. Hysteresis range
docs.text:
Set the hysteresis range for noise immunity.

Purpose: Hysteresis prevents false triggering on noisy signals by requiring different thresholds for low-to-high and high-to-low transitions.

Typical value: 100-300 mV

docs.title: Resistance settings
docs.text: Configure pull-up resistors for the I2C bus.

docs.title: 1. Pull-up enabled
docs.text:
Check the checkbox to activate internal pull-up resistors.

When to enable:

  • No external pull-up resistors on the bus
  • Testing pull-up resistance effects
  • Standalone exerciser testing without external components

When to disable:

  • External pull-up resistors are present
  • Device under test provides pull-ups
  • Avoiding conflicts with existing pull-ups

docs.title: 2. Pull-up resistance
docs.text:
Set the pull-up resistance value.

Input methods:

  • Type a custom value directly
  • Select from common resistance values in the dropdown

Common values:

  • 2.2 kΩ - High-speed I2C
  • 4.7 kΩ - Fast-mode I2C (typical)
  • 10 kΩ - Standard-mode I2C

Selection guidelines:

  • Lower resistance: Faster rise times, higher current consumption
  • Higher resistance: Slower rise times, lower current consumption
  • Match resistance to bus capacitance and speed requirements

docs.title: Voltage configuration
docs.text:
• Always verify Vdd matches your device specification
  • Set threshold carefully - incorrect values cause decode errors
  • Use a multimeter to measure actual bus voltage if uncertain

docs.title: Pull-up resistors
docs.text:
• Calculate required resistance based on bus capacitance and speed
  • Formula: R = (tr × 0.8473) / (Cb × 0.8473) where tr is rise time, Cb is bus capacitance
  • When in doubt, start with 4.7 kΩ for fast-mode I2C

docs.title: Internal nodes
docs.text:
• Use internal nodes to simulate multi-device scenarios
  • Test controller behavior with multiple targets
  • Verify proper arbitration and addressing

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: Follow these steps to set up and use I2C Protocol Exerciser:

docs.title: Setup steps
docs.text:
1. Select bus - Choose which bus to use for your I2C communication
  2. Configure PX pair parameters - Set controller/target mode, voltage, and pull-up resistors
  3. (Optional) Add internal nodes - Create virtual I2C devices in your topology
  4. (Optional) Configure DC output - Power your device under test
  5. Configure decode settings - Set Logic Analyzer parameters for I2C signal analysis
  6. Assign topology - Upload configuration to the exerciser device

docs.title: Controller mode operations
docs.text:
In Controller mode, you can perform additional operations:

  1. (Optional) Scan for devices - Scan all available addresses (0x08 ~ 0x77) to detect connected devices
  2. Send commands - Use the I2C wizard to send READ/WRITE transactions

docs.title: Target mode
docs.text: Configure the exerciser to act as an I2C target device responding to controller commands.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Target mode allows the exerciser to simulate an I2C target device. The device responds to transactions initiated by external controllers.

docs.title: Available functions
docs.text:
Target mode includes the same functions as Controller mode, except:

  • Timing Settings - Not available (controller sets timing)
  • Scan External Node - Not available (only controllers scan)

For descriptions of available functions, see:

  • Assign - Upload topology to device
  • Reload - Refresh topology from device
  • Decode Settings - Configure signal decoding

docs.title: Wizard interface
docs.text:
In Target mode, the I2C wizard interface is displayed but all packet sending functions are disabled.

Why: Target devices respond to controller commands; they do not initiate transactions. The wizard is disabled because:

  • Targets cannot send unsolicited data
  • Targets only respond when addressed by a controller
  • Bus protocol requires controller to initiate all transactions

docs.title: Responding to transactions
docs.text:
The target device automatically responds to:

  • Address match: ACKs when its address is called
  • READ requests: Sends data from internal registers
  • WRITE requests: Stores data to internal registers

docs.title: Internal node configuration
docs.text:
Even in Target mode, you can add internal nodes to simulate multiple target devices on the bus.

See: Add Internal Node

Use cases:

  • Simulate multiple sensors on one bus
  • Test controller multi-device handling
  • Create complex test scenarios

docs.title: Setup for testing
docs.text:
1. Configure target address and register behavior
  2. Add internal nodes if simulating multiple devices
  3. Connect external controller (or use another exerciser as controller)
  4. Start Logic Analyzer or Protocol Analyzer capture
  5. External controller sends transactions
  6. Verify target responses in captured data

docs.title: Common test scenarios
docs.text:
Controller development:

  • Connect your controller under test
  • Exerciser acts as target device
  • Verify controller sends correct commands
  • Check timing and protocol compliance

System integration:

  • Simulate missing devices
  • Test with partial hardware
  • Verify bus operation with multiple targets

docs.title: Limitations in Target mode
docs.text:
• Cannot initiate transactions (controller-only function)
  • Cannot send packets using wizard
  • Cannot set bus timing (follows controller timing)
  • Cannot scan for devices (controller-only function)

docs.title: Register configuration
docs.text:
• Configure internal registers to match the device you're simulating
  • Use appropriate sub-address behavior (increment, repeat, etc.)
  • Pre-load register data if testing specific read sequences

docs.title: Address selection
docs.text:
• Choose addresses that don't conflict with other devices on the bus
  • Use standard address range (0x08-0x77) unless testing reserved addresses
  • Document which addresses are used for each test scenario

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• Always capture transactions during testing
  • Verify ACK/NACK behavior is correct
  • Check data integrity in read/write operations
  • Confirm timing meets I2C specification

docs.title: Bus select
docs.text: Choose the bus configuration for MIPI I3C operations.

docs.title: Available bus configurations
docs.text: MIPI I3C supports two main bus configurations:

docs.title: 1. Multi-lane MIPI I3C
docs.text:
Uses multiple data lanes in addition to the standard clock and data signals, following MIPI Alliance specifications.

Features:

  • Increased bandwidth
  • Additional data lines beyond SCL and SDA
  • Enhanced performance for high-speed applications

Status: Multi-lane function will be released in a future version1

docs.title: 2. Traditional two-wire MIPI I3C
docs.text:
Standard I3C configuration using only SCL (clock) and SDA (data) lines.

Features:

  • Compatible with I2C legacy devices
  • Standard MIPI I3C operation
  • Support for up to four buses

Status: Additional buses (beyond one) will be released in a future version1

docs.title: Channel assignments
docs.text: Important: Channel assignments for each bus are fixed and cannot be adjusted manually. The device automatically assigns channels based on your bus selection.

docs.title: Selecting a bus
docs.text:
1. Click on the desired bus in the topology diagram
  2. The selected bus is highlighted
  3. Configure the bus using PX Pair Settings
  4. Add devices and set up topology

docs.title: Current limitations
docs.text:
• Only one bus is currently supported for operation
  • Multi-lane configuration is not yet available
  • Channel assignments are fixed per bus

  1. Multi-lane function and additional buses will be released in future software versions. ↩↩

docs.title: Controller mode
docs.text: Configure I3C controller settings, manage device addresses, and send transactions.

docs.title: Address table
docs.text: Manage addresses for I3C and legacy I2C devices on the bus.

docs.title: I3C address table
docs.text:
Reserve dynamic addresses for I3C devices by specifying their device characteristics.

Configuration fields:

  • PID (Provisional ID): 48-bit unique device identifier
  • BCR (Bus Characteristics Register): Device capabilities and role
  • DCR (Device Characteristics Register): Device type classification
  • Dynamic Address: Preferred address for assignment

Address assignment:

If the requested dynamic address is already in use, the controller automatically increments the value until an available address is found.

Use X (Don't Care): Enter X in fields where the specific value doesn't matter for your test.

docs.title: I2C address table
docs.text:
Add legacy I2C devices to the controller's device list.

When to use:

  • External I2C devices are connected to the bus
  • Testing mixed I3C and I2C configurations
  • Maintaining legacy device compatibility

Note: I2C devices use static addresses and do not participate in dynamic address assignment.

docs.title: In-used table
docs.text:
View I3C devices that have been assigned dynamic addresses and are currently active on the bus.

Displayed information:

  • Dynamic addresses currently assigned
  • Device PID
  • Device BCR and DCR
  • Assignment status

docs.title: Decode settings
docs.text: Configure Logic Analyzer parameters for I3C signal decoding.

docs.title: Configuration options
docs.text:
1. Color: Select colors for Logic Analyzer decode elements
  2. Customize for better visual distinction

  3. Match your preferred color scheme

  4. Startup mode: Select the initial decode mode for the Logic Analyzer

  5. SDR mode (default): Standard Single Data Rate - keep this for normal operation

  6. HDR modes: High Data Rate modes (DDR, TSP, TSL, etc.)

  7. Extended specification: Enable MIPI I3C debug information

  8. Shows additional protocol details
  9. Useful for compliance testing

  10. Provides deeper insight into I3C operation

  11. Report detail option: Enable detailed decoding information

  12. More verbose decode output
  13. Includes timing margins and protocol details
  14. Helpful for debugging complex issues

docs.title: Timing settings
docs.text:
Configure I3C timing parameters to match device requirements or test specific timing scenarios.

Base timing unit: 5 ns minimum

Important: All timing values must be multiples of 5 ns. Values below 5 ns are not permitted.

docs.title: Common settings
docs.text:
Configure core I3C timing parameters.

1. I3C clock speed range: 100 Hz to 13 MHz

2. Open drain clock speed range: 100 Hz to 5 MHz

3. Timing parameters (base unit: 5 ns):

  • tCAS: Clock-to-data setup time
  • tCBP: Clock-to-data valid time
  • tCASr: Clock-to-data setup time (read)
  • tCBSr: Clock-to-data valid time (read)

docs.title: Push-pull header
docs.text:
Configure timing for push-pull mode headers.

Use for: High-speed I3C transactions using push-pull drivers on both SCL and SDA.

docs.title: Optimized header
docs.text: Configure timing for optimized push-pull headers with enhanced performance.

docs.title: Open drain modes
docs.text: I3C uses open drain for legacy I2C compatibility and some control operations.

docs.title: 1. Open drain fast
docs.text: Fast open-drain timing for I2C-compatible operations at higher speeds.

docs.title: 2. Open drain slow
docs.text: Slower open-drain timing for maximum I2C compatibility.

docs.title: 3. Open drain read 8 bytes
docs.text: Optimized timing for reading 8-byte blocks in open-drain mode.

docs.title: I3C read
docs.text:
Push-pull speed mode

Configure timing parameters for I3C READ transactions.

Use for: High-speed private READ operations from I3C targets.

docs.title: I3C write
docs.text:
Push-pull speed mode

Configure timing parameters for I3C WRITE transactions.

Use for: High-speed private WRITE operations to I3C targets.

docs.title: Legacy I2C
docs.text:
Configure timing for legacy I2C device communication.

Speed range: 100 Hz to 1 MHz

I2C standard speeds:

  • Standard mode: 100 kHz
  • Fast mode: 400 kHz
  • Fast-mode Plus: 1 MHz

Use for: Communicating with I2C devices on an I3C bus.

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
Upload the configured topology to the exerciser device and activate the bus.

What's uploaded:

  • Controller and internal node configurations
  • Device addresses (static and dynamic)
  • Internal node types and characteristics
  • Timing settings
  • All topology parameters

Purpose: The exerciser needs this complete configuration to properly initiate transactions and respond to device requests.

docs.title: Run process
docs.text:
The Run process executes several steps. Some steps are optional depending on your configuration.

Status indicators:

Error occurred - Check status message for details

Wait for processing - Step is currently executing

Skip this process - Step not needed for current configuration

Process succeeded - Step completed successfully

docs.title: Successful activation
docs.text:
When all steps complete successfully, the exerciser is active and ready to send commands.

What this means:

  • Topology is loaded
  • Device is initialized
  • Bus is operational
  • Ready to send transactions

docs.title: Reload
docs.text:
Refresh the topology display from the exerciser device.

Use cases:

  • Verify current device configuration
  • Sync after external changes (e.g., Python API updates)
  • Refresh after device reset
  • Check dynamic address assignments

When building topology via Python code: Use Reload to update the GUI with the current exerciser state.

docs.title: Address table management
docs.text:
• Define all known devices in address tables before running
  • Use PID, BCR, DCR values from device datasheets
  • Test with simple topology first, then add complexity
  • Verify addresses don't conflict

docs.title: Timing configuration
docs.text:
• Start with default timing values
  • Adjust only if devices require specific timing
  • Verify timing meets MIPI I3C specification
  • Test timing margins if validating device compliance

docs.title: Run process troubleshooting
docs.text:
If Run fails:

  • Check error message for specific issue
  • Verify all required fields are filled
  • Confirm addresses don't conflict
  • Check internal node configurations
  • Ensure timing values are valid (multiples of 5 ns)

docs.title: MIPI I3C Protocol Exerciser
docs.text:
Supports MIPI I3C specification version 1.2 and below

The MIPI I3C Protocol Exerciser allows you to generate and respond to I3C bus traffic, including legacy I2C compatibility.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Use MIPI I3C Protocol Exerciser to:

  • Act as an I3C controller with dynamic address assignment
  • Simulate I3C target devices
  • Test I3C Common Command Codes (CCC)
  • Support legacy I2C devices on the same bus
  • Create virtual internal nodes for multi-device testing

Key features:

  • Dynamic address assignment (DAA)
  • In-band interrupts (IBI)
  • Hot-join capability
  • HDR (High Data Rate) modes
  • Backward compatible with I2C

docs.title: Specification support
docs.text:
MIPI I3C version: 1.2 and below

Supported features:

  • SDR (Single Data Rate) mode
  • HDR-DDR, HDR-TSP, HDR-TSL modes
  • Dynamic address assignment (ENTDAA)
  • Common Command Codes (CCC) - Broadcast and Direct
  • Legacy I2C device support
  • In-band interrupts (IBI)
  • Hot-join

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Follow the Quick Start guide for step-by-step setup instructions.

docs.title: Documentation sections
docs.text:
• Quick Start - Step-by-step setup guide
  • Bus Select - Choose bus configuration
  • Px Pair Settings - Configure mode, voltage, and pull-up resistors
  • Controller Mode - Send I3C and CCC commands
  • Target Mode - Respond to controller transactions
  • Internal Node - Create virtual I3C/I2C devices
  • Wizard - Quick send and packet builder interface

docs.title: Internal node
docs.text: Create virtual I3C and legacy I2C target devices for comprehensive bus testing.

docs.title: I3C node configuration
docs.text: Configure virtual I3C target devices with complete device characteristics.

docs.title: 1. Name
docs.text:
Set a descriptive name for this internal node for easy identification.

Examples:

  • "Sensor_1"
  • "EEPROM_0x50"
  • "Test_Target_A"

docs.title: 2. Static address
docs.text:
Set the static I3C address (if the device supports static addressing).

Range: 0x08 to 0x7D (I3C allows limited static addresses)

Note: Many I3C devices use dynamic addressing only. Leave blank if not using static address.

docs.title: 3. Register settings
docs.text: Configure how the internal node's registers behave.

docs.title: Register type
docs.text:
Current support: 32-bit register only

The internal node simulates a device with 32-bit register storage.

docs.title: Sub-address type
docs.text: Choose whether the node uses register addressing:

docs.title: Without sub-address
docs.text:
No sub-addressing (register addressing) is used.

Behavior: Direct data READ/WRITE without register selection.

docs.title: 8-bit sub-address
docs.text:
Uses 8-bit sub-addressing for register access.

Current support: 8-bit sub-address only

Behavior: First byte after address selects the register, subsequent bytes are data.

docs.title: Sub-address data format
docs.text: Configure multi-byte transaction behavior. Available only when 8-bit Sub-Address is selected.

docs.title: Repeat sub-address
docs.text:
All bytes in the transaction access the same register.

Example: Write 4 bytes to register 0x10 - All 4 bytes → Register 0x10

docs.title: Increment sub-address
docs.text:
Sub-address increments by 1 for each byte.

Example: Write 4 bytes starting at register 0x10 - Byte 1 → 0x10, Byte 2 → 0x11, Byte 3 → 0x12, Byte 4 → 0x13

docs.title: Increment loop sub-address
docs.text:
Sub-address increments and wraps at register boundary.

Example: Write 4 bytes starting at 0xFE - Byte 1 → 0xFE, Byte 2 → 0xFF, Byte 3 → 0x00, Byte 4 → 0x01

docs.title: Ignore sub-address
docs.text:
Sub-address byte is acknowledged but ignored.

Use for: Testing edge cases or non-compliant behavior.

docs.title: 4. I3C node information
docs.text: Configure I3C-specific device characteristics.

docs.title: PID (Provisional ID)
docs.text:
Build the 48-bit unique device identifier.

Components:

  • Manufacturer ID
  • Part ID
  • Instance ID

Source: Obtain from device datasheet or MIPI I3C specification.

docs.title: BCR (Bus Characteristics Register)
docs.text:
Configure the Bus Characteristics Register.

Important: BCR settings affect available options in other settings.

Defines:

  • Device role (I3C vs. I2C)
  • Advanced capabilities
  • IBI support
  • Offline capability
  • Maximum data speed

docs.title: DCR (Device Characteristics Register)
docs.text:
Set the Device Characteristics Register value.

Options:

  • Predefined classes: Select from standard device types
  • Custom: Type a specific value in the spinbox

Defines: Device class (sensor, memory, etc.)

docs.title: 1. GETCAPS (Get Capabilities)
docs.text:
Configure how the internal node responds to GETCAPS CCC.

Version 1.0:

Available when I3C specification version 1.0 is selected.

Format 1 (Simple):

Basic capabilities response.

Enable Format 2:

  • Set CAPS Defining bit to enable GETCAPS Format 2
  • Set STATUS Defining bit to enable GETSTATUS Format 2

Format 2 (Defining Byte):

Currently supports one type of defining byte per configuration.

Includes base GETCAPS Format 1 fields plus additional capability bytes:

TESTPAT (Test Pattern):

CRCAPS (Clock Rate Capabilities):

VTCAPS (Virtual Target Capabilities):

DBGCAPS (Debug Capabilities):

docs.title: 2. GETSTATUS (Get Status)
docs.text:
Configure how the internal node responds to GETSTATUS CCC.

Format 1 (Simple):

Basic status response with standard status fields.

Format 2 (Defining Byte):

Currently supports one type of defining byte per configuration.

Includes base GETSTATUS Format 1 fields plus additional status bytes:

NASTAT (Not Acknowledged Status):

PRECR (Pending Read Error Count Report):

SCMSTAT (Secondary Controller Mode Status):

docs.title: 3. GETMXDS (Get Max Data Speed)
docs.text:
Configure maximum data speed capabilities response.

Format 1 & 2 (Simple):

Basic max data speed response.

Enable Format 3:

Select Support in the Defining Byte field to enable defining byte format (Format 3).

Format 3 (Defining Byte):

Currently supports one type of defining byte per configuration.

Includes base GETMXDS fields plus:

WRRDTURN (Write-Read Turnaround): Shown above

CRHDLY (Clock-to-Data Turnaround Delay):

docs.title: 4. MWL & MRL (Max Write/Read Length)
docs.text:
Configure maximum write length (MWL) and maximum read length (MRL) for the device.

IBI Size: Only available when BCR IBI-related bits are set to Support.

Purpose:

  • Define buffer size limits
  • Prevent overflow conditions
  • Match actual device capabilities

docs.title: Legacy I2C node configuration
docs.text:
Create virtual legacy I2C devices that operate on the I3C bus.

Use cases:

  • Test mixed I3C and I2C bus scenarios
  • Simulate legacy device compatibility
  • Verify backward compatibility behavior

docs.title: 1. Name
docs.text: Set a descriptive name for identification.

docs.title: 2. Static address
docs.text:
Set the I2C address for this legacy device.

Range: 0x08 to 0x77 (standard I2C device range)

Note: I2C devices always use static addresses, not dynamic assignment.

docs.title: 3. Register settings
docs.text: Configure register behavior for the legacy I2C node.

docs.title: Register type
docs.text: Current support: 32-bit register only

docs.title: Without sub-address
docs.text: No register addressing is used.

docs.title: 8-bit sub-address
docs.text:
Uses 8-bit sub-addressing for register access.

Current support: 8-bit sub-address only

docs.title: Sub-address data format
docs.text: Available only when 8-bit Sub-Address is selected.

docs.title: Repeat sub-address
docs.text: All bytes access the same register.

docs.title: Increment sub-address
docs.text: Sub-address increments for each byte (common for EEPROMs).

docs.title: Increment loop sub-address
docs.text: Sub-address increments with wraparound.

docs.title: Ignore sub-address
docs.text: Sub-address is acknowledged but not used.

docs.title: I3C stress test
docs.text:
Test controller IBI handling under stress conditions.

Function: Continuously sends IBI (In-Band Interrupt) packets from the internal node.

Purpose: Test the controller's ability to handle a high volume of IBI requests.

Use cases:

  • Stress testing controller IBI handling
  • Verifying IBI queue management
  • Testing IBI priority mechanisms
  • Validating controller performance under load

docs.title: I3C vs. I2C nodes
docs.text:
Use I3C nodes when:

  • Testing I3C-specific features (DAA, IBI, HDR)
  • Simulating modern I3C devices
  • Need dynamic addressing

Use I2C legacy nodes when:

  • Testing backward compatibility
  • Simulating legacy devices on I3C bus
  • Verifying mixed-mode operation

docs.title: Device characteristics
docs.text:
• Use realistic PID values from actual devices or create unique test values
  • BCR should accurately reflect device capabilities
  • DCR should match the type of device you're simulating
  • Configure GETCAPS, GETSTATUS, GETMXDS to match real device behavior

docs.title: Sub-addressing
docs.text:
• Increment mode: Most common (EEPROMs, registers)
  • Repeat mode: FIFO-like devices
  • Loop mode: Circular buffers
  • Ignore mode: Edge case testing

docs.title: Stress testing
docs.text:
• Use IBI stress test to validate controller robustness
  • Start with slow IBI rate, increase to find limits
  • Monitor bus performance under stress
  • Verify no lost IBI packets

docs.title: PX pair settings
docs.text: Configure operating mode, voltage levels, and pull-up resistors for the I3C bus.

docs.title: Accessing settings
docs.text: Click the large button on the left side of the topology dialog to open the PX Pair Settings dialog.

docs.title: Mode settings
docs.text: The Acute PX device supports multiple targets and controllers on the same bus. Select the appropriate mode for your testing scenario.

docs.title: 1. Disable
docs.text:
Deactivate I3C bus functions on this bus.

Use when:

  • Bus is not needed for current test
  • Preventing accidental bus activity
  • Isolating other buses

docs.title: 2. Controller mode
docs.text:
Exerciser simulates an I3C controller with optional target nodes on this bus.

Features:

  • Initiate all bus transactions
  • Perform dynamic address assignment
  • Send CCC commands
  • Control bus timing
  • Accept in-band interrupts (IBI) from targets

IBI Size configuration:

Define the maximum amount of IBI data the virtual controller will accept from targets.

Use cases:

  • Testing target device implementations
  • Simulating a controller with multiple targets
  • Verifying protocol compliance

docs.title: 3. Target mode
docs.text:
Exerciser simulates I3C target devices on this bus.

Features:

  • Respond to controller commands
  • Accept dynamic address assignment
  • Send IBI requests (if enabled)
  • Operate in HDR modes when commanded

Use cases:

  • Testing controller implementations
  • Simulating sensors or peripherals
  • Verifying target behavior

docs.title: Internal nodes
docs.text:
In both Controller and Target modes, you can create virtual internal nodes to simulate multiple target devices on the bus.

See: Internal Node

docs.title: Voltage settings
docs.text:
Configure voltage levels for proper I3C operation and signal decoding.

All voltage values are in millivolts (mV).

docs.title: 1. Vdd
docs.text:
Set the working voltage for the I3C bus.

Typical I3C voltages:

  • 3300 mV (3.3V) - Most common
  • 1800 mV (1.8V) - Low-power I3C
  • 1200 mV (1.2V) - Ultra-low-power applications

docs.title: 2. Logic Analyzer threshold
docs.text:
Set the threshold voltage for the Logic Analyzer to properly decode I3C signals.

Recommendation: Set to approximately Vdd/2 for optimal signal detection.

Examples:

  • Vdd = 3300 mV → Threshold = 1650 mV
  • Vdd = 1800 mV → Threshold = 900 mV

docs.title: 3. Hysteresis range
docs.text:
Set the hysteresis range for noise immunity on I3C signals.

Purpose: Prevents false signal detection on noisy or slow-transitioning signals.

Typical value: 100-300 mV

docs.title: Resistance settings
docs.text: Configure internal pull-up resistors for the I3C bus.

docs.title: 1. Pull-up enabled
docs.text:
Check the checkbox to activate internal pull-up resistors.

When to enable:

  • No external pull-up resistors on the bus
  • Standalone testing without external hardware
  • Testing pull-up effects on signal quality

When to disable:

  • External pull-up resistors are present
  • Device under test provides pull-ups
  • Avoiding conflicts with existing pull-ups

docs.title: 2. Pull-up resistance
docs.text:
Set the pull-up resistance value.

Input methods:

  • Type a custom value directly
  • Select from common preset values in the dropdown

Common I3C pull-up values:

  • 1.0 kΩ - High-speed I3C (push-pull modes)
  • 2.0 kΩ - Typical I3C
  • 4.7 kΩ - I2C legacy compatibility

Selection guidelines:

  • Lower resistance: Faster transitions, higher current
  • Higher resistance: Lower power, slower transitions
  • I3C typically uses lower resistance than I2C due to push-pull operation

docs.title: Mode selection
docs.text:
Choose Controller mode when:

  • Testing target devices
  • Need to initiate transactions
  • Performing dynamic address assignment
  • Sending CCC commands

Choose Target mode when:

  • Testing controller implementations
  • Simulating sensors or peripherals
  • Verifying target response behavior

docs.title: Voltage configuration
docs.text:
• Always match Vdd to your device specifications
  • Verify mixed-voltage devices are compatible
  • I3C devices must tolerate the bus voltage
  • Legacy I2C devices must operate at the same voltage

docs.title: Pull-up resistors
docs.text:
• Calculate based on bus capacitance and speed requirements
  • I3C uses push-pull for high-speed, open-drain for legacy I2C
  • Pull-ups primarily affect open-drain (I2C legacy) operation
  • Test with recommended 2.0 kΩ first, adjust as needed

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: Follow these steps to set up and use MIPI I3C Protocol Exerciser:

docs.title: 1. Select bus
docs.text:
Activate the bus by clicking the left box in the topology dialog.

See: Bus Select

docs.title: 2. Configure PX pair parameters
docs.text:
Set up pull-up resistance, Vdd, threshold, and operating mode.

See: PX Pair Settings

docs.title: 3. Controller-specific settings
docs.text:
Note: These settings are only available in Controller mode, not in Target mode.

Configure:

  • Address Table - Define I3C and I2C device addresses
  • Timing Settings - Adjust I3C timing parameters

docs.title: 4. Configure decode settings
docs.text:
Set up Decode Settings for Logic Analyzer waveform decoding.

This ensures captured I3C signals are properly interpreted.

docs.title: 5. (Optional) Add internal nodes
docs.text:
Create virtual I3C or I2C devices using Internal Nodes.

Use cases:

  • Simulate multiple target devices
  • Test with mixed I3C and legacy I2C devices
  • Verify dynamic address assignment behavior

docs.title: 6. (Optional) Enable DC power supply
docs.text: Turn on the DC Power Supply to power your device under test.

docs.title: 7. Run
docs.text:
Press Run to activate the exerciser and upload the topology configuration.

What happens:

  • Topology is validated
  • Settings are uploaded to the device
  • Exerciser becomes active on the bus
  • Status indicators show progress

docs.title: 8. Send commands (Controller mode only)
docs.text:
Use the MIPI I3C Wizard to send:

  • CCC (Common Command Codes)
  • Private READ/WRITE transactions
  • Legacy I2C transactions
  • HDR mode transfers

docs.title: Target mode
docs.text: Configure the exerciser to act as an I3C target device responding to an external controller.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Target mode allows the exerciser to simulate one or more I3C target devices. Use this mode when you have an external controller and want to test its behavior with simulated targets.

Use cases:

  • Test controller implementations
  • Simulate sensors, memory, or peripheral devices
  • Verify dynamic address assignment from controller perspective
  • Test IBI (In-Band Interrupt) handling

docs.title: Decode settings
docs.text:
Configure Logic Analyzer parameters for I3C signal decoding.

Configuration is identical to Controller mode.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
1. Color: Select colors for Logic Analyzer decode elements
  2. Customize visual appearance

  3. Improve readability

  4. Startup mode: Select initial decode mode

  5. SDR mode (default): Standard operation - recommended for normal use

  6. HDR modes: High Data Rate variants

  7. Extended specification: Enable MIPI I3C debug information

  8. Additional protocol details

  9. Useful for compliance and debugging

  10. Report detail option: Enable detailed decode information

  11. Verbose output with timing details
  12. Helpful for in-depth analysis

docs.title: Run
docs.text:
Upload the topology configuration to the exerciser device.

What's uploaded:

  • Internal node configurations
  • Target device characteristics (PID, BCR, DCR)
  • Register settings

Note: Some controller-specific steps (like address table setup and timing configuration) are not available in Target mode.

docs.title: Run process
docs.text:
The Run process executes configuration steps for Target mode.

Status indicators:

Error occurred - Check status message

Wait for processing - Step executing

Skip this process - Not needed

Process succeeded - Step complete

docs.title: Successful activation
docs.text:
When the process completes successfully:

  • Target devices are active
  • Exerciser awaits controller commands
  • Ready to respond to bus transactions

docs.title: Reload
docs.text:
Refresh the topology from the exerciser device and display it in the software.

Identical to Controller mode functionality.

Use cases:

  • Verify current device configuration
  • Sync after programmatic changes (e.g., Python API)
  • Check dynamic address assignments received from controller
  • Refresh display after manual device updates

docs.title: Responding to commands
docs.text:
In Target mode, the exerciser:

  • Waits for controller to assign dynamic addresses (DAA)
  • Responds to Common Command Codes (CCC)
  • Handles private READ/WRITE transactions
  • Can generate IBI requests (if configured)
  • Supports hot-join (if enabled)

docs.title: Address assignment
docs.text:
Static address (optional):

  • Target announces static address during bus initialization
  • Controller may assign a dynamic address during ENTDAA

Dynamic address:

  • Received from controller during dynamic address assignment
  • Stored and used for subsequent transactions
  • Can be reassigned by controller using SETNEWDA CCC

docs.title: Limitations in Target mode
docs.text:
Not available:

  • Address table configuration (controller function)
  • Timing settings (controller sets bus timing)
  • Initiating transactions (only controller can initiate)
  • Scanning for devices (controller function)

Available:

  • Internal node configuration
  • Decode settings
  • Run and Reload operations
  • Response to all controller commands

docs.title: Setup for controller testing
docs.text:
1. Configure target device characteristics (PID, BCR, DCR)
  2. Add internal nodes if simulating multiple targets
  3. Set up decode settings for capture
  4. Click Run to activate targets
  5. Connect external controller
  6. Start capture
  7. Controller performs DAA and sends commands
  8. Verify target responses in captured data

docs.title: Device characteristics
docs.text:
• Use realistic PID, BCR, DCR values from actual devices
  • Configure BCR to match device capabilities you're simulating
  • DCR should match the device type class

docs.title: Internal nodes
docs.text:
• Create multiple internal nodes to test multi-target scenarios
  • Mix I3C and I2C legacy devices
  • Test edge cases with unusual device combinations

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• Always capture during target testing
  • Verify dynamic address assignment succeeds
  • Check IBI behavior if configured
  • Confirm CCC responses are correct
  • Validate private transaction handling

docs.title: IBI
docs.text: IBI (In-Band Interrupt) in MIPI I3C is a mechanism that lets a target device interrupt or notify the controller (master) using the same SDA/SCL lines as normal I3C data transfers—no extra interrupt pin is needed.

docs.title: Hot Join
docs.text: Hot-Join is a feature of MIPI I3C that allows a target device to be added to an active I3C bus after the system is already powered and running, without resetting or disturbing existing devices.

docs.title: Private RW
docs.text:
