In MIPI I3C, Private Read and Private Write are the basic point-to-point data transfer operations between the controller and a single target device using that target’s dynamic address. They are called private because only one specific target participates in the transfer, unlike broadcast or group operations.

  1. Private Read with SubAddress

  2. Private Write with SubAddress

docs.title: Broadcast CCC
docs.text:
1. Broadcast CCC - ENEC Broadcast CCC, ENEC allows the controller to enable specific event types simultaneously on all I3C target devices on the bus. The ENEC Broadcast CCC tells all targets which events they are allowed to generate, such as:

    • In-Band Interrupts (IBI)
    • Hot-Join
    • Controller Role Request (CRR)

    Without ENEC, targets are not allowed to issue these events.

  2. Broadcast CCC - DISEC Broadcast CCC, DISEC allows the controller to disable specific event types on all I3C target devices on the bus. The Broadcast DISEC CCC tells all targets to stop generating certain in-band events, including:

    • In-Band Interrupts (IBI)
    • Hot-Join
    • Controller Role Request (CRR)

    After DISEC, targets must not attempt to issue the disabled events.

  3. Broadcast CCC - ENTAS0 Broadcast CCC, ENTAS0 instructs all I3C target devices on the bus to enter Activity State 0, which is a defined low-activity / low-power state. The Broadcast ENTAS0 CCC tells all targets to:

    • Transition into Activity State 0
    • Reduce internal activity and power consumption
    • Maintain bus awareness so they can resume normal operation later

    Activity State 0 is typically the lowest-power activity state defined for I3C targets.

  4. Broadcast CCC - ENTAS1 Broadcast CCC, ENTAS1 instructs all I3C target devices on the bus to transition into Activity State 1, a moderate-activity / reduced-power operating state. The Broadcast ENTAS1 CCC tells all targets to:

    • Enter Activity State 1
    • Reduce power compared to full active mode
    • Remain responsive to normal I3C bus operations

    Activity State 1 balances power savings with bus availability.

  5. Broadcast CCC - ENTAS2 Broadcast CCC, ENTAS2 instructs all I3C target devices on the bus to transition into Activity State 2, which is a high-activity / near-full-performance state. The Broadcast ENTAS2 CCC tells all targets to:

    • Enter Activity State 2
    • Operate with higher internal activity than state 1
    • Be ready for high-throughput or low-latency communication

    Activity State 2 is typically just below the fully unrestricted active state.

  6. Broadcast CCC - ENTAS3 Broadcast CCC, ENTAS3 instructs all I3C target devices on the bus to transition into Activity State 3, which represents the highest activity and performance state defined by the I3C specification. The Broadcast ENTAS3 CCC tells all targets to:

    • Enter Activity State 3
    • Operate at full internal performance
    • Be fully ready for maximum bus speed and lowest latency

    Activity State 3 corresponds to unrestricted, fully active operation.

  7. Broadcast CCC - RSTDAA Broadcast CCC, RSTDAA instructs all I3C target devices on the bus to clear their currently assigned dynamic addresses and return to an unaddressed state. The Broadcast RSTDAA CCC tells all targets to:

    • Forget their dynamic address
    • Return to the default, unaddressed condition
    • Prepare for a fresh Dynamic Address Assignment (DAA) process

    After RSTDAA, no target is addressable by private transfers until DAA is performed again.

  8. Broadcast CCC - ENTDAA Broadcast CCC, ENTDAA tells all unaddressed I3C target devices on the bus to participate in the Dynamic Address Assignment (DAA) process, so the controller can assign each device a unique dynamic address. The Broadcast ENTDAA CCC allows the controller to:

    • Start the Dynamic Address Assignment (DAA) sequence
    • Assign unique dynamic addresses to all unaddressed targets
    • Ensure no conflicts between devices on the bus

    Targets that already have a dynamic address ignore ENTDAA.

  9. Broadcast CCC - DEFTGTS Broadcast CCC, DEFTGTS allows the controller to define timing parameters or slot assignments for all targets on the bus, particularly in grouped or time-slotted operations. The Broadcast DEFTGTS CCC allows the controller to:

    • Assign timing slots to target devices for coordinated operations
    • Control grouped transfer schedules, e.g., for multiple sensors
    • Ensure deterministic data reporting in systems with many devices

    DEFTGTS is particularly important for high-speed or synchronized operations, where multiple targets may need to transmit data in a pre-defined order.

  10. Broadcast CCC - SETMWL Broadcast CCC, SETMWL instructs all target devices on the bus to adopt a minimum number of bytes for write transactions before they will respond with an acknowledgment. The Broadcast SETMWL CCC allows the controller to:

    • Specify a minimum number of bytes that a target must receive in a write transfer before it can process or respond
    • Prevent targets from being triggered by partial or incomplete writes
    • Improve data integrity and bus efficiency

    Essentially, SETMWL sets a threshold for write transaction length.

  11. Broadcast CCC - SETMRL Broadcast CCC, SETMRL allows the controller to define the maximum number of data bytes that target devices are allowed to return in a single read transaction. The Broadcast SETMRL CCC tells all targets to:

    • Limit the length of private read transfers
    • Never return more than the specified number of bytes per read
    • Ensure predictable and controlled read behavior

    This protects the controller from unexpectedly long read responses.

  12. Broadcast CCC - ENTTM Broadcast CCC, ENTTM tells all targets to enter a special test or compliance mode, which is used for:

    • Manufacturing and production testing
    • Electrical and signal integrity validation
    • Protocol compliance and stress testing

    Only targets that support Test Mode respond to ENTTM; other devices safely ignore the command.

  13. Broadcast CCC - SETBUSCON Broadcast CCC, SETBUSCON allows the controller to configure bus-level operating conditions simultaneously for all I3C target devices on the bus. The SETBUSCON Broadcast CCC tells all targets how the bus will operate, including parameters such as:

    • Bus speed and timing constraints
    • Clocking and mode-related behavior
    • Other global bus configuration settings defined by the controller

    By issuing SETBUSCON as a broadcast, the controller ensures that all targets use a consistent view of the bus configuration, avoiding mismatches between devices.

  14. Broadcast CCC - ENDXFER Broadcast CCC, ENDXFER allows the controller to simultaneously terminate an ongoing data transfer or special bus operation for all I3C target devices on the bus. The ENDXFER Broadcast CCC tells all targets that the current transfer context has ended, and that they must:

    • Stop participating in the current data phase or extended transfer
    • Return to an idle or command-ready state
    • Clear any temporary transfer-related state

    ENDXFER is used to cleanly close or abort a bus operation that may involve multiple targets, ensuring all devices are synchronized and no target remains in a partial or undefined transfer state.

  15. Broadcast CCC - ENTHDR0 Broadcast CCC, ENTHDR0 allows the controller to simultaneously switch all I3C target devices on the bus into HDR-DDR (High Data Rate – Double Data Rate) mode. The ENTHDR0 Broadcast CCC tells all targets that support HDR-DDR to:

    • Exit Standard Data Rate (SDR) mode
    • Enter HDR-DDR signaling
    • Use double-data-rate transfers for higher throughput

    Only targets that support HDR-DDR mode respond to ENTHDR0. Devices that do not support this HDR mode safely ignore the command and remain in SDR mode. In this command, you can choose to turn on HDR Repeat.1

  16. Broadcast CCC - ENTHDR1 Broadcast CCC, ENTHDR1 allows the controller to simultaneously switch all I3C target devices on the bus into HDR-TSP (High Data Rate – Ternary Symbol Pattern) mode. The ENTHDR1 Broadcast CCC tells all targets that support HDR-TSP to:

    • Exit Standard Data Rate (SDR) mode
    • Enter HDR-TSP signaling
    • Use ternary symbol–based transfers to achieve higher data rates

    Only targets that support HDR-TSP mode respond to ENTHDR1. Devices that do not support this HDR mode safely ignore the command and remain in SDR mode. In this command, you can choose to turn on HDR Repeat.1

  17. Broadcast CCC - ENTHDR2 Broadcast CCC, ENTHDR2 allows the controller to simultaneously switch all I3C target devices on the bus into HDR-TSL (High Data Rate – Ternary Symbol Level) mode. The ENTHDR2 Broadcast CCC tells all targets that support HDR-TSL to:

    • Exit Standard Data Rate (SDR) mode
    • Enter HDR-TSL signaling
    • Use ternary symbol–level encoding for higher-throughput transfers

    Only targets that support HDR-TSL mode respond to ENTHDR2; devices that do not support this HDR mode safely ignore the command and remain in SDR mode. In this command, you can choose to turn on HDR Repeat.1

  18. Broadcast CCC - ENTHDR3 Broadcast CCC, ENTHDR3 allows the controller to simultaneously switch all I3C target devices on the bus into HDR-BT (High Data Rate – Burst Type) mode. The ENTHDR3 Broadcast CCC tells all targets that support HDR-BT to:

    • Exit Standard Data Rate (SDR) mode
    • Enter HDR-BT signaling
    • Use burst-mode transfers for high-speed data communication

    Only targets that support HDR-BT mode respond to ENTHDR3; devices that do not support this HDR mode safely ignore the command and remain in SDR mode. In this command, you can choose to turn on HDR Repeat.1

  19. Broadcast CCC - ENTHDR4 Broadcast CCC, ENTHDR4 allows the controller to simultaneously switch all I3C target devices on the bus into HDR-DY (High Data Rate – Dynamic) mode. The ENTHDR4 Broadcast CCC tells all targets that support HDR-DY to:

    • Exit Standard Data Rate (SDR) mode
    • Enter HDR-DY signaling
    • Use dynamic high-speed transfer modes that adapt to bus conditions for optimized throughput

    Only targets that support HDR-DY mode respond to ENTHDR4; devices that do not support this HDR mode safely ignore the command and remain in SDR mode.

  20. Broadcast CCC - ENTHDR5 Broadcast CCC, ENTHDR5 allows the controller to simultaneously switch all I3C target devices on the bus into HDR-TSV (High Data Rate – Ternary Symbol Variable) mode. The ENTHDR5 Broadcast CCC tells all targets that support HDR-TSV to:

    • Exit Standard Data Rate (SDR) mode
    • Enter HDR-TSV signaling
    • Use variable ternary-symbol encoding to achieve high-speed, adaptive data transfers

    Only targets that support HDR-TSV mode respond to ENTHDR5; devices that do not support this HDR mode safely ignore the command and remain in SDR mode.

  21. Broadcast CCC - ENTHDR6 Broadcast CCC, ENTHDR6 allows the controller to simultaneously switch all I3C target devices on the bus into HDR-BT1 (High Data Rate – Burst Type 1) mode. The ENTHDR6 Broadcast CCC tells all targets that support HDR-BT1 to:

    • Exit Standard Data Rate (SDR) mode
    • Enter HDR-BT1 signaling
    • Use burst-type high-speed transfers optimized for single-cycle or low-latency operations

    Only targets that support HDR-BT1 mode respond to ENTHDR6; devices that do not support this HDR mode safely ignore the command and remain in SDR mode.

  22. Broadcast CCC - ENTHDR7 Broadcast CCC, ENTHDR7 allows the controller to simultaneously switch all I3C target devices on the bus into HDR-BT2 (High Data Rate – Burst Type 2) mode. The ENTHDR7 Broadcast CCC tells all targets that support HDR-BT2 to:

    • Exit Standard Data Rate (SDR) mode
    • Enter HDR-BT2 signaling
    • Use an alternative burst-type high-speed transfer mode, typically optimized for higher throughput or multi-cycle burst operations

    Only targets that support HDR-BT2 mode respond to ENTHDR7; devices that do not support this HDR mode safely ignore the command and remain in SDR mode.

  23. Broadcast CCC - SETXTIME Broadcast CCC, SETXTIME allows the controller to simultaneously configure the timing parameters for extended data transfers on all I3C target devices on the bus. The SETXTIME Broadcast CCC tells all targets to:

    • Set the maximum duration or timeout for ongoing or upcoming transfers
    • Adjust internal timers to ensure synchronized transfer completion
    • Prepare for operations that may require longer or extended data phases

    Only targets that support extended transfer timing respond to SETXTIME; devices that do not support this feature safely ignore the command.

  24. Broadcast CCC - SETAASA Broadcast CCC, SETAASA allows the controller to simultaneously configure all I3C target devices on the bus to use a specific Activity-Aware Slave Address (AASA). The SETAASA Broadcast CCC tells all targets to:

    • Enable Activity-Aware Slave Addressing, allowing devices to respond to a secondary address based on activity patterns
    • Set the AASA value that targets will recognize for specific operations
    • Support coordinated or selective communication in multi-target or power-optimized bus scenarios

    Only targets that support AASA respond to SETAASA; devices that do not support this feature safely ignore the command.

  25. Broadcast CCC - RSTACT Broadcast CCC, RSTACT allows the controller to simultaneously reset the activity state of all I3C target devices on the bus. The RSTACT Broadcast CCC tells all targets to:

    • Clear their current activity state
    • Reset any activity counters, timers, or internal flags used for Activity-Aware Slave Addressing (AASA) or other activity-based operations
    • Return to a default idle or ready state for bus communication

    Only targets that support activity state tracking respond to RSTACK; devices that do not support this feature safely ignore the command.

  26. Broadcast CCC - DEFGRPA Broadcast CCC, DEFGRPA allows the controller to simultaneously define or assign a Group Address (GADDR) to all I3C target devices on the bus. The DEFGRPA Broadcast CCC tells all targets to:

    • Accept a specific Group Address for future group-directed commands
    • Enable devices to respond collectively to broadcasts or group-targeted operations
    • Support coordinated communication for power optimization, event notification, or synchronized data transfers

    Only targets that support group addressing respond to DEFGRPA; devices that do not support this feature safely ignore the command.

  27. Broadcast CCC - RSTGRPA Broadcast CCC, RSTGRPA allows the controller to simultaneously reset the Group Address (GADDR) of all I3C target devices on the bus. The RSTGRPA Broadcast CCC tells all targets to:

    • Clear any previously assigned Group Address
    • Remove the device from any group-targeted communications
    • Return to a default state where they respond only to individual or broadcast commands

    Only targets that support group addressing respond to RSTGRPA; devices that do not support this feature safely ignore the command.

  28. Broadcast CCC - MLANE Broadcast CCC, MLANE allows the controller to simultaneously configure all I3C target devices on the bus for Multi-Lane operation. The MLANE Broadcast CCC tells all targets to:

    • Enable or configure multi-lane communication, allowing multiple physical lanes to be used for higher data throughput
    • Coordinate lane mapping and synchronization across all capable devices
    • Prepare devices for parallel high-speed data transfers using multiple I3C lanes

    Only targets that support multi-lane operation respond to MLANE; devices that do not support this feature safely ignore the command.

  29. Broadcast CCC - Customized You can send a customized packet for a specific purpose.

docs.title: Direct CCC
docs.text:
1. Direct CCC - ENEC Direct CCC, ENEC allows the controller to enable specific event types for an individual I3C target device on the bus. The ENEC Direct CCC tells a particular target which events it is allowed to generate, such as:

    • In-Band Interrupts (IBI) – for asynchronous notifications to the controller
    • Hot-Join – indicating that a new device has joined the bus
    • Controller Role Request (CRR) – requesting a change in controller role

    Without ENEC, the target cannot issue these events, even if it supports them.

  2. Direct CCC - DISEC Direct CCC, DISEC allows the controller to disable specific event types for an individual I3C target device on the bus. The DISEC Direct CCC tells a particular target to stop generating certain events, such as:

    • In-Band Interrupts (IBI) – preventing the device from sending asynchronous notifications
    • Hot-Join – ignoring indications when a new device joins
    • Controller Role Request (CRR) – stopping requests to change the controller role

    By using DISEC, the controller can selectively block events from a single device without affecting other devices on the bus.

  3. Direct CCC - ENTAS0 Direct CCC, ENTAS0 instructs certain I3C target devices on the bus to enter Activity State 0, which is a defined low-activity / low-power state. The Direct ENTAS0 CCC tells certain targets to:

    • Transition into Activity State 0
    • Reduce internal activity and power consumption
    • Maintain bus awareness so they can resume normal operation later

    Activity State 0 is typically the lowest-power activity state defined for I3C targets.

  4. Direct CCC - ENTAS1 Direct CCC, ENTAS1 instructs certain I3C target devices on the bus to transition into Activity State 1, a moderate-activity / reduced-power operating state. The Direct ENTAS1 CCC tells certain targets to:

    • Enter Activity State 1
    • Reduce power compared to full active mode
    • Remain responsive to normal I3C bus operations

    Activity State 1 balances power savings with bus availability.

  5. Direct CCC - ENTAS2 Direct CCC, ENTAS2 instructs certain I3C target devices on the bus to transition into Activity State 2, which is a high-activity / near-full-performance state. The Direct ENTAS2 CCC tells certain targets to:

    • Enter Activity State 2
    • Operate with higher internal activity than state 1
    • Be ready for high-throughput or low-latency communication

    Activity State 2 is typically just below the fully unrestricted active state.

  6. Direct CCC - ENTAS3 Direct CCC, ENTAS3 instructs certain I3C target devices on the bus to transition into Activity State 3, which represents the highest activity and performance state defined by the I3C specification. The Direct ENTAS3 CCC tells certain targets to:

    • Enter Activity State 3
    • Operate at full internal performance
    • Be fully ready for maximum bus speed and lowest latency

    Activity State 3 corresponds to unrestricted, fully active operation.

  7. Direct CCC - SETDASA Direct CCC, SETDASA instructs a specific I3C target device on the bus, identified by its static I2C address, to adopt a new dynamic 7-bit address assigned by the controller. The Direct SETDASA CCC tells the target to:

    • Accept the new dynamic address provided by the controller
    • Switch from using its static address to the assigned dynamic address for future communications
    • Acknowledge the assignment so that normal I3C bus communication can proceed

    This allows the controller to efficiently assign dynamic addresses to known devices without performing a full broadcast ENTDAA procedure.

  8. Direct CCC - SETNEWDA Direct CCC, SETNEWDA instructs a specific I3C target device, identified by its current dynamic address, to adopt a new dynamic 7-bit address assigned by the controller. The Direct SETNEWDA CCC tells the target to:

    • Change its current dynamic address to the new dynamic address provided by the controller
    • Update its internal address mapping so future communications use the new dynamic address
    • Acknowledge the address change so the controller knows the operation was successful

    This command allows the controller to reassign dynamic addresses to devices already on the bus, for example, to resolve address conflicts or reorganize bus addressing without resetting devices.

  9. Direct CCC - SETMWL Direct CCC, SETMWL instructs a specific I3C target device on the bus to set its Maximum Write Length (MWL), which defines the largest number of data bytes the controller is allowed to write to that target in a single I3C write transaction. The Direct SETMWL CCC tells the target to:

    • Update its internal Maximum Write Length value to the value provided by the controller
    • Limit future write transfers from the controller to this specified maximum length
    • Enforce flow control by rejecting or managing writes that exceed the configured limit

    This command allows the controller to optimize bus performance and ensure compatibility with targets that have internal buffering or processing constraints.

  10. Direct CCC - SETMRL Direct CCC, SETMRL instructs a specific I3C target device on the bus to set its Maximum Read Length (MRL), which defines the largest number of data bytes the controller is allowed to read from that target in a single I3C read transaction. The Direct SETMRL CCC tells the target to:

    • Update its internal Maximum Read Length value to the value provided by the controller
    • Limit future read transfers to the specified maximum length
    • Ensure that read operations do not exceed the target’s internal buffering or data availability constraints

    This command allows the controller to manage read transaction sizes, improving reliability and efficiency while preventing data overruns or incomplete transfers.

  11. Direct CCC - GETMWL Direct CCC, GETMWL instructs a specific I3C target device on the bus to report its Maximum Write Length (MWL), which indicates the largest number of data bytes the controller is permitted to write to that target in a single I3C write transaction. The Direct GETMWL CCC tells the target to:

    • Return its currently configured Maximum Write Length value to the controller
    • Allow the controller to determine safe write transaction sizes
    • Support optimal bus scheduling and flow control decisions

    This command allows the controller to query a target’s write capacity, either before issuing write transfers or to confirm the value previously set using SETMWL.

  12. Direct CCC - GETMRL Direct CCC, GETMRL instructs a specific I3C target device on the bus to report its Maximum Read Length (MRL), which indicates the largest number of data bytes the controller is permitted to read from that target in a single I3C read transaction. The Direct GETMRL CCC tells the target to:

    • Return its currently configured Maximum Read Length value to the controller
    • Allow the controller to determine safe and efficient read transaction sizes
    • Support proper flow control and bus scheduling

    This command allows the controller to query a target’s read capacity, either before performing read operations or to verify the value previously configured using SETMRL.

  13. Direct CCC - GETPID Direct CCC, GETPID instructs a specific I3C target device on the bus to report its Provisional ID (PID), which uniquely identifies the device according to the MIPI I3C specification. The Direct GETPID CCC tells the target to:

    • Return its 48-bit Provisional ID to the controller
    • Allow the controller to identify the device vendor, part, and instance
    • Support device discovery, enumeration, and validation

    This command allows the controller to uniquely identify a target device without relying on static addresses, and is commonly used during device discovery or for verification after dynamic address assignment.

  14. Direct CCC - GETBCR Direct CCC, GETBCR instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to report its Bus Characteristics Register (BCR), which describes the target’s fundamental bus-related capabilities. The Direct GETBCR CCC tells the target to:

    • Return its Bus Characteristics Register value to the controller
    • Indicate whether the device supports key I³C features such as I³C target mode, I2C legacy compatibility, and in-band interrupt capability
    • Allow the controller to understand how the device behaves on the I³C bus

    This command allows the controller to determine basic bus capabilities and protocol support of a target device, which is essential during device discovery and initialization.

  15. Direct CCC - GETDCR Direct CCC, GETDCR instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to report its Device Characteristics Register (DCR), which describes the device’s functional classification. The Direct GETDCR CCC tells the target to:

    • Return its Device Characteristics Register value to the controller
    • Indicate the general device type or functional category
    • Allow the controller to identify the intended role of the device on the bus

    This command allows the controller to understand what kind of device a target is, enabling appropriate driver selection and configuration during device discovery and initialization.

  16. Direct CCC - GETSTATUS Direct CCC, GETSTATUS instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to report its Status Register, which provides current operational and interrupt-related status information. The Direct GETSTATUS CCC tells the target to:

    • Return its current status information to the controller
    • Indicate pending events such as interrupts or errors
    • Allow the controller to determine the target’s operational state

    This command allows the controller to query real-time device status, often as a follow-up to an In-Band Interrupt (IBI) or during diagnostic and monitoring operations.

  17. Direct CCC - GETACCCR Direct CCC, GETACCCR instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to report its Advanced Capabilities Control Register (ACCCR), which describes the target’s support for advanced I³C features and capabilities. The Direct GETACCCR CCC tells the target to:

    • Return its Advanced Capabilities Control Register value to the controller
    • Indicate support for optional and advanced I³C features
    • Allow the controller to determine how to enable or use advanced bus functionality with the target

    This command allows the controller to discover advanced target capabilities beyond the basic bus and device characteristics, helping optimize performance and feature usage.

  18. Direct CCC - ENDXFER Direct CCC, ENDXFER instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to terminate the current data transfer sequence and return to an idle or ready state. The Direct ENDXFER CCC tells the target to:

    • End the ongoing transfer or transaction sequence
    • Clear any internal state related to the current transfer
    • Prepare to accept new commands or transfers from the controller

    This command allows the controller to cleanly abort or conclude a transfer, ensuring both the controller and target return to a known, synchronized state on the I³C bus.

  19. Direct CCC - SETBRGTGT Direct CCC, SETBRGTGT instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to configure its bus-related timing or behavior as a bridge target, which is relevant when the device participates in bridging or multi-segment bus topologies. The Direct SETBRGTGT CCC tells the target to:

    • Set or update its bridge target configuration parameters
    • Adjust its behavior to properly forward or manage signals between bus segments
    • Acknowledge the configuration so the controller knows the bridge target is ready

    This command allows the controller to manage bus segmentation and bridge devices, enabling proper communication across complex I³C topologies while maintaining timing and protocol integrity.

  20. Direct CCC - GETMXDS Direct CCC, GETMXDS instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to report its Maximum Data Speed (MXDS), which indicates the highest data rate the device can reliably support on the I³C bus. The Direct GETMXDS CCC tells the target to:

    • Return its current Maximum Data Speed value to the controller
    • Inform the controller of the fastest speed at which it can communicate
    • Allow the controller to optimize bus timing and overall performance

    This command allows the controller to query a target’s speed capability, ensuring that data transfers are conducted within the device’s supported limits and preventing communication errors due to excessive speed.

  21. Direct CCC - GETCAPS Direct CCC, GETCAPS instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to report its capabilities, providing a summary of the device’s supported features and functional options. The Direct GETCAPS CCC tells the target to:

    • Return a value indicating which I³C features it supports
    • Include information such as support for In-Band Interrupts (IBIs), HDR modes, multi-master capability, and other optional features
    • Allow the controller to determine how best to communicate with and utilize the device

    This command allows the controller to discover the functional capabilities of a target device, enabling proper configuration, optimized bus usage, and compatibility checks before performing advanced operations.

  22. Direct CCC - SETROUTE Direct CCC, SETROUTE instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to configure its routing path, which is particularly relevant in complex or multi-segment I³C topologies where certain devices act as bridges or routing points. The Direct SETROUTE CCC tells the target to:

    • Set or update its internal routing configuration
    • Determine which bus segment or downstream devices it should forward traffic to
    • Acknowledge the new routing path so the controller knows the device is ready for communication

    This command allows the controller to manage traffic paths and device connectivity, ensuring proper communication in multi-segment or bridged I³C networks.

  23. Direct CCC - D2DXFER Direct CCC, D2DXFER instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to perform a direct-to-direct data transfer between two devices on the bus, without requiring the controller to relay all the data. The Direct D2DXFER CCC tells the target to:

    • Transfer a specified block of data directly from a source device to a destination device
    • Use the target device as a facilitator for the transfer if needed
    • Acknowledge completion of the transfer to the controller

    This command allows the controller to offload data movement between devices, reducing bus traffic and improving overall efficiency for large data transfers.

  24. Direct CCC - SETXTIME Direct CCC, SETXTIME instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to set a transfer timeout value, defining the maximum allowed duration for certain data transfer operations. The Direct SETXTIME CCC tells the target to:

    • Configure its internal transfer timeout according to the value provided by the controller
    • Limit how long a read or write transaction can remain active before the target considers it failed
    • Acknowledge the new timeout setting so future transfers comply with the configured limit

    This command allows the controller to enforce reliable and predictable timing on the I³C bus, helping prevent stalled transfers or bus lockup due to slow or unresponsive devices.

  25. Direct CCC - GETXTIME Direct CCC, GETXTIME instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to report its current transfer timeout value, which defines the maximum allowed duration for certain data transfer operations. The Direct GETXTIME CCC tells the target to:

    • Return its currently configured transfer timeout value to the controller
    • Allow the controller to determine how long the target will wait during a read or write transaction before timing out
    • Support bus scheduling and error management by providing accurate timing information

    This command allows the controller to query a target’s transfer timing constraints, helping ensure that data transfers are performed reliably and within the expected time limits.

  26. Direct CCC - RSTACT Direct CCC, RSTACT instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to reset its Activity State to the default or inactive state as defined by the I³C specification. The Direct RSTACT CCC tells the target to:

    • Transition from its current activity state to the default or idle state
    • Clear any temporary operational conditions related to activity state (e.g., performance level, internal counters)
    • Acknowledge the reset so the controller knows the device is back in a known state

    This command allows the controller to reinitialize or normalize a device’s activity state, which is useful for power management, performance tuning, or recovering devices that are in a higher activity state than required.

  27. Direct CCC - SETGRPA Direct CCC, SETGRPA instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to assign it to a particular group address (Group Address A), enabling group communication and selective broadcast operations. The Direct SETGRPA CCC tells the target to:

    • Store the specified group address in its internal configuration
    • Respond to future group-targeted broadcast commands sent to that group address
    • Acknowledge the assignment so the controller knows the device is successfully grouped

    This command allows the controller to organize devices into functional or logical groups, enabling efficient broadcast communication without addressing each device individually.

  28. Direct CCC - RSTGRPA Direct CCC, RSTGRPA instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to clear or reset its assigned Group Address A (GRPA), removing it from the group. The Direct RSTGRPA CCC tells the target to:

    • Delete or invalidate its stored Group Address A
    • Stop responding to broadcast commands sent to that group address
    • Acknowledge the reset so the controller knows the device is no longer part of the group

    This command allows the controller to dynamically manage group memberships, ensuring that devices only respond to group-targeted operations when appropriate.

  29. Direct CCC - MLANE Direct CCC, MLANE instructs a specific I³C target device on the bus to configure or report its Multi-Lane operation settings, which are used in systems that support multiple physical lanes for parallel data transfer. The Direct MLANE CCC tells the target to:

    • Enable or configure multi-lane operation parameters (such as lane assignment or activation)
    • Adjust internal settings to participate correctly in multi-lane transfers
    • Acknowledge the configuration so the controller knows the target is ready for multi-lane communication

    This command allows the controller to optimize data throughput by coordinating devices that support multiple parallel lanes, enabling higher-speed communication or load balancing across lanes.

  30. Direct CCC - Customized You can send a customized packet for a specific purpose.

  31. Legacy I2C RW

    1. Legacy I2C Read with SubAddr

    2. Legacy I2C Write with SubAddr

    You can send a legacy I2C packet for a specific purpose.

docs.title: Quick Send
docs.text:
1. Choose which bus to send the packet from.
  2. Choose the input data format for readability. The supported formats are:
    1. Hexadecimal
    2. Decimal
    3. Binary
    4. Binary (space separated): use a space to separate each binary value.
    5. ASCII In Binary format, values are grouped by the bit size, and any remaining bits are padded with zeros. For example, if the bit size is 4 and the data is 10101, the data sent is 0001 0101.
  3. Enter the data to send, in the selected input format.
  4. Send the packet.

docs.title: Packet Constructor
docs.text: Switch to the Bus tab and click the Add button at the bottom right to create a packet. After editing the packets, click Execute to send them.

docs.title: Edit Packet
docs.text:
1. Adjust the packet order.

  2. Open the detail editing dialog.

    1. Add a UART packet.

    2. Edit the packet in detail.

      1. Data Format: as described in Quick Send.
      2. Data: the data to send. The same notes as in Quick Send apply.
      3. Parity Error: you can deliberately send a parity error.

    3. Delete the packet.

    4. Adjust the order of packets.

    5. Change the display format. Two formats are supported:

      1. Packet Mode: displays the data along with the START and STOP bits.

      2. Data Mode: displays only the data.

docs.title: Px Pair Settings
docs.text: Click the button on the left side of this dialog (in the red box) to open the PX Pair Settings dialog.

docs.title: Mode Settings
docs.text: Set the mode to one of: 1. Enable: let the exerciser transmit data. 2. Disable

docs.title: Voltage Settings
docs.text: All units for these settings are in mV. 1. Vdd: set the working voltage. 2. LA Threshold: set the LA threshold for decoding. 3. Hysteresis Range: set the Hysteresis range.

docs.title: Quick Setup
docs.text:
Follow these steps:

  1. Set up the PX pod parameters.
  2. (Optional) Set up your DC output.
  3. Configure Decode and Timing Settings for UART signal analysis.
  4. Establish the connection.
  5. Send data using the UART wizard.

docs.title: 1-Wire
docs.text:
Developed by Dallas Semiconductor, the 1-Wire protocol defines signal types such as Reset Pulse, Presence Pulse, Write 1, Write 0, Read 1, and Read 0, and combines them into command sequences. Transmission is LSB (Least-significant bit) to MSB (Most-significant bit); speeds include Overdrive and Standard.

Timing Setting units are µs; wrong values mis-detect Reset / Presence / Write. See Settings for channel prefixes.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
1-Wire Decode Settings
  • Channel: Set the data channel source.
  • ChipSet: Select the chipset to decode. Default: Raw Data.
  • Bit Order: LSB first or MSB first. Default: LSB first.
  • Data Byte Column Amount: Bytes per Data row in the Report (8 / 16 / 32). Field enabled (Enable) only when ChipSet is Raw Data. Default: 8.
  • Timing Setting: All units are µs.
    • Slot Time:
      • Min: Minimum slot duration. Default: 60 µs.
      • Max: Maximum slot duration. Default: 120 µs.
    • Slot Interval:
      • Min: Minimum interval between slots. Default: 1 µs.
      • Max: Maximum interval between slots. Default: 5 µs.
    • Reset Time:
      • Min: Minimum Low time of the Reset pulse. Default: 480 µs.
      • Max: Maximum Low time of the Reset pulse. Default: 640 µs.
    • Presence Time:
      • Min: Minimum Low time of the Presence pulse. Default: 60 µs.
      • Max: Maximum Low time of the Presence pulse. Default: 240 µs.
    • Write One:
      • Min: Minimum Low time when writing 1. Default: 1 µs.
      • Max: Maximum Low time when writing 1. Default: 15 µs.
    • Write Zero:
      • Min: Minimum Low time when writing 0. Default: 60 µs.
      • Max: Maximum Low time when writing 0. Default: 120 µs.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
1-Wire decode result
  • Reset pulse: Reset pulse.
  • Presence pulse: Presence pulse, followed by data.

docs.title: 10BASE-T1S
docs.text:
10BASE-T1S names this Ethernet technology for 10 Mbit/s baseband signaling on a single pair. Unlike conventional Ethernet with four pairs, T1S targets single-pair environments.

Mismatching Sync/Beacon/MAC display options can omit or overfill report fields. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
10BASE-T1S Decode Settings
  • Show Sync Code: Show Commit and SSD. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Hide BEACON: Hide Beacon data. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • FCS in Byte order: Present FCS in the report in byte order. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Display 5B Code: Show special-code values. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Show MAC Data for each row: Show MAC Address, Data, FCS, and related fields. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared. (The Show MAC Data group can be opened separately; Default for the group is checked.)
    • Transport Layer Data: For IPv4 (0800h), the Data column shows transport-layer data only. Default show type index: 0.
    • Transport Layer Data & Header: Data column includes the header (about 20 bytes for IPv4).
  • Data filter: Show only a specified number of data bytes (minimum 20). Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared; filter value Default: 20.
  • Report format: Limit how many bytes appear in the Data column before wrapping. Default index: 0 (typically 8 bytes).
  • Export PCAP: Export PCAP. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.

docs.title: BiSS (Bidirectional Serial Synchronous)
docs.text:
BiSS, from iC-Haus, is an open point-to-point synchronous serial interface for absolute encoders. The master drives the clock on MA and the slave returns data on SLO. There is no chip select, so each frame is delimited by the gap after the clock stops. Both BiSS-C and BiSS-B are supported.

Besides the position data (Single Cycle Data), BiSS carries a slow bidirectional control channel for register access. It borrows one bit from every frame — CDM on the master side, CDS on the slave side — so one register transaction spans dozens of frames. Choose which side to inspect with Mode.

See Settings for channel prefixes.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
BiSS Decode Settings
  • MA / SLO: Assign the clock (MA) and data (SLO) channels.
  • Mode: Single Cycle Data (SCD) for position data, or Register Access - Master (CDM) / Register Access - Slave (CDS) for the control channel. Default: Single Cycle Data (SCD).
  • Data Channel: Number of data blocks in one frame. Default: 1.
  • Serial Data Length (bits): Total position data length, 1 ~ 64. With Auto checked the length is detected from the waveform and the field is read-only; clear it to enter the value by hand. Default: Auto.
  • Alignment (bits): Alignment bits appended after the position data. Default: 0.
  • Combine Multi-Turn and Single-Turn: Show the position as one value instead of two. Default: cleared.
  • Single-Turn(ST): Single-Turn bit count. Multi-Turn(MT) takes the remaining bits and is shown beside it. Default: 8.
  • CRC Bit amount / CRC Polynomial / CRC Initial Value: Sensor CRC parameters. The BiSS specification does not fix them, so set them from the encoder datasheet. Defaults: 6 / 0x43 / 0x0.
  • Protocol: BiSS-C or BiSS-B. BiSS-B has no CDS bit and its status-bit polarity is inverted. Default: BiSS-C.
  • SLO Phase (samples): Shift the SLO sampling point when the data is skewed against the clock. Default: 0.
  • Register Data Columns: Data bytes per row in the register report, 8 or 16. Default: 8.

docs.title: CAN 2.0B/FD (Controller Area Network, CAN with Flexible Data-Rate)
docs.text:
CAN (Controller Area Network) is a field bus from Bosch for automotive and industrial use. The physical layer uses differential CAN_H / CAN_L; the decode itself takes one digital channel, normally the logic Rx signal after the transceiver. Frame types include Data, Remote, Error, and Overload. CAN FD (Flexible Data-Rate) adds a faster data phase and longer payloads (up to 64 bytes) with CRC17 / CRC21.

A wrong Data Rate or the wrong signal polarity fails decode. With CAN FD checked, Auto detect Data Rate and Show scale are field disabled (Disable). For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
CAN Decode Settings
  • Invert: Invert the input signal. Check it when the signal has the reverse polarity. Default: cleared.
  • Auto detect Data Rate: Auto-calculate the data rate. Field enabled (Enable) when checked; manual rate field disabled (Disable). Default: checked. When cleared, choose a preset or enter 5 Kbps–1 Mbps; manual Default: 125 Kbps. Field disabled (Disable) when CAN FD is enabled.
  • Show scale in the waveform: Show bit scale on the waveform. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared. Field disabled (Disable) when CAN FD is enabled.
  • CAN FD: Enable CAN FD decode. When checked, ISO-CRC / Non ISO-CRC and Data phase are field enabled (Enable). Default: cleared.
    • ISO-CRC / Non ISO-CRC: CRC analysis rule. Default: ISO-CRC.
    • Data phase: Data-phase rate (Kbps). Default: 1000 Kbps.
    • Sample Point: Sampling position inside the data-phase bit, 70–80%. Field enabled (Enable) when CAN FD is checked. Default: 80%.
  • Data Filter: Show only Data within a length (8–60 bytes); longer Data is omitted. When checked, the length field is enabled (Enable). Default: cleared (show all); length often 8 bytes.
  • Report Data: Report data width (8-byte / 16-byte / 32-byte). Default: 8-byte.
Report Data width example (e.g. 16-byte)

docs.title: CXPI (Clock Extension Peripheral Interface)
docs.text: CXPI is an automotive single-wire network standardised as ISO 20794 (from JASO D015, via SAE J3076). It sits between LIN and CAN and is used for body and HMI networks — switches, sensors, actuators and instrument clusters. The master node embeds its clock in the data waveform through PWM encoding, which is where the name comes from, so slave nodes need no crystal; slaves may also transmit on their own initiative, which LIN cannot do. The bus runs at 2.4 to 20 kbit/s as a single-ended bus, with recessive HIGH and dominant LOW and non-destructive bit arbitration.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
Decode Settings
  • Configuration Channel: Select the logic analyzer channel the CXPI bus is connected to. CXPI uses a single wire, so only one channel is needed.
  • Color: Set the background color of the ID, DLC/NM/CT, Data and Error fields. Default: ID orange, DLC/NM/CT peach, Data light green, Error light blue.
  • Bit Rate: Select 20, 19.2, 10, 9.6, 4.8 or 2.4 kbps, Custom, or Auto. Auto automatically detects the signal bit rate. The detected rate is shown in the report Information column. If no plausible CXPI rate is found, decoding falls back to 20 kbps and reports Auto, not detected. Default: 20 kbps.
    • Custom (bps): Enter any bit rate in bit/s. Enabled only when Bit Rate is set to Custom. Default: 20000.
  • Encoding: Select the line coding. PWM starts every bit with a falling edge that carries the clock — logic 1 is a short dominant pulse (25 %) and logic 0 a long one (75 %). NRZ holds the level for the whole bit. Both are sampled at mid-bit. Default: PWM.
  • Polarity: CXPI idles recessive HIGH. Select Idle Low (Inverted) if the capture was taken through an inverting probe. Default: Idle High (Recessive).
  • Sample Point: Position of the sample moment inside a bit, 20 % to 80 %. 50 % suits both line codings. Default: 50 %.
  • Tolerance: Permitted deviation of the measured bit width from the selected bit rate, 5 % to 50 %. Raise it for a signal with a loose clock. Default: 20 %.
  • CRC-8: Generator polynomial used for the normal frame checksum. Select None to skip the check. Default: 0x2F, init 0xFF (AUTOSAR).
  • CRC-16: Initial value used for the long frame checksum (CCITT 0x1021). Select None to skip the check. Default: CCITT 0x1021, init 0x0000.
  • Detect PTYPE (0x80): Treat a leading 0x80 byte as the PTYPE byte of the polling method. The byte is excluded from the CRC and is reported in the Information column. Default: checked.
  • Check Counter (CT) sequence: Verify that the CT field advances by one (modulo 4) between two frames carrying the same frame ID, so a lost or duplicated frame becomes visible. A break is reported as a Counter error. Default: checked.
  • Data Column: Number of payload columns in the report, 8 (D0..D7) or 16 (D0..D15). A frame with more data bytes than this wraps onto continuation rows, so a long frame carrying up to 255 bytes stays readable. Default: 8 Columns.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The report shows one row per frame: ID, DLC, NM/CT, the payload spread over D0..Dn, CRC, Error and Information. The CRC cell is green when the checksum matches and red when it does not; the Error cell turns red whenever it is not empty. The Information column states the signal bit rate on the first row and afterwards carries frame notes that are not faults, such as PTYPE and Wake-up Pulse.

A frame carrying more data bytes than the selected Data Column count continues on the next row. Only the payload cells are repeated — the ID, DLC and NM/CT stay on the frame's first row, and the CRC and Error land on the row that closes it. The second frame below has DLC 12, the normal-frame maximum, so its payload wraps after D7.

docs.title: HDQ
docs.text:
HDQ was defined by Texas Instruments for battery-management display applications in consumer electronics. It supports 8-bit and 16-bit data widths with a fixed 7-bit address. A packet mainly consists of Break, 7-bit Address, 1-bit R/W, and 8-bit or 16-bit Data. Transmission is LSB to MSB; maximum rate is 5 Kbit/s.

For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

  • Show Battery Information: Show command exchange between the battery monitor IC and the battery. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Inverse Waveform (IDLE Low): Invert the waveform. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.

docs.title: HID over I2C (Human interface device Over I2C)
docs.text:
HID Over I2C (Human Interface Device Over I2C) is mainly used on Windows 8 ARM platforms; HID Over USB is used on x86 systems. On Windows 8, a common device that supports the HID Over I2C bus protocol is the touch panel.

Wrong Address Mode or Ignore Glitch settings can yield incorrect address/data decode. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
HID over I2C Decode Settings
  • Channel: Assign Logic Analyzer channels for SCL, SDA, and ATTN.
  • Custom Format: Customize part of the parse content. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Setting: Opens Notepad to edit the decode format: CMD, {Name of parse field 1, Number of bytes in parse field 1, Arrangement of parse field 1}, ……
  • Address Mode:
    • 7-bit addressing: Show a 7-bit address and 1-bit Rd/Wr. Default: this mode selected.
    • 8-bit addressing (Include R/W in Address): Show an 8-bit address (7-bit address plus 1-bit Rd/Wr).
    • 10-bit addressing: Show a 10-bit address.
  • Ignore Glitch: Ignore glitches caused by slow transitions. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: checked, < 2 sample points.

docs.title: HID over SPI
docs.text:
HID Over SPI (Human Interface Device Over SPI) is mainly used on Windows 8 ARM platforms. Compared with HID Over I2C, HID Over SPI uses more pins and offers higher bandwidth, higher clock rates, and lower latency.

Wrong channel assignment prevents correct decode. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings

docs.title: HTSensor (Humidity & Temperature sensor)
docs.text:
An HTSensor measures and monitors environmental conditions such as temperature and humidity, and provides the data to a system or device for processing or control. These sensors are widely used in smart homes, automation systems, climate control, medical devices, and similar applications.

Wrong Model or timing parameters versus the device under test cause decode failures. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
HTSensor Decode Settings
  • Data: Assign the Logic Analyzer channel for the sensor data signal.
  • Chip Setting: Select a supported chip model or define custom chip timing parameters.
    • Model: Chip model (AM2120 / AM2320 / CHTA30 / DHT11 / Custom). Default: AM2120. With Custom, timing and Calculate Type fields are enabled (Enable); other models disable (Disable) those fields and load that model’s parameters.
    • Display: Temperature display unit. Default: Celsius.
    • Tolerance: Allowed error percentage. Default: 0%.
    • Calculate Type: Humidity/temperature calculation method. Default follows the Model (AM2120: (High Low) / 10).

docs.title: HyperBus
docs.text:
HyperBus is a high-performance memory interface technology designed to increase data transfer rates, especially in embedded systems such as smartphones, tablets, and IoT devices. Proposed by Micron Technology and adopted by several device manufacturers, HyperBus can support many memory types—most commonly Flash and DRAM—while providing faster read/write speeds than traditional SPI and parallel memory interfaces.

Wrong Mode / Bus Width or HyperRAM options cause decode failures. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
HyperBus Decode Settings
  • Mode: Switch between HyperFlash and HyperRAM. Default: HyperFlash. HyperFlash enables (Enable) HyperFlash options and disables (Disable) HyperRAM options; HyperRAM does the opposite.
  • Bus Width: Set bus width (8 / 16). Default: 8. Width 8 disables (Disable) D8–D15 / RWDS2 channel spins; width 16 enables (Enable) them.
  • Channel: Assign Logic Analyzer channels for each signal on the device under test.
  • Display CA[47:0] in report: Show CA[47:0] (48 bits) in the report. Available only in HyperFlash mode. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • HyperRAM Options: Valid only in HyperRAM mode.
    • Invert CLK: Invert CLK. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
    • Phase Delay (CMD, Write Data): Delay sample-point count. Default: 0.
    • Latch Method and Phase Delay (Read Data): CLK or RWDS delay sample points. Default Latch Method: RWDS (also set for HyperFlash); Delay: 0.
    • Latency Count: Delay CLK count. Default: 0.
    • Data Arrangement: One of two arrangement modes. Default: the second mode.
    • Address Format: Address display format. Default: System Byte Addr.

docs.title: I2C(EEPROM) (Inter-Integrated Circuit for EEPROM 24X series)
docs.text:
EEPROM, or E2PROM (Electrically-Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory), typically uses a serial or parallel interface. I2C EEPROM is a 2-wire serial EEPROM in the 24x series.

Wrong address mode / Word Address width or Ignore Glitch settings cause decode failures. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
I2C EEPROM Decode Settings
  • Clock Channel (SCL): Transfer clock of the I2C EEPROM.
  • Data Channel (SDA): Transfer data of the I2C EEPROM.
  • Device Address:
    • Control Code: Display Control Code. Default: this mode selected; enables (Enable) the 24LCS61 / 24LCS62 checkbox.
    • 7-bit Addressing: Display a 7-bit-wide address. Forces 24LCS61 / 24LCS62 cleared and disabled (Disable).
    • 8-bit Addressing (Include R/W in Address): Display an 8-bit address (7-bit address plus 1-bit Rd/Wr). Forces 24LCS61 / 24LCS62 cleared and disabled (Disable).
  • Word Address: Valid bit count of the I2C EEPROM address. Default: 8. Disabled (Disable) when 24LCS61 / 24LCS62 is checked.
  • 24LCS61 / 24LCS62: Analyze 24LCS61 / 24LCS62. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Ignore Glitch: Ignore glitches caused by slow transitions. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: checked.

docs.title: I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit)
docs.text:
I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) is a two-wire serial bus with a multi-master/multi-slave architecture, introduced by Philips in the 1980s for connecting low-speed peripherals. It uses SCL (clock) and SDA (data). Frames include Start, Address, Data, and Read/Write; address modes are commonly 7-bit / 8-bit (R/W included) / 10-bit.

Wrong SCL/SDA wiring or address mode yields incorrect addresses in the report. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
I2C Decode Settings
  • Clock Channel (SCL): Assign the I2C clock (SCL) channel.
  • Data Channel (SDA): Assign the I2C data (SDA) channel.
  • Address Mode:
    • 7-bit Addressing: Show a 7-bit address and 1-bit Rd/Wr. Default: this mode selected.
    • 8-bit Addressing (Include R/W in Address): Show an 8-bit address (7-bit address plus 1-bit Rd/Wr).
    • 10-bit Addressing: Show a 10-bit address.
  • Report:
    • Show data in report: Data columns in the report (8 Column / 16 Column). Default: 8 Column.
    • Show NACK: Mark that byte as NACK. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
    • Unwrap the ASCII frame: Add an ASCII column in the report. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Clock Stretching: Detect clock stretching. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Ignore Glitch: Ignore short glitches. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: checked, < 2 sample points.

docs.title: I2S (Inter-Integrated Circuit Sound)
docs.text:
I2S (Inter-Integrated Circuit Sound) is a Philips digital-audio interface using SCK (clock), WS (word select), and SD (data) for left/right channels; data width up to 32 bits.

Wrong Mode / Data Bits misaligns decode. See Settings.

docs.text:

  • Mode: I2S Justified / MSB Justified / LSB Justified / PCM / TDM. Default: I2S Justified.
  • Report columns: Default: index 0.
  • Audio restore:
    • Draw waveform: Draw audio in the waveform area. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
    • Playback: Play after analysis. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
    • Save .WAV: Save as WAV. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
    • Align common sample rate: Align to 44.1 kHz / 48 kHz, etc. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
    • Enable meet full scale: Pad width to a multiple of 8. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • TDM: Channel size / Length / Word Length Default 16; Channel offset Default 0; Latch Default index 0.

docs.title: I80 (Intel 8080)
docs.text:
The Intel 8080-series interface is mainly used for LCM data transfer (I80 interface). Analyzing 8080-series requires 3 or 4 control lines (WR, RD, CS, and optionally D/C) and a data bus of at least 4 bits, so at least 7 channels are needed (WR, RD, CS, D0–D3); with D/C, 8 channels. An 8-bit data bus needs 11 signals (WR, RD, CS, D0–D7), and so on. Channel numbers can be adjusted.

Wrong Data Bus / Bit Order or On D/C settings cause decode failures. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
I80 Decode Settings
  • Select Channel: Assign Logic Analyzer channels for WR, RD, CS, and DATA pins.
  • On D/C: Use the D/C pin as Command (Low) or Data (High). When checked, the D/C channel and Cmd/Data colors are enabled (Enable); when cleared, those fields are disabled (Disable). Default: checked.
  • Data Bus: DATA pin width (4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 20 / 24 Bit). Default: 8 Bit. Wider buses enable (Enable) matching D* channels; unused channels are disabled (Disable).
  • Bit Order: LSB First or MSB First. Default: LSB First.
  • Report Data: Columns per report row (8 Column / 16 Column). Default: 8 Column.

docs.title: IDE (Integrated Device Electronics)
docs.text:
IDE (Integrated Device Electronics) is a standard interface for hard disks, solid-state drives, CD-ROMs, and similar storage. The name was first used by Western Digital in the U.S. for hard-disk sales. The official specification is ATA/ATAPI (Advanced Technology Attachment / AT Attachment Packet Interface). ATA continued to expand as capacity and transfer-speed needs grew. In 1998, ATA-4 added ATAPI so ATA could connect optical drives and other media. In 2003, SATA (Serial ATA) was published, and the original parallel ATA was retrospectively renamed PATA (Parallel ATA).

Because IDE is parallel, many channels are required. They are grouped into three types:

Normal channel (11 pin): DASP-, DIOR-:HDMARDY-:HSTROBE, DIOW-:STOP, DMACK-, DMARQ, INTRQ, IORDY:DDMARDY-:DSTROBE, PDIAG-:CBLID-, RESET-, CSEL, and IOCS16-.

Register channel (5 pin): CS(0:1)- and DA(2:0).

Data channel (16 pin): DD(15:0).

Recommended IDE bus wiring to the Logic Analyzer:

Recommended IDE wiring

Wrong Transferring Mode may affect command interpretation; analysis can still run if not specified correctly. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
IDE Decode Settings
  • Channel: Assign channel numbers on three pages (General, Register, and Data Bus).
  • Transferring Mode: Specify which specification the device under test uses so IDE analysis can interpret commands correctly. If not specified correctly, analysis can still run. Default: ULTRA DMA Mode 6. With UDMA Mode 6, the IOCS16 channel is disabled (Disable).
  • Analysis Report: Choose which registers appear in the report window. For example, if Data Register is cleared, data-register content is filtered out of the report. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: all checked (Command, Alternate, Status, Sector Count, LBA Low/Mid/High, Features, Error, Dev Ctrl, Device, Data).

docs.title: IOLink
docs.text:
IO-Link connects smart sensors and actuators to automation systems per the Single-drop digital communication interface for small sensors and actuators (SDCI) in IEC 61131-9. The specification covers electrical connections and digital protocols so smart sensors and actuators can interact with automation systems.

Wrong Transmission Timeout / Response Time or analysis mode affects Master/Device decode and report content. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
IO-Link Decode Settings

  • Timing Constraints:
    • Transmission Timeout: If IDLE is greater than this value, the next data is decoded as Master. Default: 30 TBIT.
    • Response Time: If IDLE is less than this value and greater than 3 TBIT, the next data is decoded as Device. Default: 10 TBIT.
  • Analysis Mode: Report analysis mode (Overview, Frame, ISDU, Event). Default: Overview.

docs.title: IrDA (Infrared Data Association)
docs.text:
The Infrared Data Association (IrDA) was formed in 1993 by about 50 companies including HP, IBM, Sharp, and Sony. IrDA defines point-to-point infrared wireless transfer.

docs.title: ITU-R BT.656 (CCIR656)
docs.text:
ITU-R BT.656 (CCIR656), from the ITU Radiocommunication Sector, is a digital video data format. It uses YUV color coding (luminance and two chrominance signals), which needs less bandwidth than RGB coding.

Data Bits or channel assignment must match the source; otherwise decode fails. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
ITU-R BT.656 Decode Settings
  • Channel: Assign the DUT signal pins to logic analyzer channels.
  • Data Bits: Data bus width (8/10). Default is 8. In 8-bit mode, D8/D9 are Field disabled (Disable); in 10-bit mode those channels are Field enabled (Enable).
  • Save Raw Data: Save the analysis result as a .bin file. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default is unchecked.

docs.title: JTAG (Joint Test Action Group)
docs.text:
JTAG (Joint Test Action Group) is an international test protocol (IEEE 1149.1) for on-chip testing; many advanced devices (DSP, FPGA, etc.) support it. Interfaces: TCK, TMS, TDI, TDO, and TRST (TDO is output). A TAP (Test Access Port) is defined inside the device and exercised with a JTAG tool.

With cJTAG enabled, TDI/TDO are field disabled (Disable); TCK/TMS act as TCKC/TMSC in OScan1. Instruction decode may decide whether TRST is required. See Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
JTAG Decode Settings
  • Channel: Assign TCK / TMS / TDI / TDO / TRST. TRST is optional; field enabled (Enable) when checkedchecked.
  • cJTAG: Disables TDI/TDO fields; TCK/TMS as TCKC/TMSC. Default: cleared.
Advanced settings
  • Show test data: In Shift-IR / Shift-DR, show TDI or TDO in hex. Default: show TDO.
    • Test data bit order: LSB First / MSB First. Default: index 0 (LSB First).
    • Interpreter Instruction: Enable the instruction list; show IR contents at Update-IR. Edit JtagInst.txt, then Refresh. Default: checked.
    • Acute Jtag Instruction table (JtagInst.txt): Provided by the Jtag DLL; editable; BSDL can be added. See appendix.
Report display
  • Show TDI or/and TDO: “Show TDI and TDO” shows both. Default: Show 1 data.
  • TAP state display: Default: all states checked.

docs.title: Result
docs.text: JTAG decode result

docs.title: Appendix: Acute JTAG Instruction table (JtagInst.txt)
docs.text:
Numbers are hexadecimal.

  • ##: comment
  • #ID: list ID 00–FF; must be sequential
  • #NAME: set name (max 32 bytes)
  • #LENGTH: instruction length in bits
  • #CAPTURE: Capture-IR value
  • #INST: code, name; empty #INST: ends the list
  • #TRST: 1 if TRST needed; 0 or omit if not
  • #BSDL: full BSDL path

Example: same as the traditional sample (#ID:00 … #BSDL:C:\3256at144_1532.bsd).

docs.title: LCD1602 (Liquid Crystal Display 1602)
docs.text:
LCD1602 is a common liquid-crystal display interface for 5×8 or 5×11 character glyphs. Variants share the same basic principle. The bus uses 11 lines: Instruction/Data Register Select (RS), Read/Write Select (RW), Enable (E), and 8-bit or 4-bit data lines (DB0–DB7 / DB0–DB3). There is no fixed frequency range.

Wrong Data Mode yields incorrect data-line decode; in 4 Lines mode, DB4–DB7 are field disabled (Disable). For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.text:

  • Data Mode: Choose data lines by transfer width.
    • 8 Lines: Use DB0–DB7. Default: this mode selected.
    • 4 Lines: Use DB0–DB3; DB4–DB7 are field disabled (Disable) when selected.
  • To merge the same command: Merge identical commands after analysis. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: checked.

docs.title: LED_CTRL (LED Driver TM1814)
docs.text:
LED Controls target digital LEDs with on-chip drivers so an MCU can drive a single LED or a section of LEDs.

Wrong Model, timing (T0 / T1 / Reset), or Bit Size yields decode failure; non-Custom models often field-disable (Disable) timing fields. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
LED_CTRL Decode Settings
  • Channel (Data): Assign the LED data signal channel.
  • Waveform Display: Show decode as numeric values or RGB color in the waveform.
    • value: Show numeric values. Default: this mode selected.
    • color: Show RGB color.
  • Chip Setting:
    • Model: IC model (Custom, TM1814, WS2811, WS2812, RT7905, HZ0028). Non-Custom often field-disables (Disable) T0 / T1 / Reset / Bit Size and applies that model’s preset. Default: Custom.
    • Timing (Idle high): Waveform idle is high. A low pulse between T0 Min and T0 Max decodes as 0; between T1 Min and T1 Max as 1. Custom Default: T0 Min 300 µs, T0 Max 400 µs, T1 Min 600 µs, T1 Max 1000 µs.
    • Reset: Holding high longer than the set time resets the start bit (Reset High / Reset Low). Custom Default: Reset High, 200 µs.
    • Bit Size: 24-Bit (RGB) / 32-Bit (WRGB) / 48-Bit. Default: 24-Bit.
    • RGB Order: RGB byte order. Default index: 0.
    • Display: Value / Percentage (tied to waveform display). Default: Value.

docs.title: Line Decoding
docs.text:
Digital information can be encoded as a digital signal. Choice of line code depends on requirements, medium, and equipment. The simplest mapping assigns voltage levels to binary 0 and 1; more complex codes improve performance.

Common codes:

NRZI (Non return to zero, inverted): Two modes:

NRZI (Transition occurs for a one): A 1 causes a level transition; a 0 does not. Example: "110100110" with initial 1 → "011000100".

NRZI (Transition occurs for a zero): A 0 causes a transition; a 1 does not. Example: "001011001" with initial 1 → "011000100".

Manchester: A mid-bit transition every bit period. Three modes:

Manchester (Thomas): High-to-low is 1; low-to-high is 0. Example: "0010110010" → "01 01 10 01 10 10 01 01 10 01".

Manchester (IEEE802.3): High-to-low is 0; low-to-high is 1. Example: "0010110010" → "10 10 01 10 01 01 10 10 01 10".

Differential Manchester: Always a mid-bit transition; a transition at the bit start means 0, otherwise 1. Example: "0011101011" → "10 10 01 10 01 01 10 10 01 10".

Biphase Mark: Each bit becomes two halves (1 → 01/10, 0 → 00/11) with a mandatory end-of-bit inversion. Example: "0010110010" → "11 00 10 10 10 11 01 00 10 10".

Miller: Used in RFID. A 1 transitions mid-bit; a 0 holds level, with a transition between consecutive 0s. Example: "0010110010" → "11 00 01 11 10 01 11 00 01 11".

Modified Miller: Idle stays high; a 0 pulses at the start, a 1 mid-bit; a 0 immediately after a 1 does nothing. Example: "1011001010":

Modified Miller encoding example

Wrong Format or Data Rate yields decode failure; with Auto-Detect Data Rate checked, the manual rate field is disabled (Disable). For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
Line Decoding Decode Settings
  • Channel: Assign the signal channel.
  • Format: Select the line code. Default: NRZI (Transition occurs for a one).
    • NRZI (Transition occurs for a one)
    • NRZI (Transition occurs for a zero)
    • Manchester (Thomas)
    • Manchester (IEEE802.3)
    • Differential Manchester
    • Biphase Mark Decode
    • Miller
    • Modified Miller
  • Show Unknown: Show unknown data. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Show Bus: Show bus data. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Auto-Detect Data Rate: Auto-detect the data rate; when checked, the manual Data Rate field is disabled (Disable). Default: checked. Manual placeholder text: 1 MHz.

docs.title: Line Encoding
docs.text:
Digital information can be encoded as a digital signal. Choice of line code depends on requirements, medium, and equipment. The simplest mapping assigns voltage levels to binary 0 and 1; more complex codes improve performance.

Common codes:

NRZI (Non return to zero, inverted): Two modes:

NRZI (Transition occurs for a one): A 1 causes a transition; a 0 does not. Example: "110100110" with initial 1 → "011000100".

NRZI (Transition occurs for a zero): A 0 causes a transition; a 1 does not. Example: "001011001" with initial 1 → "011000100".

Manchester: A mid-bit transition every bit period.

Manchester (Thomas): High-to-low is 1; low-to-high is 0. Example: "0010110010" → "01 01 10 01 10 10 01 01 10 01".

Manchester (IEEE802.3): High-to-low is 0; low-to-high is 1. Example: "0010110010" → "10 10 01 10 01 01 10 10 01 10".

Differential Manchester: Always a mid-bit transition; a start-of-bit transition means 0, otherwise 1. Example: "0011101011" → "10 10 01 10 01 01 10 10 01 10".

AMI (Alternate Mark Inversion): Three levels (positive / zero / negative).

AMI (Standard): 0 is level 0; 1 alternates +/-.

AMI (B8ZS): Special substitution for eight consecutive zeros (e.g. if 1 is +, 00000000 → 000+-0-+).

AMI (HDB3): Special handling for four consecutive zeros (by parity and prior 1 polarity).

MLT-3: 0 holds level; 1 steps through 0, +, 0, -.

Pseudoternary: 0 alternates +/-; 1 is level 0.

CMI: 0 is "01"; 1 alternates "00" / "11".

Biphase Mark: Example: "0010110010" → "11 00 10 10 10 11 01 00 10 10".

Miller: Used in RFID. Example: "0010110010" → "11 00 01 11 10 01 11 00 01 11".

Modified Miller: Idle high; example "1011001010":

Modified Miller encoding example

Wrong Format or Data Rate yields incorrect encode/display; with Auto-Detect Data Rate checked, the manual rate field is disabled (Disable). For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
Line Encoding Decode Settings
  • Channel: Assign the signal channel0.
  • Format: Select the line code. Default: NRZI (Transition occurs for a one).
    • NRZI (Transition occurs for a one)
    • NRZI (Transition occurs for a zero)
    • Manchester (Thomas)
    • Manchester (IEEE802.3)
    • Differential Manchester
    • AMI (Standard)
    • AMI (B8ZS)
    • AMI (HDB3)
    • Pseudoternary

docs.title: LPC (Low pin count)

The LPC (Low pin count) bus was developed by Intel to replace the ISA bus for legacy I/O data transfers.

docs.title: LPT (Parallel Port)
docs.text:
LPT (Line Printer Terminal Port) has been a common PC parallel interface since the 1980s, primarily for printers and other peripherals. This decode supports EPP Mode only.

When /nInit or /nIntr is cleared, that channel is field disabled (Disable). For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: LTPI (LVDS Tunneling Protocol & Interface)
docs.text:
LTPI (LVDS Tunneling Protocol & Interface) carries low-speed signals between the HPM and SCM. It supports GPIO, I2C/SMBus, UART, and related channels via TDM over LVDS. GPIO has low- and normal-latency types; I2C/SMBus handles single-controller links; UART supports flow control; OEM is for proprietary interfaces; a data channel supports memory-mapped transfers.

Wrong Interface mode or waveform direction/type yields incorrect decode content. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Math
docs.text:
Math performs arithmetic and logic operations on captured signals—single channels or multi-channel buses: +, −, ×, ÷, AND, XOR, OR, NAND, NOR, XNOR, and Bit Shift.

On OK, settings are written to AqMath.bin in the working directory (overwritten each OK). Save a copy with the waveform file, and place it in the working directory before reopening. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.text:

      • Arithmetic: +, −, ×, ÷.
      • Logic: AND, XOR, OR, NAND, NOR, XNOR, >>, <<.
    • “=” button: Add the equation to the Math List.
    • Invert Bit Order: New buses default to smaller channel number as lsb; check to reverse. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.

Operating methods

  • Select operands and operator, then “=” to add to the Math List

docs.title: MCTP over I3C (Management Component Transport Protocol over I3C)
docs.text:
MCTP (Management Component Transport Protocol) over I3C lets system management controllers (such as BMC, EC, NIC, GPU) communicate over the MIPI I3C bus. Versus MCTP over I2C, it offers higher speed, lower power, and more flexible device management.

MCTP is transport-independent and can run over PCIe, I2C, I3C, UART, Ethernet, and similar layers. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: MCTP over SMBus/I2C (Management Component Transport Protocol over SMBus/I2C)
docs.text:
MCTP (Management Component Transport Protocol) over SMBus/I²C is a DMTF management transport binding that lets management controllers (such as BMC, EC, NIC) communicate over SMBus or I²C for monitoring, remote management, power, and thermal control. It is commonly used in servers, embedded systems, and hardware monitoring.

SMBus and I²C share the same electrical bus and the same MCTP binding, so a single decode covers both. Select this decode whether the bus is described as SMBus or as I²C.

MCTP is transport-independent and can run over PCIe, I²C, SMBus, I3C, UART, Ethernet, and similar interfaces. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

This decoder is based on VESA Mobile Display Digital Interface Standard Version 1.2; only Type I communication is supported.

docs.title: MII / RMII / RGMII / GMII (Media Independent Interface)
docs.text:
MII: Media Independent Interface

RMII: Reduced Media Independent Interface

RGMII: Reduced Gigabit Media Independent Interface

GMII: Gigabit Media Independent Interface

Formulated by 802.3u and applied to Fast Ethernet, connecting the MAC of the Data Link Layer and the PHY layer. Clock frequency is either 25 MHz or 2.5 MHz (Ethernet); signals are TX_CLK and RX_CLK. TX[0:3] and RX[0:3] are 4-bit buses; TX_EN/RX_EN enable IN/OUT; TX_ER/RX_ER detect bus errors; RX_DV indicates valid received data; COL detects collision. Serial Management Interface (SMI), also known as MDIO, is also an important part of MII.

Wrong protocol/mode, Data Edge, or RGMII/RMII options yields incorrect decode. For channel-prefix differences, see Settings.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
MII Decode Settings
  • Protocol: MII/RMII/GMII/RGMII. Except BusFinder/LA, TravelLogic and MSO do not support GMII. Default: MII.
  • Mode: Transmit (TX) or Receive (RX). Default: Transmit (TX).
  • Channel: Assign each signal end on the DUT to a logic analyzer channel.
  • Data Edge: Rising/Falling latch on the clock edge. Default: Rising.
  • Report Column: 8 columns/16 columns. Default: 8 columns.
  • RGMII Speed: 1 Gbps or 100/10 Mbps; valid only when Protocol is RGMII. Default: 1 Gbps.
  • RMII Clock: Normal or Decrease Latch Frequency (x10); valid only when Protocol is RMII. Default: Normal.
  • Decode Ethernet Packet (MAC): Decode MAC packets. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Timing Specifics: Delay or advance of the data latch; available only when Protocol is GMII. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.
  • Export as PCAP: Export decode result as PCAP. Field enabled (Enable) when checked. Default: cleared.

docs.title: MIL-STD-1553
docs.text:
MIL-STD-1553 is a 1 Mb/s Manchester II encoded, transformer-coupled bus used in aircraft avionics, spacecraft and ground military vehicles. A Bus Controller issues Command Words; a Remote Terminal answers with a Status Word and whatever Data Words the command asked for. Command and Status words are indistinguishable on the wire — which is which is resolved by tracking the message.

Probing. The bus is differential and transformer-coupled, while the analyzer measures one wire against ground, so set the threshold to 20–30 % of the peak amplitude rather than 0 V — the standard tolerates a residual level between messages that a comparator sitting on zero will chatter through. Check which of the two wires the measured signal is on: a signal taken from the inverted wire cannot be decoded, and the report says so rather than inventing words.

docs.title: Decode Settings
docs.text:
MIL-STD-1553 Decode Settings
  • View: Which layer the waveform strip shows — Field (Sync, RT Address, T/R, SubAddress, Word Count …), Word (Command / Status / Data), or Transfer (one block per transfer). All three come from the same analysis; open a second instance of the decode on the same capture to see more than one layer at once. Default: Field.
  • Tolerance: How much bit-time deviation to accept. A receiver must tolerate ±150 ns of zero-crossing deviation out of a 500 ns half bit, which is 30 %. Default: 30%.
  • Version: MIL-STD-1553B or MIL-STD-1553A. The two revisions differ only in what the Status Word's bits are called. Everything used to recover the bits from the waveform — the sync patterns, the Manchester decoding, the 16 data bits and the parity bit — is the same in both, so this setting changes the names in the report and nothing else. Default: MIL-STD-1553B.
  • Response From / Response To: The window a Remote Terminal must answer in. The measured time is always shown; these bounds decide when it is flagged. Default: 4 us / 12 us.
  • Gap Minimum: The shortest intermessage gap accepted between transfers. Default: 4 us.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
Field view — a BC-to-RT transfer with its Status Word response

Errors are reported at two levels. Word level: Invalid Sync, Manchester Error and Parity Error. Transfer level: Bad Word Count, Address Mismatch, Non-contiguous Data, Response Time and Intermessage Gap. Each fault is flagged once, on the field it is about.

When most words fail to decode the report opens with a warning instead of listing words that were never really there — check the probe connection, the threshold, and which wire of the pair is being probed.
